💡 Key Takeaways
  • The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread.
  • It has been revealed that while scroll-state(), with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one.
  • In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The CSS scroll-state() query, surprisingly, has nothing to do with whether you’re doom-scrolling in a state of existential dread. It does, however, allow you to change the CSS used based on scrolling behavior. Far from doom, that’s pretty neat-o speedo. (Okay, you’re right, there’s nothing neat-o about a speedo). You can do lots of things that used to require JavaScript, like revealing the navigation when a user scrolls up or animating in a back to top link once the user scrolls down.

It has been revealed that while scroll-state(), with those slimming parentheses, looks like a function, it’s not technically one. It’s a container query (@container) like style(). Since scroll-state() is a query, the website is basically asking the browser whether a particular feature of a container has a specific value. If it does, the styles within the brackets will apply. If it doesn’t have that feature at all or has the feature, but the value is different, the @container query is false and the styles in the brackets will not apply.

In the following demo (which we’ll dissect in a bit), a “Back to Top” link slides in from the bottom as you scroll down the page.

scroll-state() has four possible features and each of those has a variety of possible values.

Asks if a container has been scrolled in a given direction:.

Asks if a container can be scrolled in a given direction:.

Asks if a sticky-positioned element is stuck:.

Asks if a snap target has been snapped on a particular axis:.

Industry observers note that first let’s look at the scrolled feature. This is the demo we saw at the beginning where we animate a back-to-top link when we scroll down:.

Sources indicate that when the scroll container is scrolled toward the block-end (downward in this case) the translate applies and the .toplink element animates up into the visible area. Because we’re using a transition, when we scroll a different direction (up and down/block-start and block-end are the only options here), it nicely animates out.

It has been revealed that while the scrolling direction in the demo above is pretty clear, what if this page was translated into a different language? Or we had a hero image that covered the entire viewport? One way we could indicate the scroll direction would be to have an arrow or other signifier animating and pointing in the correct direction. (I’m more a believer in constructing your page such that scroll direction is pretty obvious; however, I can foresee situations where an indicator was the best user experience or where translations/writing-mode changes could obscure what scrolling direction was appropriate.).

One nice thing about the scrollable feature is that when you scroll to the end of the scrollable area, it shuts off. So when we scroll to the block-end of the page (bottom of the page in this instance) scrollable: block-end is no longer true and our scroll indicator will revert to its default (in this case, display: none).

You could also combine the scrollable and scrolled features to remove the scroll indicator once the container has been scrolled either in the block-start or block-end direction. (We need both, because if we’re down in the middle of the page and we scroll up, scrolled: block-end will no longer be true and the scroll indicator will appear again.).

Industry observers note that another way we could enhance our demo is to have our navigation stick at the top while we’re scrolling down and change the look of the navigation once it’s stuck. The stuck feature must be on the element that gets stuck (as opposed to the scroll container, as was the case above). Also, because the container is set on the element that gets stuck, you cannot select the element itself from within the container query. You’ll need to position: sticky a wrapper element and “demote” all styles you want to change to the child.

Sources indicate that the work of setting up the stuck feature happens in that .header-wrapper, but since we can’t apply styles to the container from within the container (not even with :has()). We need most of the styling to be in the element.

According to recent reports, changing the size of an element in the header that affects the size of the header can lead to conflicting results. i.e. you scroll to a position where the header is stuck, which initiates the size change, but that reduces the size, which pulls it away from the stuck point, which cancels the size change which makes it stuck again, which initiates the size change and round and round we go. Even a small change can make it impossible to even scroll past the stuck point. Adding a transition can help with this and make scrolling work again, but you can still scroll to a place where the resizing happens in a loop. In the following demo, if you scroll down to a pixel or so past where the header touches the top of the viewport, you should see the stutter step.

According to recent reports, there is one weird trick to fix this, though. No, really, there is! (shakes fist at the internet for making “one weird trick” an unbelievable phrase.) The one weird trick is to set a height on the element that’s getting stuck (.header-wrapper in the case above). Ideally, set it smaller than the final size of the header if you’re making the header smaller. This prevents the element from resizing because of a change in its content’s size. This does require the header content to overflow. If that’s a no-go for you, you’ll have to change its size with transformations. The transformed element has a sort of placeholder that stays in the DOM where the transformed element originally lived. This placeholder is what’s used to determine the sticky position and does not change based on what happened in the animation.

In a recent development, we can also add some styles when scroll snapping has been applied and that scroll has snappity-snapped (technical term). Similar to the stuck feature, snapped should be defined on the element that is snapped, not on the scroll container. If scroll snapping has not been applied to the element, then the snapped feature returns false and the container query does not apply.

First, we set up our scroll snapping in the scrolled container.

Note: As with most scrolling CSS (scrolling animations, etc.), if you’re using the document’s default scroll, the element is what’s being scrolled, not the .

The slide s are what we’re going to snap to the size of the viewport:.

Recent findings suggest that as stated above, the container type and name go on the snapped item. And then we modify descendants of the slide once it snaps:.

Again, as with stuck, you cannot apply styles directly to the snapped element/the container, but only to the children of that element/container.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Proposal.
  • Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency.
  • Industry observers note that the most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which reveals the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Proposal. We took this opportunity to (re-)assert the fundamental role that open AI systems and open science play in enabling the technology to be more performant and efficient, broadly and reliably adopted, and meeting the highest standards of security. This blog post provides a summary of our response, the full text is available here.

Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency. Our team's recent OlympicCoder outperforming Claude 3.7 on complex coding tasks with 7B parameters and an open-source post-training recipe, or AI2's fully open OLMo 2 models (with open training data) matching o1-mini performances, are two of the most recent compelling examples. These successes show that a robust AI strategy must leverage open and collaborative development to best drive performance, adoption, and security of the technology. We make three major recommendations in this direction.

Industry observers note that the most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which reveals the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress. Investment in systems that can freely be re-used and adapted has also been shown to have a strong economic impact multiplying effect, driving a significant percentage of countries' GDP. As AI systems with open weights and training techniques become increasingly attractive options for developers in terms of both performance and cost, prioritizing public research infrastructure and broad access to compute, customizable models, and trusted open datasets — especially for smaller developers and researchers — will be essential to the further technical and economic success of AI technology.

Addressing the resource constraints of organizations adopting and adapting AI technology will be essential to supporting its diffusion and fostering innovation from adopters across the entire development chain. Smaller models (that may even be used on edge devices), techniques to reduce computational requirements at inference, and efforts to facilitate mid-scale training for organizations with modest to moderate computational resources all support the development of models that meet the specific needs of their use context, especially in high-risk settings such as healthcare where fully generalist models have proven unreliable. More efficient and purpose-designed AI systems facilitate better in-context evaluation, better resource utilization, and enable organizations to build technical capacity at all stages of the AI development chain to ensure that all users can leverage the system that best fits their needs.

Finally, if decades of information security and cybersecurity in open source software are any indication, open and transparent AI systems will have a fundamental role to play in securing AI development and deployment especially in the most critical settings — with different levels of openness needed for different security requirements. Fully transparent models providing access to their training data and procedures can support the most extensive safety certifications. Open infrastructure and open-source tooling implementing the latest training techniques can empower organizations to train the models they need in fully controlled environments. Open-weight models that can be run in air-gapped environments can be a critical component in managing information risks. Prioritizing adoption of the most transparent systems, supporting the development of the open resources outlined, and building capacity to leverage them especially in critical settings of AI adoption are essential to enabling more secure AI adoption.

Please refer to the full response for our more detailed recommendations!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web, a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites.
  • The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience.
  • I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web, a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites.

The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience. It explores how storytelling, color, typography, imagery, and layout can work together to create websites that people recognize and remember. We asked Andy a few questions about the book and the ideas that went into it.

I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them. Yet, somehow, so many websites look remarkably similar.

Sources indicate that I’m not suggesting every website needs a novelty design. Far from it. But I do think that — somewhere along the way—designers have become a little too comfortable with familiar patterns and predictable layouts.

I wrote Standout Designs for the Web to encourage designers to rediscover the creativity and personality that made me fall in love with the web in the first place.

Industry observers note that absolutely. Familiarity helps people understand how websites work, and there’s no reason to make something difficult to use just to be different. The problem is when familiarity makes every design look alike. When you visit a hotel website, an insurance company, or an online shop, you should be able to recognise something of the company behind it.

I call this sameness “commodity design,” and it’s perfectly fine when all you want is fine, but it does little to make a organization recognisable or its website memorable. I’m not arguing against using conventions. I’m asking designers to make more thoughtful decisions about when to use them.

When I talk about storytelling, I don’t mean writing a lengthy organization history or filling a website with marketing messages.

It has been revealed that every tech giant has a story worth telling. It might be how it started, the people behind it, its personality, or something unexpected about what it does. Those details can influence everything from the words you write to the colours, typography, illustrations, and layouts you choose.

I spend a lot of time talking to clients because I’m looking for what makes them different. Sometimes, something they mention almost in passing becomes the inspiration for an entire design. The trick is recognising which details are worth developing and turning them into something visual.

Sources indicate that ha! Because I wanted a vehicle for my explanations and to have some fun. Wheelman is a fictional company for getaway drivers, and it gave me the freedom to explore ideas without worrying too much about the practical constraints of a real client project. Its characters, criminal connections, and rather questionable business activities gave me plenty of opportunities to experiment with personality.

According to recent reports, but there’s a serious point behind the silliness. I use Wheelman to demonstrate how a firm’s character can influence ordinary business pages, e-commerce, editorial content, and even transactional forms. If I can make a donation form for retired criminals interesting, designers have no reason not to bring more personality to everyday websites.

I think twelve-column grids have become the default setting for web design. They’re familiar and useful, but they’re only one way to organise content. When designers begin every project with twelve columns, they’re already limiting their possibilities before they’ve considered what the content needs.

In the book, I explore column, compound, and modular grids; ratios; symmetry versus asymmetry; and other ways to create rhythm and movement across a page. I’m not suggesting designers abandon column grids, but I want them to understand layout well enough to choose the right type and combine several—to make their layouts more interesting.

Recent findings suggest that I’d like them to approach their next project with a little more curiosity. Before opening Figma or Sketch, choosing a typeface, or deciding on a layout, I’d like them to spend more time discovering what makes the company they’re designing for interesting.

According to recent reports, then I’d encourage them to question their first design decisions. Does this layout suit the content, or is it just familiar? Does this typography express the manufacturer’s personality? Can an illustration communicate something more effectively than an AI-generated image or a stock photo?

It has been revealed that I don’t expect every website to be extraordinary, and I certainly don’t think every design needs to break conventions. But I’d like designers to feel more confident making decisions that give their work character.

Sources indicate that the first sign of trouble is rarely a crash. It is the invoice.

Sources indicate that A small team ships a Node.js app on a serverless platform because it is quick to set up. Traffic grows, and the bill grows with it, in ways that are hard to forecast. Some visitors also wait a beat longer for their first response, because the function has to start up before it can answer.

According to recent reports, the usual alternative is a virtual private server (VPS). The price is fixed, but the work is not. Someone has to patch the operating system (OS), configure the web server, renew SSL certificates and keep backups running.

Between the two sits a third option: managed hosting for Node.js. Here is how the three compare, and how to choose.

Industry observers note that platforms such as AWS Lambda charge for what runs. Lambda's event functions are priced on the number of requests and on duration, measured in GB-seconds, and the memory you choose sets the CPU and the cost per second.

In a recent development, that suits small or spiky workloads. A fresh app with little traffic can sit inside the free tier, which covers one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds a month.

The surprises come with growth. Billed duration is multiplied by the number of requests, so even small inefficiencies in a handler can turn into significant costs at scale.

Then there is the cold start. When the platform has to create a new execution environment, the first request waits. AWS's own decision guide puts Lambda cold starts at roughly 100 milliseconds to over 1 second.

Since August 2025, AWS bills for that initialization (INIT) phase across all function configurations, so a cold start now demonstrates up on the invoice as well as in the response time.

AWS's own analysis found they occur in under 1% of invocations, so steady traffic makes them far less. For a checkout page that does hit one, it is still a pause the customer feels.

Industry observers note that there are fixes. Provisioned concurrency keeps functions initialized and ready, but it is billed for the time it is enabled. Newer options let one execution environment handle several requests at once, which means fewer cold starts.

Sources indicate that limits matter, too. A Lambda function can run for 15 minutes at most, and accounts start with a default of 1,000 concurrent executions. Long-running jobs need a different home.

A VPS fixes the pricing problem. A initiative costs the same every month, whatever traffic does.

Industry observers note that on an unmanaged VPS, the team owns everything above the hardware. That means operating system updates, a firewall, a web server such as NGINX in front of the app, a process manager such as PM2 to restart it if it crashes, SSL certificate renewals and backups that someone has to test.

Sources indicate that none of it is exotic. All of it is a job. Left undone, it is how small teams end up with unpatched servers and no way to restore one.

For a team without a sysadmin, the real price of a VPS is the hours.

Recent findings suggest that managed Node.js hosting sits between the two. The app runs on a persistent infrastructure, so there is no scale-to-zero and no cold start between requests. The price is a flat monthly proposal. The provider handles the work around it.

Cloudways Velocity is one example. It patches the OS, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically.

The stack is NGINX and PM2, pre-configured with caching, and PostgreSQL is provisioned on all looks. Deployment is by Git push with built-in CI/CD, and a WAF, malware protection, DDoS mitigation and Cloudflare Enterprise CDN are included.

Recent findings suggest that it ships presets for 12 project types, including Next.js, Remix, Express, Fastify, Astro, Nuxt, Angular and n8n. Anything that builds to SSR or a static bundle and starts with a Node command can run under "Other". Runtime versions are selectable, with Node.js LTS 22.x and 24.x listed.

It has been revealed that the trade-off is scaling. Velocity scales vertically: you pick a server size and move up when the app outgrows it. A traffic spike beyond that server's capacity is a capacity problem, not something the platform absorbs by adding instances.

Look at the traffic first. If it comes in bursts with long quiet gaps, serverless often wins. If it is steady, a server is usually simpler to reason about.

Take one handler and keep the assumptions the same throughout. Each request runs for half a second on 1 GB of memory. The rates are AWS's published x86 prices: $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second, after the free tier, as shown earlier.

Recent findings suggest that now compare Velocity's looks, which use a pay-as-you-go model billed on an hourly basis according to the selected strategy, ranging from Starter at $20 a month (2 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 5 apps) to Business at $400 (64 GB RAM, 16 vCPU, 150 apps). More importantly billing is strictly tied to the server plan rather than incoming traffic, a sudden spike in visits will not automatically raise your hourly compute rate.

Sources indicate that the Lambda figures leave out API gateway charges, data transfer and logging. A single server has a ceiling, so load-test before assuming one plan carries 100 million requests.

And Velocity has metered extras: $0.033/GB for offsite backup storage, $0.02/GB for CDN bandwidth beyond the initiative's allocation, and $1 per 10 GB of extra disk.

If you want to test managed hosting, you can try Cloudways Velocity during Black Friday with the promo code BFCM802 for 80% off for 2 months plus unlimited migrations, valid through December 4, 2026.

Sources indicate that the point is the shape, not a winner. Serverless cost tracks usage. A server's cost tracks its size. Choose the one you can forecast.

The strongest case is also the most common one: steady traffic, a small team and a budget that has to be forecast.

When cloud hosting costs have to fit a budget, a flat monthly plan beats a meter. Velocity's intends give you Node.js hosting with predictable pricing, so finance can see the number in advance and it does not move with every spike.

Because the server stays on, there is no cold start between requests, and the first visitor after a quiet spell is not left waiting.

Cloudways says Velocity patches the operating system, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically. The people who built the product keep building it.

It has been revealed that APIs, full-stack apps and automation workflows such as n8n need a process that stays up. A persistent server is built for exactly that.

When the app outgrows its server, you move up a size, and you can move back down if you don't need it.

For most small teams, that adds up to a simple choice. Velocity trades the theoretical ceiling of serverless for something many teams value more: costs they can forecast and an app that stays ready, without a DevOps hire.

Teams whose traffic is extreme, or who need code running at the edge, may still prefer a specialist platform, but that is the exception.

According to recent reports, serverless is strongest when work is irregular. A VPS is strongest when you want control and have the time. Managed Node.js hosting suits the large group in between: teams with steady traffic, a small headcount and no appetite for server upkeep.

Teams looking for managed hosting can explore Cloudways Velocity to deploy and scale Node.js applications efficiently.

  • That’s why it’s vital to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our users.
  • In a recent development, the issue of robustness is so vital that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd. It illustrates just how fragile the technical infrastructure of a website or app can be.

That’s why it’s vital to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our users.

In a recent development, the issue of robustness is so vital that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)! So how can we provide a modern front end without excluding people who use browsers and hardware that are only partially compatible or not compatible at all?

The answer lies in implementing multiple safety nets in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so that we are prepared for the worst-case scenario and can provide our consumers with the best possible experience.

The main difference between the use of fallbacks and progressive enhancement lies in the directions in which the two approaches aim.

While progressive enhancement is about automatically making certain features available as long as they are supported (forward), fallbacks are about what happens when something is not available or accessible (backward).

For example, we can offer a shiny new CSS feature that makes interacting with our website even more enjoyable. But if this feature isn’t available in some browsers, no one will notice, because a version that’s supported by older browsers is available instead. Progressive enhancement in action!

Another example: If JavaScript cannot be loaded for a critical application, we provide a fallback that either offers basic functionality or, at the very least, displays a message explaining what the problem is.

While one doesn’t necessarily exclude the other, their approaches are quite different. My personal recommendation is to always work with progressive enhancement as a guiding principle and to consider fallbacks whenever possible.

To evaluate newly introduced features intended for production, we must first determine the extent to which a feature is supported.

Since 2023, the Interop project has been in place, in which major browser vendors collaborate to release newly introduced features for the web platform more or less simultaneously. This serves as a general overview.

Related to this is the Baseline project, which shows, for specific features, the extent to which they are supported and how long they have been available. However, it is extremely vital to note that it does not track browser support for accessibility features built into the web platform!

Another important resource for checking compatibility is Can I Use. Here, you can get a quick overview of browser support for various features.

Let’s start with the foundation of the World Wide Web: HTML. Modern tech stacks place a strong emphasis on client-side rendered JavaScript, which can offer many benefits to users in more complex applications. However, there can be just as many reasons why JavaScript might fail to load, so we need a strategy to address this.

Industry observers note that in the event of a total failure, we should redirect owners to an appropriate error page where they receive information about what went wrong and what not only they, but also we, can do to prevent this in the future. If you want to know how to write error messages that actually help users rather than frustrate them, check out Amy Hupe’s amazing article.

Because this kind of error feedback is so essential, the static site generator Astro, for example, offers the ability to add custom 404 and 500 error pages. You could discuss other possible error codes with your back-end team to implement additional safeguards.

Sources indicate that but what if we also want to make individual sections or components more robust in case JavaScript isn’t available? For this, we can use the  tag, which, according to Can I Use, has excellent browser support. Here’s a highly simplified example of a fictional dashboard component:.

If JavaScript is not available, we will still display the components, but explain in simple and clear terms that they cannot be loaded at the moment and why that is the case.

Sources indicate that we give customers the option to reload that specific component so they can resolve the concern themselves. We also offer them the option to contact us directly via email if the problem persists.

Here, you could add a pre-written text to the  tag, which could include, for example, an internal error code specific to that component in the subject line and have a corresponding body text. This way, they would only need to click the button and could send the email directly using their email program of choice. Support would then have all the necessary information to resolve the issue without needing to ask for additional details.

No matter what your use case is, this pattern can be universally adapted and extended, and ensures that it works even if everything else goes wrong.

Let’s stick with our fictional dashboard component. Say we want to use the CSS anchor() function to display the data, which is fairly fresh and has solid, but not great, browser support.

Recent findings suggest that since this is a feature that can include multiple attributes, we need to check whether the ones we want to use are actually available. This is exactly where the @supports CSS rule comes into play! Here, it’s recommended to use the and operator: It should only be used if all attributes are available. If not, the more robust CSS with better browser support is used.

Here’s another fictional, simplified example:.

This approach also serves as documentation: Once the feature has been around for a while and is more well-established, you can look directly for the @supports rule in your code base and check whether it is still necessary, along with its fallback.

It has been revealed that javascript offers us the ability to make our front end even more resilient with minimal effort. To do this, we can use the if…else statement to check whether a specific feature is available. For example, if we want to use the relatively newly introduced Navigation API, we could check for it as follows:.

If we use a component-based approach, where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are all contained in a single file, we can also use the conditional ternary operator to display this component or parts of it, or do nothing at all.

According to recent reports, our fictional dashboard component relies on data from the back end, and it only makes sense to display it once the data has successfully reached the front end. So, for example, we could do the following:.

According to recent reports, depending on the use case, it makes sense to display a fallback or even nothing at all. You could also define the conditions more specifically, depending on how robust you want it to be.

My experience so far at various companies has been that the topics of fallbacks and robustness haven’t played as prominent a role as they really should have.

This is surprising, because as we’ve learned, it doesn’t take much to implement various safety nets on the front end, as long as you think ahead about what (shouldn’t) happen if something goes wrong.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide us with specific elements and functions to ship robust code and thus avoid upsetting our owners and, in the worst case, causing them to turn away from us.

Access entire row data in select events for more intuitive interactivity and data manipulation.

Customise the interactivity of your dataframe by specifying non-editable columns using the static_columns parameter.

Quickly find the data you need with our powerful search feature by setting the show_search parameter to "search".

Breaking: Style Queries as Conditional Modifiers

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in Kevin’s course, CSS Demystified.
  • Modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors.
  • For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in Kevin’s course, CSS Demystified. The module covers configuration options with custom properties, math functions, relative colors, :has(), style queries, and more, all put to work in practical, reusable patterns. The course is 32% off until December 2, 2026.

Modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors. Some common examples are things like different versions of alerts and buttons.

For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things.

A card is a nice example of this, where we might have several versions.

The glitch here is, if I’m using .card--compact, I probably want to do that for all the cards within a section. That can be annoying to apply to each card, but that’s rendered moot since most people are doing some sort of looping in a template like this these days.

And this works great, as long as we always want the cards to be compact.

Industry observers note that however, you might put this together and send it off to the design team for approval, only for them not to like that when the compact cards are lower down the page, the smaller padding isn’t needed to create visual separation between the two sections. Instead of helping with the hierarchy, it’s simply creating a strange visual inconsistency.

We could use something like a resize observer to try and deal with this, but we have a better tool at our disposal: Container Style Queries, which are now Baseline Newly Available.

While they all start with container, for the rest of this article I interchangeable use container query or size query for a container size query, and style query for what we’re talking about here.

Before we get into the good stuff, a quick look at the basics of style queries.

You’re probably familiar with size queries, which work similar to @media but look at the size of a container, rather than the viewport. Container style queries use the same @container at-rule as container size queries, but instead of looking at a size, they look at the value of a custom property.

This reads as, “if the nearest container has --theme: high-contrast, style the .card like this.”.

A couple of important notes about them:.

Just like with size queries, style queries look at an ancestor, not the element itself. That means this won’t work:.

In a recent development, the custom property needs to be set on something above the card. Sometimes this can be annoying, and it always tends to catch people out, but because of how I use them, I don’t find this to be much of a limitation.

Sources indicate that if() is also on the way, and allows for style queries as well, but if() is able to see the value of custom properties on the element it’s being used. The big difference is it can only be used for a single property, while style queries can be used for rules with multiple properties.

Let’s take a look at a card again, first with a modifier like we might do now. To change it up, we’ll use an attribute modifier instead of a class.

Switching this up to use a style query, we could do something like this instead:.

Industry observers note that if we’re in the mindset of how we’re used to using modifiers, this feels like a lot more work with no real payoff, but now, anything that can set a custom property can switch it: a media query, a container query, a :has() selector, or a parent section. The styles for the alternative layout are written once, and there are lots of ways to switch them on, making it so much more versatile.

One easy win here is if you’re working with a CMS. Now, the author of the page can chose from an option, which just sets one custom property value for a section of the page, and the appropriate styles kick in.

Where I feel like this has the most potential is when dealing with conditional styles like the sidebar we looked at earlier, where we can enable the compact card layout however we want:.

Here’s an overflow grid pattern I use quite a bit:.

Sources indicate that the problem is that it always overflows, even if I don’t have enough children to warrant it. Like here, the first row, the third card is just barely overflowing, making it awkward more than anything.

One solution is to use a container query and :has(), where we let the items fill the space when there are fewer than five of them, and there’s enough space:.

And this works really well! But sometimes, we might need to make some bigger changes depending on where the elements are being used.

Let’s say, for example, our page has a hero component that goes to two columns on larger screens, with a heading on one side and a set of featured articles in an overflow grid on the other. The container query is making sure the overflow is on in the narrow space, but horizontal scrolling there seems a little awkward.

When the split happens, I’d rather the grid scrolled vertically instead, and we can leverage style queries to pull this off.

First, we give the overflow grid a configuration option for its direction, defaulting to columns:.

Now the split can change when it goes to two columns:.

And this works, but the result isn’t great. The grid is still sized for horizontal scrolling, so we end up with a tall, awkward column, and no overflow at all.

It has been revealed that this is where style queries come in. The overflow grid can “listen” for the direction change and adjust its own styles to match.

Recent findings suggest that the split section isn’t styling the overflow grid directly, which is possible, but always awkard, and leads to fragile code bases. Instead, we created some configurable settings on that grid, and simply adjusted them as needed.

In a recent development, I don’t think style queries mean it’s time to throw out modifier classes (or data modifiers). They still work great, especially since a style query can’t look at the element it’s styling. If I simply want my button to be an accent button, or a pill shape, then a modifier makes a lot of sense.

On top of that, a regular media query or container query, or even an intrinsic pattern might get the job done, and that’s great too.

Industry observers note that where style queries shine is when the condition and the styles need to live in different places, or when one condition needs to affect several things at once, like the split above. Instead of a layout reaching in and styling its children, it changes a few settings, and each component decides how to respond.

That’s a substantial part of what I think of as writing resilient CSS: components that keep working, and adapt sensibly, no matter where they end up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a reranker model (also known as a cross-encoder) that beats all existing options on exactly your data. This method can also train extremely strong new reranker models from scratch.

Finetuning reranker models involves several components: datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class itself. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong reranker models.

Sources indicate that lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my small finetuned tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce reranker model that I trained alongside this blogpost easily outperforms the 13 most commonly used public reranker models on my evaluation dataset. It even beats models that are 4x bigger.

Repeating the recipe with a bigger base model results in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce, a reranker model that blows all existing general-purpose reranker models out of the water on my data.

If you're interested in finetuning embedding models instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost as well.

Sources indicate that reranker models, often implemented using Cross Encoder architectures, are designed to evaluate the relevance between pairs of texts (e.g., a query and a document, or two sentences). Unlike Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. bi-encoders, embedding models), which independently embed each text into vectors and compute similarity via a distance metric, Cross Encoder process the paired texts together through a shared neural network, resulting in one output score. By letting the two texts attend to each other, Cross Encoder models can outperform embedding models.

However, this strength comes with a trade-off: Cross Encoder models are slower as they process every possible pair of texts (e.g., 10 queries with 500 candidate documents requires 5,000 computations instead of 510 for embedding models). This makes them less efficient for large-scale initial retrieval but ideal for reranking: refining the top-k results first identified by faster Sentence Transformer models. The strongest search systems commonly use this 2-stage "retrieve and rerank" approach.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "reranker model" and "Cross Encoder model" interchangeably.

Reranker models are often tasked with a challenging problem:.

Which of these kkk highly-related documents answers the query the best?

According to recent reports, general-purpose reranker models are trained to perform adequately on this exact question in a wide range of domains and topics, preventing them from reaching their maximum potential in your specific domain. Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

In the Evaluation section end of this blogpost, I'll show that training a model on your domain can outperform any general-purpose reranker model, even if those baselines are much bigger. Don't underestimate the power of finetuning on your domain!

Training reranker models involves the following components:.

Let's take a closer look at each component.

The CrossEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use your local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

According to recent reports, note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

According to recent reports, some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

You can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

In a recent development, it is vital that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format and model). Verifying whether a dataset format and model work with a loss function involves three steps:.

For example, given a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"] where the "label" column has float similarity score ranging from 0 to 1 and a model outputting 1 label, we can use it with BinaryCrossEntropyLoss because:.

Be sure to re-order your dataset columns with Dataset.select_columns if your columns are not ordered correctly. For example, if your dataset has ["good_answer", "bad_answer", "question"] as columns, then this dataset can technically be used with a loss that requires (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, but the good_answer column will be taken as the anchor, bad_answer as the positive, and question as the negative.

In a recent development, additionally, if your dataset has extraneous columns (e.g. sample_id, metadata, source, type), you should remove these with Dataset.remove_columns as they will be used as inputs otherwise. You can also use Dataset.select_columns to keep only the desired columns.

According to recent reports, the success of training reranker models often depends on the quality of the negatives, i.e. the passages for which the query-negative score should be low. Negatives can be divided into two types:.

Industry observers note that the strongest CrossEncoder models are generally trained to recognize hard negatives, and so it's valuable to be able to "mine" hard negatives to train with. Sentence Transformers supports a strong mine_hard_negatives function that can assist, given a dataset of query-answer pairs:.

Loss functions help evaluate a model's performance on a set of data and direct the training process. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of available loss functions in the Loss Overview.

Most loss functions are easy to set up - you just need to provide the CrossEncoder model you're training:.

Industry observers note that you can customize the training process using the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

For more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Cross Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

Here's an example of how to set up CrossEncoderTrainingArguments:.

To track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the CrossEncoderTrainer. However, you might want more detailed metrics beyond just the evaluation loss. That's where evaluators can help you assess your model's performance using specific metrics at various stages of training. You can use an evaluation dataset, an evaluator, both, or neither, depending on your needs. The evaluation strategy and frequency are controlled by the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators:.

You can also use SequentialEvaluator to join multiple evaluators into one, which can then be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainer. You can also just pass a list of evaluators to the trainer.

Sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

The STS Benchmark (a.k.a. STSb) is a commonly used benchmarking dataset to measure the model's understanding of semantic textual similarity of short texts like "A man is feeding a mouse to a snake.".

Feel free to browse the sentence-transformers/stsb dataset on Hugging Face.

Preparing data for CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator can be difficult as you need negatives in addition to your query-positive data.

It has been revealed that the mine_hard_negatives function has a convenient include_positives parameter, which can be set to True to also mine for the positive texts. When supplied as documents (which have to be 1. ranked and 2. contain positives) to CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator, the evaluator will not just evaluate the reranking performance of the CrossEncoder, but also the original rankings by the embedding model used for mining.

Note that by default, if you are using CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator with documents, the evaluator will rerank with all positives, even if they are not in the documents. This is useful for getting a stronger signal out of your evaluator, but does give a slightly unrealistic performance. After all, the maximum performance is now 100, whereas normally its bounded by whether the first-stage retriever actually retrieved the positives.

It has been revealed that you can enable the realistic behaviour by setting always_rerank_positives=False when initializing CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator. Repeating the same script with this realistic two-stage performance results in::.

Industry observers note that the CrossEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

According to recent reports, in this example I'm finetuning from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, a base model that is not yet a Cross Encoder model. This generally requires more training data than finetuning an existing reranker model like Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-reranker-base. I'm using 99k query-answer pairs from the GooAQ dataset, after which I mine hard negatives using the sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 embedding model. This results in 578k labeled pairs: 99k positive pairs (i.e. label=1) and 479k negative pairs (i.e. label=0).

I use the BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, which is well suited for these labeled pairs. I also set up 2 forms of evaluation: CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator which evaluates against the NanoBEIR benchmark and CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator which evaluates the performance of reranking the top 30 results from the aforementioned static embedding model. Afterwards, I define a fairly standard set of hyperparameters, including learning rates, warmup ratios, bf16, loading the best model at the end, and some debugging parameters. Lastly, I run the trainer, perform post-training evaluation, and save the model both locally and on the Hugging Face Hub.

After running this script, the tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce model was uploaded for me. See the upcoming Evaluation section with evidence that this model outperformed 13 commonly used open-source alternatives, including much bigger models. I also ran the model with answerdotai/ModernBERT-large as the base model, resulting in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce.

Industry observers note that evaluation results are automatically stored in the generated model card upon saving a model, alongside the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential consumers would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The CrossEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the CrossEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:.

Industry observers note that each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:.

Cross Encoder models have their own unique quirks, so here’s some tips to help you out:.

CrossEncoder models overfit rather swiftly, so it’s recommended to use an evaluator like CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator or CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator together with the load_best_model_at_end and metric_for_best_model training arguments to load the model with the best evaluation performance after training.

CrossEncoders are particularly receptive to strong hard negatives (mine_hard_negatives). They teach the model to be very strict, useful e.g. when distinguishing between passages that answer a question or passages that relate to a question.

Don’t underestimate BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, it remains a very strong option despite being simpler than learning-to-rank (LambdaLoss, ListNetLoss) or in-batch negatives (CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MultipleNegativesRankingLoss) losses, and its data is easy to prepare, especially using mine_hard_negatives.

Industry observers note that I ran a reranking evaluation of my model from the Trainer section against several baselines on the GooAQ development set with both always_rerank_positives=False and with always_rerank_positives=True in the reranking evaluator. These represent the realistic (only rerank what the retriever found) and evaluation (rerank all positives, even if the retriever didn't find it) formats, respectively.

As a reminder, I used the extremely efficient sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 static embedding model to retrieve the top 30 for reranking.

Recent findings suggest that which uses the rerank subset from my tomaarsen/gooaq-reranker-blogpost-datasets dataset. This dataset contains:.

Recent findings suggest that with just 99k out of 3 million training pairs from the gooaq dataset and just 30 minutes of training on my RTX 3090, my small 150M tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce was able to handily outperform every single <1B parameter general-purpose reranker. The larger tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce took less than an hour to train, and is in a league of its own with a massive 79.42 NDCG@10 in the realistic setting. The GooAQ training and evaluation dataset aligns very well with what these baselines were trained for, so the difference should be even larger when training for a more niche domain.

It has been revealed that note that this does not mean that tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce is the strongest model here on all domains: It's simply the strongest in our domain. This is totally fine, as we just need this reranker to work well on our data.

Sources indicate that don't underestimate the power of finetuning reranker models on your domain. You can improve both the search performance and the latency of your search stack by finetuning a (small) reranker!

Recent findings suggest that these pages have training examples with explanations as well as links to training scripts code. You can use them to get familiar with the reranker training loop:.

For further learning, you may also want to explore the following resources on Sentence Transformers:.

And here is an advanced page that might interest you:.

For training other Sentence Transformers model types, or techniques that pair with a reranker:.

Industry observers note that @tomaarsen ,kindly let us know how to to carryout finetuning qlora-peft combinations? It helps a lot.

The distinction between reranking retrieved candidates and injecting all positives is especially helpful. We saw the same evaluation problem in our own BM25 + semantic-judgment experiment: the raw-verse reranking result is conditional on the gold verse being in the five-candidate pool, while the separate 160-query structured-record set had full top-5 recall. Our write-up is here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this week, a latest model from DeepSeek silently landed on the Hub.
  • In a recent development, the model has the same architecture as the original DeepSeek-V3 and now also comes with an MIT license, while the previous V3 model had a custom model license.
  • The DeepSeek team has evaluated the model on a range of math and coding tasks and we can see the model’s strong capabilities compared to other frontier models:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week, a latest model from DeepSeek silently landed on the Hub. It’s an updated version of DeepSeek-V3, the base model underlying the R1 reasoning model. There isn’t much information shared yet on this new model, but we do know a few things!

In a recent development, the model has the same architecture as the original DeepSeek-V3 and now also comes with an MIT license, while the previous V3 model had a custom model license. The focus of this model release was on improving the instruction following as well as code and math capabilities. Let’s have a look!

The DeepSeek team has evaluated the model on a range of math and coding tasks and we can see the model’s strong capabilities compared to other frontier models:.

Clearly, the model plays in the top league: often on par with GPT-4.5 and generally stronger than Claude-Sonnet-3.7.

To summarise the model has seen significant improvements across benchmarks.

Specifically, in the model card the DeepSeek mentions targeted improvements in the following areas:.

Sources indicate that so the question might pop-up: how did they actually do this? Let’s speculate a bit!

Sources indicate that given the naming and architecture it is fairly safe to assume that the new model is based on the previous V3 model and trained on top of it. There are two possible areas how they improved the models:.

Until the team releases a technical report we don’t know for sure what they tweaked but the post-training pipeline is quite likely and potentially also adding a bit of pretraining. So have a look at how to use the models next!

You can use Hugging Face’s Inference Providers to swiftly experiment with this model. It’s available through Fireworks, Hyperbolic, and Novita.

Here’s an example using the huggingface_hub library. You can also use the OpenAI client library like in this example.

TGI supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 with its latest release as well. You can use it directly with the tagged docker image on a node of H100s.

Sources indicate that SGLang supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 out of the box along with the Multi Latent Attention and Data Parallelism optimisations as well. To use you can simply just run the following on a node of H100s. For more information follow along here.

Dynamic Quants from Unsloth and Llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that running large LLMs like DeepSeek V3-0324 can be quite compute intensive and would require a large amount GPU VRAM to run. This is where Quantization comes in, it allows the end user to use the same model but with much lower VRAM consumption with a small trade-off in downstream performance.

Sources indicate that unsloth AI created Dynamic quantisations which allow one to run DeepSeek V3 with half the amount of compute as one node of H100 and can run with llama.cpp without as much degradation in benchmarks. Read more about it here: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V3-0324-GGUF.

It has been revealed that running language model safely has always been at the center of attention, ever since the first GPT models have been released. With the immense popularity of the DeepSeek models and their origin the question has found new interest. Let us run down the things that are safe to do and areas where some caution is a good idea. This is not DeepSeek specific but true for any open model!

First of all - is it safe to even download the model?

Industry observers note that yes, downloading the model is safe. There are a few precautions on the Hub side that make sure it’s safe to download and run models:.

So downloading the weights is safe, and upon code review so is executing the modeling code. This means you can run the DeepSeek model locally without the risk of backdoors or malicious code execution.

Industry observers note that so what would be the main risks outside of downloading and running the model? It depends on what you do with the model outputs!

The advice that follows is not specific to any model, and applies to both open and closed models: whether considering risks stemming from built-in secret behaviours in the model or from a model accidentally producing bad outputs.

We’ll cover risks in three areas: alignment, code generation and agents.

Alignment mismatch: Every model provider chooses how and to which values their models are aligned. What these values are and how they are chosen typically remains opaque and they might also change over time (see this study). The advantage of open models is that the alignment can be changed with custom fine-tuning at a later stage still as the example of Perplexity’s DeepSeek 1776 shows.

As a rule, customers should be aware that any LLM is biased in one way or another and treat the model outputs accordingly.

It has been revealed that code generation: One of the most popular use-cases of LLMs is as coding assistants. However, this is also where indiscriminate usage of the model outputs can have the most negative effects. Models are trained on vast amounts of published code, new and old. This typically includes potentially malicious code or code that contains known vulnerabilities. So models might produce similar vulnerabilities when proposing code solutions.

According to recent reports, so, how can you prevent security concerns when using LLMs for code development? Run thorough code reviews of the proposed changes and scan the code with appropriate tools for vulnerabilities, as you would with any other code contribution.

Agents: In the past few months agent applications have gained significant interest, giving LLMs more autonomy and agency also bears risks. It’s crucial to be careful about what kind of system access agents have and which information you provide them. Some good practices:.

In a recent development, TL;DR: Is it safe to run the models? Yes, downloading and running the models is safe, but, as with any model, you should take precautions to use the models generations with the appropriate safety measures.

According to recent reports, that’s why it matters even more to use truly free software models, which are free software licenses are promoted by projects like GNU and Free Software Foundation: They allow for inspection by anyone involved in their development or maintenance.With such a model of transparency—where code is Free Software so others may see and change the program it becomes easier to make sure that there aren’t any hidden backdoors lurking inside. 👩‍💻✨.

What is Free Software? - GNU Project - Free Software Foundationhttps://www.gnu.org/philosophy/free-sw.html.

We're excited to announce the native integration of Intel Gaudi hardware support directly into Text Generation Inference (TGI), our production-ready serving solution for Large Language Models (LLMs). This integration brings the power of Intel's specialized AI accelerators to our high-performance inference stack, enabling more deployment options for the open-source AI community 🎉.

According to recent reports, we've fully integrated Gaudi support into TGI's main codebase in PR #3091. Previously, we maintained a separate fork for Gaudi devices at tgi-gaudi. This was cumbersome for customers and prevented us from supporting the latest TGI features at launch. Now using the fresh TGI multi-backend architecture, we support Gaudi directly on TGI – no more finicking on a custom repository 🙌.

This integration supports Intel's full line of Gaudi hardware:.

You can also find more information on Gaudi hardware on Intel's Gaudi product page.

The Gaudi backend for TGI provides several key benefits:.

Sources indicate that the easiest way to run TGI on Gaudi is to use our official Docker image. You need to run the image on a Gaudi hardware machine. Here's a basic example to get you started:.

Once the server is running, you can send inference requests:.

For comprehensive documentation on using TGI with Gaudi, including how-to guides and advanced configurations, refer to the fresh dedicated Gaudi backend documentation.

We have optimized the following models for both single and multi-card configurations. This means these models run as fast as possible on Intel Gaudi. We've specifically optimized the modeling code to target Intel Gaudi hardware, ensuring we offer the best performance and fully utilize Gaudi's capabilities:.

🏃‍♂️ We also offer many advanced features on Gaudi hardware, such as FP8 quantization thanks to Intel Neural Compressor (INC), enabling even greater performance optimizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hugging Face has become synonymous with advancing AI at scale. With over 4 million builders deploying models on the Hub, the rapid growth of the platform necessitated a rethinking of how sensitive configuration data —secrets— are managed.

Last year, the engineering teams set out to improve the handling of their secrets and credentials. After evaluating tools like HashiCorp Vault, they ultimately chose Infisical.

This case study details their migration to Infisical, explains how they integrated its powerful features, and highlights how it enabled engineers to work more efficiently and securely.

It has been revealed that as Hugging Face's infrastructure evolved from an AWS-only setup to a multi-cloud environment that includes Azure and GCP, the engineering team needed a more agile, secure, and centralized way to manage secrets. Instead of reworking legacy systems or adopting heavyweight solutions like HashiCorp Vault, they turned to Infisical due to its developer-friendly workflows, multi-cloud abstraction, and robust security capabilities.

The key challenges they faced were:.

In addition, the team needed a solution that adhered to infrastructure-as-code practices, supported project-by-project secret management, and provided a smooth balance between automation and manual control during deployments.

It has been revealed that infisical’s flexible architecture was an ideal solution. The engineering team seized the opportunity to re-examine their internal project structure, splitting projects into distinct infrastructure and application domains. This allowed them to implement a clearer separation of concerns and standardize secret rotation practices—a priority in the wake of a recent security incident.

By leveraging Terraform, which was previously used to create Kubernetes secrets from AWS configurations, they found the transition to the Infisical Kubernetes Operator exceptionally smooth. This integration enabled security improvements while standardizing secrets management across all environments.

Kubernetes is at the heart of Hugging Face’s production environment, and Infisical's Kubernetes Operator has been instrumental in automating secret updates. The Operator continuously monitors for changes to any secret in Infisical and ensures that these updates are propagated to the corresponding Kubernetes objects. Whenever a change is detected, it can automatically reload dependent Deployments, ensuring that containers always run with the most recent secrets.

Recent findings suggest that A new secret is required by an application running in Kubernetes. The secret can be created via the Infisical's CLI or the web UI, then the developer creates an InfisicalSecret resource in Kubernetes that specifies which secret from Infisical should be synced:.

Sources indicate that once the CRD is applied, the Infisical Operator continuously watches for updates. When changes are detected in Infisical, the Operator automatically updates the Kubernetes secret (my-app-k8s-secret).

Better yet, since the application's Deployment references my-app-k8s-secret as an environment variable source or mounted volume, the Operator can automatically trigger a container reload when the secret changes.

In a recent development, in practice, Hugging Face engineers favor waiting for manual redeployments despite the Operator’s ability to automatically trigger container restarts. This decision was driven by the need for precise control over deployments, particularly when high traffic (over 10 million requests per minute) and numerous replicas are involved.

For local development, Infisical’s CLI streamlines workflows by injecting secrets directly into development environments. This removes the need for insecure local .env files, aligning local configurations with production standards and reducing onboarding friction.

It has been revealed that security improvements form the backbone of this migration. By integrating Infisical with existing identity providers such as Okta, Hugging Face established a fine-grained RBAC system. Permissions are automatically mapped from Okta groups, ensuring that developers retain administrative rights over their projects, while frontend and backend teams receive appropriately restricted read or write access.

Additionally, the secret sharing functionality allows secure credentials sharing among ML/AI researchers at Hugging Face. The centralized Infisical platform also simplifies auditing and managing secret rotations—a necessity highlighted by previous security incidents.

Recent findings suggest that seamless integration with CI/CD pipelines further enhanced the overall security posture. Infisical was embedded into the deployment pipeline via GitHub Actions using OIDC authentication and Terraform integration. By operating self-hosted runners within a secure environment, every deployment adhered to production-grade security standards. This integrated approach minimized risks and ensured a uniform experience from local development to cloud deployment.

Centralizing secrets management with Infisical brought tangible improvements:.

As noted by Adrien Carreira, Head of Infrastructure at Hugging Face,.

"Infisical provided all the functionality and security settings we needed to boost our security posture and save engineering time. Whether you're working locally, running kubernetes clusters in production, or operating secrets within CI/CD pipelines, Infisical has a seamless prebuilt workflow.".

According to recent reports, hugging Face's migration to Infisical demonstrates how a technically driven, engineering-centric approach to managing secrets across multiple cloud platforms delivers significant benefits. For tackling similar challenges, using Infisical is a practical way to work more efficiently while keeping security strong.

When the secure path is made the easiest path, teams can focus on building innovative products instead of worrying about managing secrets.

#173732. Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance
