Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that serving LLMs to many applications and users in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources.
  • An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.
  • According to recent reports, why do we need a queue here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that serving LLMs to many applications and users in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources. This article is the first in a series on LLM performance, based on our experience with serving self-hosted LLMs at TNG Technology Consulting GmbH. In the first part, we focus on the impact of queuing and discuss different scheduling strategies.

An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.

According to recent reports, why do we need a queue here? Because calculations on the GPU are more performant and resource-efficient when they are done batch-wise instead of isolated for individual requests. This backend queue allows the scheduler to pick multiple requests and put them on the same batch to be processed.

Note that typically each inference engine serves only a single model, and we have multiple deployments running for different models in parallel.

Recent findings suggest that when a single user "A" sends a large number of requests, they will quickly fill up the queue. Other owners ("B" and "C") that send their requests only shortly after are blocked from using the same model (until all requests from "A" have been processed). Note that the picture focuses on vLLM as inference engine, but the problem is more general and applies to other backends as well.

At TNG, consumers don't send requests directly to the vLLM backend but to an API Server (what we call "LLM-Server"). Here we can have separate queues for each user (and model), and a scheduler that is not FIFO (first in - first out) but goes round-robin through all user queues. This achieves some "fair scheduling": for example, in the diagram users B and C send their request a bit later, when user A's first request has already been scheduled. At that time, three requests from user A had been waiting already for some time, but user C has to wait for only one request from user A to be completed.

Sources indicate that the key idea is: prioritize requests from different customers in our own component and not in the inference backend! Typically, you can't change the order of requests once they have been sent to the inference engine, so you have to bring them in the right order while they are still in the LLM-Server, where we have full control.

In a recent development, you can consider different aspects in order to decide what "fair" scheduling is. In the above example, any new user with a single request should be served before any user is served two or more times in a row. This is "fair" on a number-of-requests level. But you could also look at processing time: how long does a request keep the backend busy? Long prompts and long generations will "block" the LLM for other users for a longer time, so maybe shorter requests should have precedence? Unfortunately, it is very difficult to estimate the generation length. While there are some requests with a "max_tokens" limit, a typical chat message from an interactive AI assistant has no token limit, and can vary between a very short generation ("summarize this text") and a very long one ("tell me a story" / "write all code for xyz").

Sources indicate that depending on the prompts, there can be some benefit in arranging requests based on similarity, so that vLLM can maximize cache hits, which speeds up the performance. This kind of KV-cache-aware routing has recently gained attention by frameworks like NVIDIA Dynamo and AIBrix.

In a business context, and for hosted LLMs, the cost of individual requests can be another metric to consider, but comes with similar challenges.

In a recent development, the solution can also be extended by having not only one queue per user (and model) but several queues with different priorities. For example, interactive applications like TNG's AI Assistant with chat interface should have higher priority because users who don't see any progress within five seconds will think the application is broken. Users who generate code reviews for tens of files and several thousand lines of code, however, will expect the LLM requests to take some time. And some use cases (like benchmark runs, scheduled via a batch API) should have such low priority that they don't disturb other use cases and are just scheduled when nothing else is running.

Consider again the scenario that one user A sends a lot of requests at once, and some time later a new user C joins and wants to schedule a single request. If the scheduler on LLM-Server side sent every request (according to the fair prioritization) immediately to the backend, all requests from A would accumulate again in the FIFO queue. The new user C would have to wait again until all previously received requests have been processed. There would be almost no improvement to the initial scenario without LLM-Server.

Ideally, you could limit the number of maximum elements in the backend queue, but vLLM doesn't give you that option. Therefore, we have to dynamically adjust the rate at which the scheduler on LLM-Server side sends new requests to the backend. Here, our goal is: keep the backend queue length short in order to minimize latencies experienced by new users.

(The simplest approach would be a static rate limit, but this would likely result in underutilization when most requests are short and hard to calibrate for different models and load patterns).

In order to make the backend queue length available in the LLM-Server, we need to fetch the respective Prometheus metrics from the vLLM /metrics endpoint. Our fair scheduler is only allowed to send requests to the backend as long as the backend queue length metric is smaller than three, for example. This target length for the backend queue can be lowered for an even shorter latency for latest users, until it results in under-utilized batches and a reduced efficiency - there is a trade-off. Keep in mind, though, that the target queue length does NOT reflect maximum concurrency; there can still be more than three requests being processed in parallel; vLLM will add queuing requests to the current batch as soon as there is sufficient space ("continuous batching").

According to recent reports, once you have the feedback loop between backend queue and scheduler in the LLM-Server, you can easily extend the set of vLLM metrics used for making scheduling decisions. For example, for a good user experience in TNG's interactive AI Assistant we aim for a high token generation speed (e.g., >7 tokens/s, that is ~150ms per token), and if the reported time-per-output-token metric rises above 150ms, no upcoming requests will be scheduled.

Industry observers note that you can also program different metric thresholds for different request priorities. For example, for low-priority requests from the batch API we only schedule a request when the backend queue is completely empty: we rather risk short periods of underutilized GPUs than causing increased latencies for any later request with higher priority.

There is quite some potential for optimizations: for example, if you allow scheduling for a backend length shorter than three and the current metric is zero, you can immediately send three requests to the backend before having to fetch the metrics again. In the worst case, none of them fit into the current batch and all of them are in the backend queue (in which case the fresh length is three, just fine).

Sources indicate that recently, vLLM added a priority-based scheduling option instead of sticking with FIFO. For this new feature, requests are tagged with a priority before they are sent to the backend. And vLLM would regularly check if any higher-priority request is queuing and then sort all requests by priority (both the running batch and the waiting queue). This would not only let the high-priority request literally jump the queue but even move it directly to the processed batch. The price is (aside from some overhead due to sorting) that lower priority requests would be evicted from the running batch and put back in the waiting queue again.

In a recent development, vLLM understands the request priority as a continuous number. This does not only allow you to distinguish between default, high priority (interactive AI assistant) and low priority (batch API) but you could even make smaller decrements for every request that the user has already sent to the backend and where the response is pending. For example, owners B and C send only single requests, which will have priority zero. User A sends four requests at once; the first one has priority zero, too, but the next ones will have priorities one, two, and three, and will be processed later (higher number = lower priority).

Industry observers note that overall, backend-side priority scheduling can be a good strategy for vLLM-based systems, because it simplifies queueing logic on the upstream LLM-Server. Unfortunately, in a realistic setting you cannot get rid of the LLM-Server as an additional scheduling layer, since you need some objective instance to assign priorities to individual requests.

Queueing and scheduling are crucial for applications with multiple customers and clients of varying priorities, as they significantly impact the user experience. This is especially true in scenarios where multiple clients submit requests in parallel, benefiting from a dedicated "fair scheduling" strategy. Although backend features like priority scheduling can simplify optimization, an upstream gateway server is still necessary to fully manage these complexities.

It has been revealed that in the next part of this blogpost series, we will shift gears and focus on the token generation in the inference engine during prefill and decode phases. In particular, we will discuss resource utilization and strategies for concurrent processing of multiple requests.

Industry observers note that has Disaggregated Prefill been improved in 0.9.1? Many people use 1P and ND mode now.

yes, disaggregated prefill has improved by now, although it still takes some custom work to set it up correctly.The original challenge of multi-user serving with heterogeneous load patterns and priorities remains, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, education has always been at the heart of Hugging Face’s mission to democratize AI and we’re doubling down on that by giving hf.co/learn a big upgrade! Our NLP course has been a go-to resource for the open-source AI community for the past 3 years, and it’s now time for a refresh. We’re updating and expanding it to keep up with all the exciting stuff happening in AI (which is not easy when there are breakthroughs every week!).

We felt the excitement during the experimental smol-course and the massive agents course, where 100k students registered to learn about AI agents in a new, fun, and interactive way!

Over the last few months we’ve expanded the "NLP" course with new chapters, including fine-tuning LLMs and building reasoning models like Deepseek R1. These newer chapters don’t fit under the banner of ‘NLP’ so we’ve searched for a more relevant and modern title and landed on The LLM course.

In a recent development, we will maintain the existing material that focuses on classic NLP tasks like classification, named entity-recognition and retrieval. These topics are vital because:.

In fact, over the coming months we will enhancement and modernise these classic chapters to include approaches like Sentence Transformers, updates in Zero Shot classification, and ModernBert.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different organization” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different manufacturer” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Industry observers note that dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure organization.

Clarke stated he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Recent findings suggest that dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

Sources indicate that HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the organization’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO remarked HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Sources indicate that dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.

📅 04 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1177 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Journey to 1 Million Gradio Users!

📅 04 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 5 years ago, we rolled out Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.
  • Today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps.
  • Sources indicate that how did we get here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

5 years ago, we rolled out Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.

Today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps. This includes some of the most popular open-source projects of all time, like Automatic1111, Oobabooga’s Text Generation WebUI, Dall-E Mini, and LLaMA-Factory.

Sources indicate that how did we get here? How did Gradio keep growing in the very crowded field of open-source Python libraries? I get this question a lot from folks who are building their own open-source libraries. This post distills some of the lessons that I have learned over the past few years:.

1. Invest in good primitives, not high-level abstractions.

When we first launched Gradio, we offered only one high-level class (gr.Interface), which created a complete web app from a single Python function. We swiftly realized that developers wanted to create other kinds of apps (e.g. multi-step workflows, chatbots, streaming applications), but as we started listing out the apps owners wanted to build, we realized what we needed to do: go lower.

In a recent development, instead of building many high-level classes to support different use cases, we built a low-level API called Gradio Blocks that let customers assemble applications from modular components, events, and layouts. Despite generally being more work to use, gr.Blocks today represents 80% of the usage of Gradio—including the highly popular apps mentioned above.

Recent findings suggest that with a small team, a focus on low-level abstractions has necessarily meant that we could not chase many tempting, high-level abstractions. But this focus saved us from two common pitfalls:.

Customization-maintenance trap: high-level abstractions are easy to use, but users request extra parameters to customize them, which in turn leads to increased maintenance burden since every abstraction and parameter needs to be implemented, maintained, and tested to avoid bugs.

The productivity illusion: using high-level abstractions seems like less work, until a user needs functionality that is not supported (which can be hard to predict at the beginning of a project), forcing the developer to do a costly rewrite.

The first problem wastes our time as maintainers of Gradio, while the second problem wastes our users’ time. To this day, Gradio only includes two high-level abstractions (gr.Interface and gr.ChatInterface) which themselves are built with Blocks.

The advantage of having good primitives is even more dramatic in the age of AI-assisted coding, where we find that LLMs are generally good at combing through documentation and building complex applications out of primitives (see all the games being built with three.js for example). It doesn’t take much extra time to write low-level code if the AI is writing the code for you.

Recent findings suggest that the best ambassador for your library is not you, but an enthusiastic user. It follows, then, that you should find ways for users to share your library or its products as part of their workflow. Gradio’s early growth was fueled by our “share links” feature (which created a temporary public link for your Gradio app in a single line of code). Instead of having to worry about packaging or hosting their code on a web server with the right kind of compute, Gradio users could share their apps with colleagues immediately.

Industry observers note that after joining Hugging Face, we also benefited from being the standard UI for Hugging Face Spaces—widely used by the machine learning research community. The most viral Spaces drew millions of visitors, exposing developers to Gradio, who in turn shared and built their own Gradio apps, using those same Spaces (whose code was publicly available) as a resource to learn how to use Gradio.

3. Build for a (growing) niche use case.

Early on, we faced a critical decision: should Gradio be a general-purpose Python web framework, or should we focus specifically on building machine learning web apps? We chose the latter, and this has made all the difference.

In the crowded ecosystem of Python web libraries, we are frequently asked, "How is Gradio different from X?" Our concise answer—that Gradio is optimized for machine learning web apps—is memorable and fundamentally accurate. Each Gradio app ships with features particularly suited to ML workflows, such as a built-in queue that can manage long-running ML tasks efficiently, even with thousands of concurrent consumers. The components we have designed are specifically tailored to ML use cases. On the other hand, for a long time, Gradio did not even include features like link buttons, simply because our core users never needed it. By narrowing our focus, Gradio quickly became the go-to choice among machine learning developers—the default "UI for AI.".

According to recent reports, of course, we benefited tremendously from choosing a niche that itself was growing. The recent headwinds that have propelled all things AI-related benefited us tremendously and we likely would not have experienced the same kind of growth if we had focused on data science or dashboards for example.

4. Your only roadmap should be rapid iteration.

Unlike some other libraries, Gradio doesn’t publish roadmaps. Instead, we track emerging trends in machine learning and ship accordingly. In open-source software generally, and AI specifically, shipping features based on the needs of the community (and deprecating features that are no longer needed) is key to continuous growth. As a concrete example, in the early versions of Gradio we built specific functionality to allow developers to show the “interpretation” of their machine learning models—as this was a very popular use case around 2020-21. As interest in interpretation waned, we deprecated this and instead poured our efforts into audio/video streaming and chat-related features.

Our internal process is decentralized as well. Each of the 11 engineers and developer advocates on the Gradio team is encouraged to identify impactful ideas, prototype quickly, engage directly with the open-source community via GitHub, Hugging Face, and social media. Each team member brings these ideas back to the team and we continuously build and rebuild consensus around what ideas are likely to be impactful as we keep growing the most impactful directions.

5. Maximize ways people can consume your library's outputs.

It has been revealed that when you create a Gradio app and “launch()” it, you get a web application running in your browser. But that’s not all -- you also get an API endpoint for each Python function, as well as automatically-generated documentation for each endpoint. These endpoints can be consumed via Python or JavaScript Clients that our team has built, or directly using cURL.

The reason that we do this is because we want each minute that a developer spends with Gradio to be maximally useful. A single Gradio app should run locally or be deployed without any code changes on Hugging Face Spaces or on your server, or integrate into larger applications programmatically, or even be harnessed by AI agents through MCPs (more on that soon!). By focusing on maximum usability, we hope that developers can continue to get more and more out of the Gradio library.

📅 05 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are incredibly excited to welcome the next generation of large language models from Meta to the Hugging Face Hub: Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)!
  • Recent findings suggest that released today, these powerful, natively multimodal models represent a significant leap forward.
  • This is just the start of our journey with Llama 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are incredibly excited to welcome the next generation of large language models from Meta to the Hugging Face Hub: Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)! 🤗 Both are Mixture of Experts (MoE) models with 17B active parameters.

Recent findings suggest that released today, these powerful, natively multimodal models represent a significant leap forward. We've worked closely with Meta to ensure seamless integration into the Hugging Face ecosystem, including both transformers and TGI from day one.

This is just the start of our journey with Llama 4. Over the coming days we’ll continue to collaborate with the community to build amazing models, datasets, and applications with Maverick and Scout! 🔥.

Llama 4, developed by Meta, introduces a latest auto-regressive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. This generation includes two models:.

Sources indicate that both models leverage early fusion for native multimodality, enabling them to process text and image inputs. Maverick and Scout are both trained on up to 40 trillion tokens on data encompassing 200 languages (with specific fine-tuning support for 12 languages including Arabic, Spanish, German, and Hindi).

For deployment, Llama 4 Scout is designed for accessibility, fitting on a single server-grade GPU via on-the-fly 4-bit or 8-bit quantization, while Maverick is available in BF16 and FP8 formats. These models are released under the custom Llama 4 Community License Agreement, available on the model repositories.

To help the community leverage these state-of-the-art models immediately, we're thrilled to announce the following integrations:.

The Llama 4 models were pre-trained with a context length of 256K. The Instruct models were fine-tuned to support much larger context lengths: 1M in the large 128 experts version (Maverick), and 10M (!) for the 16 experts version (Scout).

It has been revealed that these large context lengths come with a few very interesting architecture choices. Until an official technical report is published, this is what we know so far.

NoPE (cute name, +1 charisma points), which was explored as far back as 2022, just forgoes the traditional positional encoding schemes, such as RoPE, that are most times applied in transformers models. In the case of Llama 4, NoPE layers are used every 4 layers. These layers are crucial for long context, as they use the full causal mask over the context.

For RoPE layers (three out of 4), chunked attention is used.

Meta refers to the interleaved use of NoPE layers, together with temperature scaling (as explained below), as the iRoPE architecture.

If you want to learn more about positional encodings, we recommend Chris' recent post.

In a recent development, as a way to reduce memory requirements, Llama 4 uses chunked attention in the layers that work with traditional RoPE positional encodings (three out of 4 decoder layers). The best way to visualize how chunked attention works is through this ASCII representation that was extracted from the transformers source code:.

This diagram demonstrates the attention mask that would be used if the chunked attention length was 3. In the case of Llama 4, chunked attention length is 8192. This means that RoPE layers can only keep track of context in 8K blocks, while NoPE layers have access to the full context. You can see it as a more memory and compute efficient version of Sliding Window Attention.

It has been revealed that attention blocks applied to long contexts have a problem: the attention probability scores fade closer to zero as the sequence length increases. This is a known consequence of applying the softmax function to very long sequences. To address this problem, Llama 4 uses a scaled softmax, which the model refers to as temperature tuning. This is applied in the NoPE layers, but not in the RoPE ones as these attend to shorter sub-sequences.

This method is a way to improve generalization for arbitrary context lengths, and probably one of the key factors to achieve 10M context length in Llama 4 Scout.

Llama Scout (the 16 experts version) uses an additional RMS normalization without learnable parameter of the Query and Key states in RoPE layers, after RoPE embeddings have been applied.

Recent findings suggest that llama Scout is a full MoE consisting of 16 experts. Llama Maverick uses 128 experts, but MoE and dense layers alternate. Therefore, experts are applied in half of the layers.

Llama Maverick was co-distilled from a larger model, Llama Behemoth, using a novel loss function that weight dynamically the student and teacher logit.

The models leverage MetaP, a methodology likely inspired by MuP, to optimally tune hyperparameters across different dimensions including training budget and model size.

Getting started with Llama 4 using transformers is straightforward. Make sure you have transformers v4.51.0 or later installed (pip install -U transformers huggingface_hub[hf_xet]). Here's a quick example using the instruction-tuned Maverick model responding about two images, using tensor parallel for maximum speed. You need to run this script on an instance with 8 GPUs, using a command like:torchrun –nproc-per-instance=8 script.py.

Make sure to check the model cards on the repos (Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)) for detailed usage instructions, including multimodal examples, specific prompt formats (like system prompts), quantization details, and advanced configuration options!

Sources indicate that evaluation results confirm the strength of these models, showing state-of-the-art performance that significantly outperforms predecessors like Llama 3.1 405B. For instance, on reasoning and knowledge tasks, the instruction-tuned Maverick achieves 80.5% on MMLU Pro and 69.8% on GPQA Diamond, while Scout scores 74.3% and 57.2% respectively.

Releasing a giant like Llama 4 takes a colossal effort across teams, geographies and a lot of VMs. In no particular order we’d like to thank Arthur, Lysandre, Cyril, Pablo, Marc, Mohammed from the Transformers team. We are grateful to the full vLLM team for rich discussions, insights, shared testing and debugging during this intense integration with many challenges. With larger optimisation needs, we’d like to thank Mohit for single-handedly adding support to Llama 4 in TGI. These chonky models require some serious engineering at the storage level. This took a lot of effort from Ajit, Rajat, Jared, Di, Yucheng and the rest of the Xet team too.

There are a lot of people involved in this effort, thanks a lot to the rest of the Hugging Face, vLLM and Meta Llama teams for the brilliant synergy!

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until latest hire lands, then stick around as advisor.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the organization’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami revealed his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the tech giant as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

Sources indicate that in chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami remarked he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he mentioned, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.”.

In a recent development, ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO stated the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix declared its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The tech giant added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest upcoming customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the tech giant’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • Industry observers note that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • Recent findings suggest that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

Industry observers note that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

Recent findings suggest that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

Sources indicate that the Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This concern is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In a recent development, in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

It has been revealed that streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 concerns.

Sources indicate that VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the fresh advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware customers rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication glitch VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

Sources indicate that the other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

Industry observers note that in past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At Inception, we have been working to enhance AI model evaluations within the Arabic language context.
  • As part of our ongoing efforts, we are excited to share the following updates:.
  • The following sections provide details about each of these updates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Inception, we have been working to enhance AI model evaluations within the Arabic language context. Previously, we introduced AraGen, one of the first generative Arabic leaderboards, serving as a benchmark for evaluating Arabic LLMs on generative tasks.

As part of our ongoing efforts, we are excited to share the following updates:.

The following sections provide details about each of these updates.

According to recent reports, arabic-Leaderboards is a comprehensive and unified space for all Arabic evaluations and tasks. It is meant to serve as a central hub covering a broad spectrum of evaluations, for models across modalities. Presently, it has AraGen-03-25 and Arabic Instruction Following as live leaderboards. We plan to expand this space with more leaderboards and tasks for Arabic AI models across various modalities.

We invite interested contributors to reach out to us through the community tab or directly through email in order to discuss how to integrate their work/leaderboards as additional tabs into this space.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2024, we introduced the AraGen Benchmark as the foundation for the AraGen Leaderboard. A key feature of this leaderboard is its dynamic nature, with evaluation datasets remaining private (blind testing) for three months to ensure fair and unbiased assessments. Adhering to the same philosophy, we are publicly releasing the AraGen-12-24 benchmark, along with all model responses evaluated by Claude-3.5-Sonnet following the 3C3H guidelines.

By sharing this benchmark and model responses, we aim to encourage the community to review them, identify any unexpected behaviors we may have missed and help us refine our evaluation framework.

In this latest AraGen release, we have expanded the dataset to include 340 pairs of questions and answers, up from 279 in the previous version. The distribution remains relatively similar:.

This allocation reflects the primary focus on question answering as the main use cases of any Language-Model/Chatbot/AI-Assistant, while still addressing other evaluation areas, particularly given the complexity of generating challenging queries in Arabic grammar and orthography.

Additionally, we refined the judge system prompt to enhance clarity, even for smaller/weaker judge models.

Industry observers note that maintaining consistency and reliability in our benchmark and evaluation pipeline is crucial as we introduce dynamic evaluation cycles. To ensure this, we analyzed ranking variations among the top 10 models across different dataset versions and system prompt configurations.

We analyzed model performance under two evaluation scenarios:.

According to recent reports, the overall rankings were stable, with the top-performing model (o1-2024-12-17) consistently maintaining its lead. Notably, we observed a swap in rankings between two Claude models, underscoring the sensitivity of our evaluation approach, especially given their initially close scores.

It has been revealed that the only significant change in rankings was for the gpt-4o-2024-08-06 model, whose performance markedly improved with the updated dataset and prompt. This sudden jump is right now under investigation as part of our ongoing benchmarks-design research.

In a recent development, no major variations occurred solely due to changes in the system prompt, indicating good reproducibility as long as the same judge model (claude-3.5-sonnet) is used. However, we anticipate potential variations with smaller or weaker models as judges, where employing the second system prompt (SP2) may enhance consistency.

Sources indicate that as a summary, the robust, consistently top-ranking performance of o1-2024-12-17—whose top score dropped from 82.67% to 70.25%—continues to reinforce its reliability for Arabic applications under the more challenging updated benchmark. While recent updates to the evaluation pipeline introduced minor ranking shifts, the overall framework remained stable, with top and bottom performers showing consistent positions. Many observed ranking adjustments likely reflect typical evaluation error margins due to minor score differences. Notably, scores for the second- through fifth-ranked models, previously between 70–78%, are now between 51–57%. This highlights that the updated AraGen dataset poses a markedly more difficult benchmark aligned with ongoing advances in reasoning models. Despite these shifts in absolute scores, it is encouraging that leaderboard positions remained largely consistent, underscoring the robustness of the evaluation approach moving forward.

According to recent reports, as part of our December release, we introduced 3C3H as a fresh evaluation measure of the chat capability of models, aimed at assessing both the factuality and usability of LLMs’ answers. Over the past three months, we have observed some interesting findings, which we share in this section.

One emergent trend is that the various dimensions are almost perfectly correlated. In most cases, correct answers are scored as both highly helpful and harmless, while most models fail to maintain this correlation for the conciseness dimension. This generally reflects the way we train these models today, where more verbose answers are often rewarded as more helpful. This trend has recently caught the attention of the research community, as exemplified by the release of OpenAI’s GPT-4.5 model. According to their use cases section, answers from GPT-4.5 are more concise than those from GPT-4, while still being equally helpful.

A model that stood out in this analysis is “silma-ai/SILMA-9B-Instruct-v1.0”, which exhibited a higher conciseness score compared to other open-weight models—even those with larger sizes. However, this gain in conciseness came at the cost of helpfulness and other dimensions when compared to its base model, “google/gemma-2-9b-it”. We believe that this analysis, along with optimizing for 3C3H, will enable the community to develop better models through curated datasets while maintaining the correlation across all dimensions.

It has been revealed that this is an ongoing effort to better understand how these dimensions are interconnected and how various scenarios and training recipes affect this relationship. Below, we provide a space where you can generate heatmaps for any combination of models of your choice. We hope the community finds it helpful in spotting additional trends that we may not have noticed. Ultimately, we aim for this tool to foster more discussion about evaluation and 3C3H, serving as a resource for others’ work.

It has been revealed that we believe that one limitation of this analysis is the zeroing rule, whereby we do not evaluate the other dimensions if the answer is not correct. In the future, we proposal to investigate further whether an answer can be helpful despite being incorrect, and how dimensions such as conciseness and harmlessness factor into this evaluation if the answer is not correct.

One of the core capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is their ability to understand and follow human instructions. This skill is crucial for building reliable chatbots, virtual assistants, and AI systems that do what people ask. Without strong instruction-following, a model might generate correct information but in the wrong format, ignore user-specified constraints, or produce unwanted content. Instruction-Following benchmark is standardized, objective way to measure a model's instruction adherence and compare models fairly to drive improvements.

Industry observers note that our work took inspiration from the IFEval dataset. IFEval, originally introduced by Google, provides a structured benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on their ability to follow verifiable instructions. It consists of prompts containing specific, objectively measurable commands such as “use exactly three bullet points,” “include the word ‘innovation’ twice,” or “limit your answer to 100 words.” English IFEval dataset contains around 500 prompts covering 25 different types of such verifiable instructions. Evaluation within IFEval is conducted through Python functions that automatically verify whether instructions are followed, avoiding the need for human evaluators or another AI judge. This makes the evaluations reproducible and unbiased. While IFEval has become the standard for assessing LLMs responding in English, a similarly detailed and structured resource is absent for Arabic.

It has been revealed that construction of our Arabic IFEval dataset began by carefully adapting approximately 300 prompts from the original English IFEval. This wasn't a straightforward, word-for-word translation; instead, we thoughtfully adjusted prompts to clearly reflect Arabic linguistic nuances and cultural contexts. Instructions that made little sense in Arabic, such as those involving English-specific vowel constraints, were either adapted to equivalent Arabic linguistic challenges or omitted entirely. Cultural references specific to English-speaking contexts were replaced with culturally relevant or Arabic-language equivalents to maintain contextual clarity. Additionally, we created unique Arabic-specific samples from scratch, specifically designed to emphasize distinctive Arabic phonetics, orthographic characteristics, and morphology, such as the careful use of diacritical marks (tashkīl), phonetic constraints like avoiding certain letters (e.g., writing without using the letter Alef (ا)), and leveraging root-based morphology to challenge models' word-selection abilities. All prompts underwent rigorous expert validation by Arabic linguists and domain experts who ensured grammatical accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and unambiguous clarity of each instruction.

Sources indicate that arabic IFEval dataset is publicly available for the research community to utilize, test, and contribute to. It is available on Huggingface under inceptionai/Arabic_IFEval.

It has been revealed that prompt (Ar):فسر كيف يمكن للتقنيات الحديثة مثل الذكاء الاصطناعي أن تسهم في الحفاظ على الأدب العربي، مع تضمين 12 كلمة تنتهي بأحد الحروف الرافسة (د، ذ، أ، ر، ز، و)، وأن تكون الإجابة مكتوبة بأسلوب موجز لا يتجاوز 120 كلمة. يجب أن لا تحتوي إجابتك على أي فواصل.

Industry observers note that prompt Translation (En): Explain how modern technologies, such as artificial intelligence, can contribute to preserving Arabic literature. Your answer should include at least 12 words ending with one of these specific Arabic letters (د، ذ، أ، ر، ز، و), be concise, and should not exceed 120 words. Your response must not contain any commas.

Prompt (Ar): اكتب قصة قصيرة عن الرقم 600، على أن يكتب الرقم في القصة بالكلمات وبكل الصيغ المفقطة الممكنة له على الأقل مرة (ستة مائة - ست مئة - ستمئة - ستمائة).

Sources indicate that prompt Translation (En):Write a short story about the number 600. Within the story, the number should be spelled out in Arabic in all possible written forms at least once each ("ستة مائة", "ست مئة", "ستمئة", "ستمائة").

Instructions to follow:Your response must explicitly include the following Arabic spellings at least once each:.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the models, we adopted a comprehensive methodology combining both explicit and implicit evaluation techniques. Explicit evaluation involved using automated scripts to assess whether instructions were strictly followed, focusing on elements such as correct formatting and specific word usage. Implicit evaluation addressed more nuanced linguistic expectations, such as maintaining the intended response language and avoiding repetitive patterns.

Sources indicate that additionally, we utilized scoring metrics introduced by Google in the IFEval framework, applying these metrics at both prompt-level and instruction-level granularity. These metrics were measured using strict criteria accuracy, which requires adherence to the provided instructions. The prompt-level score is notably harder, reflecting the user's viewpoint by asking, "Did I get everything I requested?" If a prompt included multiple requirements, failing to meet any single requirement would mean the user's request was not fully satisfied. In contrast, the instruction-level score is more lenient, allowing us to evaluate partial compliance.

In our analysis, we will emphasize the prompt-level strict accuracy as it provides the most rigorous assessment of a model's instruction-following capabilities.

It has been revealed that we evaluated a broad range of LLMs on both the English IFEval benchmark and our newly introduced Arabic IFEval. This encompassed closed-source models (such as OpenAI's GPT series and Anthropic's Claude models) and open-source alternatives (including the Jais series, Meta’s LLaMA-2 variants, and various open bilingual models). Below, we present a summary of results for a representative subset of these models, comparing their prompt-level accuracy on both English and Arabic IFEval. Accuracy is reported using both strict and loose criteria, with values expressed as the percentage of prompts successfully completed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

According to recent reports, this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of Latest York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision states Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors indicated evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”.

Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”.

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

It has been revealed that huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ indicates.

The feds say the Chinese manufacturer also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”.

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”.

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Industry observers note that washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese tech giant return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®.

#173720. The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1869 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • Recent findings suggest that the answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a fresh security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes vital the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

Recent findings suggest that the answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

It has been revealed that together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

According to recent reports, there is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

An agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

According to recent reports, network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

Industry observers note that for an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The notable part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

According to recent reports, MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

Recent findings suggest that docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

Here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

Recent findings suggest that this makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that one boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

It has been revealed that audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

Industry observers note that denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

Sources indicate that current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

Recent findings suggest that AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

In a recent development, in practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

It has been revealed that AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an concern, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

According to recent reports, the agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

According to recent reports, now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

Recent findings suggest that for governance activity presently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

In a recent development, if that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

According to recent reports, the model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility reveals how governed activity was handled.

Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

In a recent development, the challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

That makes the boundary around the agent just as vital as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

Industry observers note that the goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

Visual Salamandra: Pushing the Boundaries of Multimodal Understanding

📅 11 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video.
  • Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.
  • According to recent reports, the resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video. Visual Salamandra is based on the 7 billion parameters foundational model maintaining its compactness and efficiency while extending it to multimodal tasks.

Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.

According to recent reports, the resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions. This development reflects a broader commitment by the Lab to support robust, multilingual, and multimodal AI systems—especially those that prioritize European linguistic diversity.

Recent findings suggest that to adapt Salamandra for visual inputs, the Lab implemented a four-phase training process centered on late-fusion architecture. In this setup, a pre-trained image encoder (SigLIP, 14 patches at 384x384 resolution) generates image embeddings, which are then aligned with the LLM via a custom-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector.

The four training phases include:.

• Phase 1: Projector Pre-training – Only the projector is trained to map image features into the LLM’s latent space.

• Phase 2: High-Quality Vision Pretraining – Using refined datasets (e.g., OCR and re-captioned images), the entire architecture (encoder, projector, and LLM) undergoes joint training.

• Phase 3: Instruction Tuning – The model learns to follow user instructions via visual question answering (VQA), OCR, and other grounded vision tasks.

• Phase 4: Full Multimodal Tuning – Incorporates single/multi-image and video data, along with text-only examples, to optimize the model’s generalization to real-world, multi-input scenarios.

Data diversity played a crucial role throughout training. A total of 6.1 million instruction-tuning instances were used, including 842,000 text-only samples. The training corpus featured data from sources like AI2D, Cambrian, and LLaVA Next, chosen to enhance visual grounding, document understanding, mathematical reasoning, and OCR.

Figure 1. Data distribution during the Visual Salamandra 7B training process.

As with previous models from the Language Technologies Lab, Visual Salamandra continues the commitment to multilingual inclusivity, with a strong focus on European languages.

Recent findings suggest that this approach guarantees that underrepresented languages benefit from instruction tuning and alignment with vision tasks, helping to close the resource gap in multimodal AI research. Visual Salamandra is one of the first models of its kind to integrate such linguistic plurality into a multimodal instruction-tuned framework.

Figure 2. Multilingual generation examples with the model trained with Text Regularization and merged with the original backbone LLM.

Visual Salamandra unlocks a wide range of applications at the intersection of language and vision, such as:.

• Visual Question Answering (VQA): Ask questions about an image or video and receive context-aware, accurate responses.

• Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Accurately read and transcribe text from documents, scenes, and charts.

• Document and Chart Understanding: Analyze complex visual documents or graphical content with embedded text.

• Mathematical Reasoning: Solve visually grounded math problems through multimodal reasoning.

• Instruction-based Image Interaction: Follow detailed instructions in visual contexts, including image captioning and localization tasks.

The inclusion of video capabilities also opens the door for further developments in video summarization, event detection, and multimodal storytelling...

Recent findings suggest that with Visual Salamandra, the Language Technologies Lab demonstrates its ongoing leadership in creating inclusive, high-performing foundational models. By harmonizing state-of-the-art vision encoders with strong multilingual LLMs, the team is setting the stage for next-generation AI systems that see, understand, and communicate—across modalities and languages.

While Visual Salamandra demonstrates strong multimodal capabilities, it is notable to note its limitations:.

• It may hallucinate plausible but incorrect answers, especially when visual inputs are ambiguous.

• Performance on complex OCR and dense document layouts is still challenging.

• The model was trained with filtered and licensed datasets, but people should remain vigilant about potential biases or inaccuracies, particularly when deployed in sensitive applications.

We recommend using Visual Salamandra in contexts where human oversight is possible and avoiding high-stakes applications without proper evaluation.

Visual Salamandra is released under a Apache License, Version 2.0, allowing for research and non-commercial use.

Stay tunned for future releases and tools built on Visual Salamandra, and explore the full model details in our paper.

The Language Technologies Lab team.

💡 Key Takeaways
