According to recent reports, the re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a latest deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage firm (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

In a recent development, ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

According to recent reports, A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Recent findings suggest that online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Sources indicate that transfer real estate by recording new deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and upgrade both documents every 3-5 years.

Sources indicate that A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

Industry observers note that A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

According to recent reports, A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

A living trust is one of the most effective tools for protecting the wealth you have built on the path to financial independence. It avoids probate, provides incapacity protection, maintains complete privacy, and ensures your heirs receive assets quickly and efficiently. The key is actually funding the trust — transferring asset titles into it. For FI families with a net worth above $500K, the $1,500-$5,000 setup cost pays for itself many times over in avoided probate fees and time savings for your heirs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux.

Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop.

As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons.".

In a recent development, this impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well.

Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage, and X.

In a recent development, also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README states: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO.".

It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway.

Sources indicate that before any former Windows people cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us.

Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude.

We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32. The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps.

However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page shows a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps.

Sources indicate that loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant. We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page reveals updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September.

Finetuning olmOCR to be a faithful OCR-Engine

📅 22 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that recently, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence introduced olmOCR, a model that has demonstrated impressive results in converting PDFs into clean, linearized plain text while preserving structured content.
  • In this example, crucial information in the header and footer marked as red, is ignored by olmOCR.
  • Optical Character Recognition has broad applications in various business use cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that recently, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence introduced olmOCR, a model that has demonstrated impressive results in converting PDFs into clean, linearized plain text while preserving structured content. However, olmOCR's primary use case is to provide more training data for Large Language Models and therefore ignores extraneous information like headers and footers in documents. While this is beneficial for generating training data, it is insufficient for real business applications where crucial information often resides in the header and footer part of the text (think of invoices, for example). This article describes how we fine-tuned the original olmOCR-7B-0225-preview to be a faithful OCR engine, enabling it to support a broader range of applications.

In this example, crucial information in the header and footer marked as red, is ignored by olmOCR.

Optical Character Recognition has broad applications in various business use cases. For a long time, the predominant paradigm for AI-based OCR engines have been pipeline-based systems. These are comprised of multiple machine-learning components, e.g., section segmentation, table parsing, character recognition, etc., chained together. However, one fundamental flaw of this approach is that the extracted results mostly do not flatten the context in a way that adheres to logical reading order, also known as linearization. This is particularly challenging for layout-rich documents with floating elements like multi-column documents with floating diagrams, headers, footers, etc. With the recent advent of Vision Language Models, a lot of effort has been put into leveraging them as alternative OCR systems to tackle this problem.

It has been revealed that during our testing of the olmOCR model published on Hugging Face for business applications like invoice parsing, we observed a consistent omission of important information in the headers and footers. This was expected, as the dataset used to train olmOCR, olmOCR-mix-0225, intentionally excludes extraneous information in these areas to maintain a natural reading flow, as such information cannot be meaningfully predicted in the context of next-token prediction for training.

To address this limitation and enable comprehensive information extraction, we utilized Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct to generate a dataset of 8,000 documents that captures all relevant information, as one would expect from a reliable OCR engine. We based our training setup on the open-sourced olmOCR training pipeline, utilizing 4 gradient accumulation steps on an 8xH100 Nvidia node, for a total of 2.5 epochs. The default hyperparameters worked quite well for us, eliminating the need for resource-intensive hyperparameter search. The experiment tracking with MlLflow showed the following results:.

For evaluation, we utilized a customized version of the olmOCR-mix-0225 eval-datasets, which include header and footer information, also acquired with Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct.

Once the training was done, it was time to put our model to the test.

According to recent reports, we did a qualitative assessment of documents where crucial information was missing after parsing its content. Our inference setup is identical to the one by olmOCR, utilizing the special prompting strategy called document anchoring that preserves any born-digital content from each page. This technique extracts the raw tex blocks and position information to prompt VLMs alongside the rasterized image.

We provide several examples of the original response and the response of the fine-tuned model below. We marked crucial missing information in red.

Sources indicate that overall, we are happy with the results, as now all information, including extraneous data, will be extracted and the model is still able to parse simple tables. Notably, we noticed that for some examples, the quality of the resulting output can change significantly with different temperatures.

It has been revealed that OCR is crucial for extracting structured information from documents. The ability of end-to-end-systems like olmOCR to linearize content gives them a strong advantage over traditional systems. With our fine-tuned version, we can now faithfully extract text including header and footer sections from various documents, which is crucial for business use cases such as invoice parsing. We are curious about how future models will evolve in this fast-paced domain. Special thanks to the Allen Institute for AI for open-sourcing their model, dataset, and code.

If you're curious to try out our finetuned olmOCR-model, we have open-sourced it on HuggingFace.

Great article, thanks for sharing!

What made you choose the 8xH100 setup for finetuning and how was your experience with it?You did not mention how long training took, so I'm wondering if finetuning olmOCR actually requires that kind of hardware.

We chose the 8xH100 setup primarily for speed and convenience, since we had multiple experimental runs. Our final training run lasted 6 hours, so it was definitely overkill. But we rented the cluster via a cloud platform, which was a flexible, low-commitment choice; we could easily spin up/down instances as needed. Also, in terms of GPU memory, less would be definitely sufficient, probably two GPUs are already enough.

Latest Update: JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.
  • JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.
  • The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.

JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.

The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Like its predecessor, Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language, in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files.

The revised benchmark now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories.

The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request.

A 30-minute limit was set for each task.

Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60  percent on those based on closed source repositories.

Sources indicate that although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them.

Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks.

When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60  percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent.

Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however.

In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models.

Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials.

In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy.

(Kotlin consumers will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.).

One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate.

Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the glitch of integrity may go deeper.

"Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn.

Sources indicate that "On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp newly introduced hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at.".

It has been revealed that jetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also prepares to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana, against the results to check for errors.

Sireesha Pulipati, a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions.

"Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote.

So good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin owners some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®.

According to recent reports, upcoming! (May 23, '25) If you prefer Python, check out the companion post Tiny Agents in Python.

Over the past few weeks, I've been diving into MCP (Model Context Protocol) to understand what the hype around it was all about.

My TL;DR is that it's fairly simple, but still quite powerful: MCP is a standard API to expose sets of Tools that can be hooked to LLMs.

It is fairly simple to extend an Inference Client – at HF, we have two official client SDKs: @huggingface/inference in JS, and huggingface_hub in Python – to also act as a MCP client and hook the available tools from MCP servers into the LLM inference.

But while doing that, came my second realization:.

Once you have an MCP Client, an Agent is literally just a while loop on top of it.

In this short article, I will walk you through how I implemented it in Typescript (JS), how you can adopt MCP too and how it's going to make Agentic AI way simpler going forward.

If you have NodeJS (with pnpm or npm), just run this in a terminal:.

This installs my package into a temporary folder then executes its command.

You'll see your simple Agent connect to two distinct MCP servers (running locally), loading their tools, then prompting you for a conversation.

By default our example Agent connects to the following two MCP servers:.

Note: this is a bit counter-intuitive but currently, all MCP servers are actually local processes (though remote servers are coming soon).

The Tiny Agent code lives in the mcp-client sub-package of the huggingface.js mono-repo, which is the GitHub mono-repo in which all our JS libraries reside.

https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface.js/tree/main/packages/mcp-client.

The codebase uses modern JS features (notably, async generators) which make things way easier to implement, especially asynchronous events like the LLM responses. You might need to ask a LLM about those JS features if you're not yet familiar with them.

According to recent reports, what is going to make this whole blogpost very easy is that the recent crop of LLMs (both closed and open) have been trained for function calling, aka. tool use.

A tool is defined by its name, a description, and a JSONSchema representation of its parameters. In some sense, it is an opaque representation of any function's interface, as seen from the outside (meaning, the LLM does not care how the function is actually implemented).

The canonical documentation I will link to here is OpenAI's function calling doc. (Yes... OpenAI pretty much defines the LLM standards for the whole community 😅).

Sources indicate that inference engines let you pass a list of tools when calling the LLM, and the LLM is free to call zero, one or more of those tools. As a developer, you run the tools and feed their result back into the LLM to continue the generation.

Recent findings suggest that note that in the backend (at the inference engine level), the tools are simply passed to the model in a specially-formatted chat_template, like any other message, and then parsed out of the response (using model-specific special tokens) to expose them as tool calls. See an example in our chat-template playground.

Now that we know what a tool is in recent LLMs, let us implement the actual MCP client.

Industry observers note that the official doc at https://modelcontextprotocol.io/quickstart/client is fairly well-written. You only have to replace any mention of the Anthropic client SDK by any other OpenAI-compatible client SDK. (There is also a llms.txt you can feed into your LLM of choice to help you code along).

As a reminder, we use HF's InferenceClient for our inference client.

The complete McpClient.ts code file is here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓.

To connect to a MCP server, the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client TypeScript SDK provides a Client class with a listTools() method:.

StdioServerParameters is an interface from the MCP SDK that will let you easily spawn a local process: as we mentioned earlier, currently, all MCP servers are actually local processes.

For each MCP server we connect to, we slightly re-format its list of tools and add them to this.availableTools.

Easy, you just pass this.availableTools to your LLM chat-completion, in addition to your usual array of messages:.

tool_choice: "auto" is the parameter you pass for the LLM to generate zero, one, or multiple tool calls.

According to recent reports, when parsing or streaming the output, the LLM will generate some tool calls (i.e. a function name, and some JSON-encoded arguments), which you (as a developer) need to compute. The MCP client SDK once again makes that very easy; it has a client.callTool() method:.

Finally you will add the resulting tool message to your messages array and back into the LLM.

Recent findings suggest that now that we have an MCP client capable of connecting to arbitrary MCP servers to get lists of tools and capable of injecting them and parsing them from the LLM inference, well... what is an Agent?

Once you have an inference client with a set of tools, then an Agent is just a while loop on top of it.

It has been revealed that which is to say, we don't need to provide painstakingly formatted lists of tool use examples in the prompt. The tools: this.availableTools param is enough.

Loading the tools on the Agent is literally just connecting to the MCP servers we want (in parallel because it's so easy to do in JS):.

Update resolves work-blocking popup, but affected users may need an administrator command prompt to install it.

It has been revealed that microsoft has released a fix for a baffling bug that threw a blank window over Office applications and brought work to a standstill. The problem appeared when users launched an affected Office app, which could display an empty dialog box with no text and no buttons.

Because the dialog offered no way to close it, some customers were locked out of their work entirely, unable to continue until the glitch was resolved.

According to recent reports, the good news is that there's an update to fix the problem – version 2611, build 16.0.20625.20142. The bad news is that you might not be able to launch the applications to perform the update because of that blank dialog window.

Microsoft instructs affected users to save their work, close all Office applications, and open Command Prompt as administrator. They can then force the upgrade with: "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142.

The glitch affects a swathe of Microsoft 365 products – Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote.

Users reported the problem on Microsoft's forums, where volunteer moderator Stefan Blom noted that "this seems to be a common error at the moment" and suggested users try an Office repair or the more thorough Online Repair.

Online Repair reinstalls Office, however, some owners reported activation and sign-in problems alongside the blank windows, which may hint at the cause. Microsoft has yet to elucidate.

Other users found that rolling back Office resolved the issue, while several reported that signing in with another application, such as Edge, fixed things.

Recent findings suggest that for administrators preparing fleets of devices, a dialog that blocks first use creates another deployment headache. One user with E3 licensing reported: "We can't just hand off a staged machine without getting call[s] that our newly introduced users can't get Office to work because of the blank licensing window.".

Microsoft has shared a fix for the problem, but has not stated which versions of its productivity applications were affected, nor has it explained what went wrong.

It has been revealed that the fix is welcome. An explanation of how Office ended up blocking consumers with a window containing nothing at all would be welcome too. ®.

PipelineRL

📅 25 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection.
  • According to recent reports, in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm.
  • In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection. PipelineRL's key innovation is inflight weight updates during RL training (see Figure 1 below). This allows PipelineRL to achieve constantly high inference throughput and minimize the lag between the weights used for rollouts and the most recently updated model weights. The result: fast and stable RL training for large language models.

According to recent reports, in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm. We also present the modular PipelineRL architecture that facilitates trying new inference / trainer combinations.

In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection. To explain this trade-off let us first define conventional RL algorithmically:.

It has been revealed that to achieve high throughput, the inference servers must use large batch sizes and, therefore, generate data for multiple policy optimization steps. However, each optimization step increases the lag between the current policy and the data collected using the inference policy, progressively making collected data more off-policy and less effective for training. On-policy learning requires data for a single optimization step. But producing small amounts of data with many GPUs is inefficient because this means the per-GPU batch size is small. Furthermore the batch size goes down as the inference server finishes the short sequences and has only the few longest sequences in progress.

PipelineRL (Figure 1b) remediates this trade-off through inflight weight updates. We revision the weights in inference servers after each optimizer step without ever stopping inference. We only pause the inference at all inference servers for just the time needed to receive the upcoming weights. Inflight weight updates allow the inference server to constantly maintain the optimal batch size while simultaneously ensuring data remains on-policy or near on-policy, which leads to better GPU utilization and more effective learning, respectively.

Industry observers note that to demonstrate the effectiveness of PipelineRL and the benefits of inflight weight updates, we trained a 7B model and 32B model on the Open-Reasoner-Zero dataset. Looking at the learning curves we see that PipelineRL matches or exceeds the performance of Open-Reasoner on the popular reasoning test benchmarks: AIME 2024 and MATH 500 (see Figure 2 above).

Notably, our RL implementation is much simpler than Open-Reasoner-Zero. While Open-Reasoner-Zero uses a value function, our implementation is a simplified version of GRPO. In particular, we found that the trust region importance weight clamping is not needed for stable training. Neither was overlong sequence filtering or reward shaping from the DAPO paper. For normalizing the loss we just use the number of sequences in the batch as the denominator, giving equal weights to all tokens. We used no KL penalty and no entropy bonus (though our implementation does support reference model KL). Despite the simplicity of our implementation, or perhaps thanks to it, training is very stable as you can see in this wandb report.

In a recent development, one might expect that inflight weight updates would result in an unstable training process, since sequence generation proceeds with stale keys and values in the KV cache that was computed with a previous model version. However, our experiments indicate this does not adversely affect stability.

PipelineRL is built to be modular and take advantage of rapid improvements in highly-specialized inference and training software (SGLang, vLLM, Nvidia Dynamo, DeepSpeed, FSDP, TorchTitan, FastLLM, etc.). We propose clear contracts between the inference and training components, allowing easy integration of latest inference and training solutions as they become available.

The inference software must expose the following APIs to PipelineRL[1]:.

If init_process_group and request_weight_update APIs become the industry standard, one will be able to plug-and-play try using difference inference implementations with PipelineRL.

PipelineRL training code feeds freshly-generated training data to trainer workers as soon as the right number of training tokens has accumulated for each of them. One can make any training software that exposes these Python APIs work with PipelineRL:.

Recent findings suggest that pipelineRL at the moment uses the HuggingFace accelerate library to give the user a choice between DeepSpeed and FSDP. But we found that accelerate contract is too flexible and can be confusing. We will be moving to the stricter contract as described above that will make using other trainers easier.

Upcoming features. Our implementation is still experimental and lacks some important functionality. Top priorities for us include using coroutines for more precise inference batch size control, multi-modal support and sequence parallel training. We would also welcome contributions of more inference server and trainer integrations. We will not, however, try to make the pipeline-rl repo a framework that supports all possible algorithms and reward functions. Our take is that pipeline-rl should be a hackable and fast reference implementation of GRPO with easily verifiable rewards. If you'd like to do a research project using PipelineRL, you can just fork the repo and have fun hacking the code!

Recent findings suggest that more research coming soon. More analysis is needed to understand how inflight weight updates affect the training dynamics, and to carefully measure the speed-ups that PipelineRL brings. Also, much can be said about the similarities between PipelineRL and highly relevant prior work on asynchronous Reinforcement Learning for LLMs. For all this and more please stay tuned for our upcoming research paper!

Sources indicate that alexandre Piché wrote the first synchronous version of our RL code while working on TapeAgents. Dzmitry Bahdanau refactored the code to be asynchronous and distributed, and implemented inflight weight updates. Rafael Pardinas implemented sequence packing. Ehsan Kamaloo helped with running the experiments. Xiaoyin Chen helped with debugging the framework.

We acknowledge the prior RL for LLM implementations such as TRL, OpenRLHF and veRL for the many tricks we borrowed from them. Artifacts from other open-source reasoning projects, such as Simple-RL, Deepscaler, DAPO and OpenReasoner were instrumental for stabilizing PipelineRL. We would like to recognize Christopher Manning, Michael Noukhovitch for their thoughtful comments. Finally, we thank the broader ServiceNow Research team and ServiceNow CoreLLM teams for being amazing colleagues.

Introducing AutoRound: Intel’s Advanced Quantization for LLMs and VLMs

📅 29 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging.
  • Sources indicate that autoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel.
  • Recent findings suggest that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging. Quantization offers a solution by reducing model size and inference latency. Intel's AutoRound emerges as a cutting-edge quantization tool that balances accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility.

Sources indicate that autoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel. It uses signed gradient descent to jointly optimize weight rounding and clipping ranges, enabling accurate low-bit quantization (e.g., INT2 - INT8) with minimal accuracy loss in most scenarios. For example, at INT2, it outperforms popular baselines by up to 2.1x higher in relative accuracy. The image below provides an overview of the core algorithm in AutoRound. For more details, please refer to our paper.

Recent findings suggest that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode. It also supports mixed-bit tuning, lm-head quantization, GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF format exporting, and flexible tuning recipes.

AutoRound delivers highly promising results, particularly in low-bit quantization scenarios. Evaluations across a variety of tasks show that it outperforms popular methods by a wide margin at 2-bit precision (source). At 4 bits, AutoRound continues to hold a competitive edge in most cases, as demonstrated on the Low-Bit Open LLM Leaderboard.

Recent findings suggest that LLMs: AutoRound supports nearly all popular LLM architectures, including well-known models like Qwen, LLaMA, and DeepSeek. Ready-to-use quantized models are available on Hugging Face through collections such as OPEA, Kaitchup, and fbaldassarri.

Recent findings suggest that VLMs: AutoRound supports over 10 vision-language models (VLMs), including Mistral-Small-3.1, Gemma3, and more. You can find the full list in the README, and ready-to-use quantized models are available in the OPEA Hugging Face collection. For models not yet supported, you can still apply our RTN method with --iters 0. No tuning is required, but some accuracy loss is expected.

AutoRound requires only 200 tuning steps and a small calibration dataset (as few as 128 samples) to achieve high accuracy. This efficiency translates to faster quantization times and reduced resource consumption compared to other int2 methods, which are more computationally intensive.

Currently, only offline mode is supported to generate quantized models.

AutoRound also offers another two recipes, auto-round-best and auto-round-light, designed for optimal accuracy and improved speed, respectively.

Industry observers note that for 2 bits, we recommend using auto-round-best or auto-round. For a comparison of the three recipes, please refer to the table below.

W4G128 Average Accuracy of 13 tasks (mmlu-pro, if_eval, gsm8k, etc) and Time Cost Results (Testing was conducted on the Nvidia A100 80G using the version of PyTorch 2.6.0 with enable_torch_compile):.

This setting offers a better trade-off between accuracy and tuning cost, and is recommended in all scenarios.

For the best/light settings of AutoRound for API usage or mixed-bit configurations, please refer to AutoRound README.

Industry observers note that autoRound automatically selects the best available backend based on the installed libraries and prompts the user to install additional libraries when a better backend is found. For more details, please refer to HF README or AutoRound README.

Recent findings suggest that most GPTQ/AWQ models can be converted to the AutoRound format for better compatibility and support with Intel devices. Please note that the quantization config will be changed if the model is serialized.

AutoRound offers a meaningful improvement step forward in post-training quantization for large language and vision-language models. By combining high accuracy, exceptional efficiency, and broad compatibility with popular models, devices, and export formats, AutoRound makes low-bit quantization both practical and powerful. Whether you're deploying LLMs at scale or experimenting with edge inference on VLMs, AutoRound provides the tools and flexibility you need to achieve optimal performance with minimal overhead. We invite you to try it out and join the growing community pushing the boundaries of efficient AI deployment.

Contributions to AutoRound are welcome and greatly appreciated! Whether it's fixing bugs, improving documentation, adding fresh features, or suggesting improvements, your help is always valued.

If you encounter any challenges with auto-round, please open an concern on the AutoRound repository.

We would like to thank the open-source low-precision libraries including AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GPTQModel, Triton, Marlin and ExLLaMAV2, whose CUDA kernels are used in AutoRound.

Tech giant Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ sqrt(Headcount)

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lia

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture.
  • In a recent development, the results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page.
  • It has been revealed that there is a better way to measure culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.

In a recent development, the results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the firm calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.

It has been revealed that there is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.

Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of people. That’s it.

It has been revealed that the square root is key. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a organization of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.

We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.

Sources indicate that the Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.

Sources indicate that to account for this, we also measure the percentage of consumers who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).

It has been revealed that if P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.

Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.

For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:.

As with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.

It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.

If your tech giant uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.

If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.

In a recent development, culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: Today, Meta releases Llama Guard 4, a 12B dense (not a MoE!) multimodal safety model, and two fresh Llama Prompt Guard 2 models.
  • Recent findings suggest that vision and large language models deployed to production can be exploited to generate unsafe output through jail breaking image and text prompts.
  • Industry observers note that newly introduced safeguard models address this matter by evaluating image and text, and the content generated by the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: Today, Meta releases Llama Guard 4, a 12B dense (not a MoE!) multimodal safety model, and two fresh Llama Prompt Guard 2 models. This release comes with multiple open model checkpoints, along with an interactive notebook for you to get started easily 🤗. Model checkpoints can be found in Llama 4 Collection.

Recent findings suggest that vision and large language models deployed to production can be exploited to generate unsafe output through jail breaking image and text prompts. Unsafe content in production varies from being harmful or inappropriate to violating privacy or intellectual property.

Industry observers note that newly introduced safeguard models address this matter by evaluating image and text, and the content generated by the model. User messages classified as unsafe are not passed to vision and large language models, and unsafe assistant responses can be filtered out by production services.

Llama Guard 4 is a new multimodal model designed to detect inappropriate content in images and text, whether used as input or generated as output by the model. It’s a dense 12B model pruned from Llama 4 Scout model, and it can run on a single GPU (24 GB of VRAM). It can evaluate both text-only and image+text inputs, making it suitable for filtering both inputs and outputs of large language models. This enables flexible moderation pipelines where prompts are analyzed before reaching the model, and generated responses are reviewed afterwards for safety. It can also understand multiple languages.

The model can classify 14 types of hazard defined in the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, along with code interpreter abuse.

The list of categories detected by the model can be configured by the user on inference, as we’ll see later.

Recent findings suggest that llama Guard 4 employs a dense feedforward early-fusion architecture, in contrast to Llama 4 Scout, which uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers with one shared dense expert and sixteen routed experts per layer. To leverage Llama 4 Scout pre-training, the architecture is pruned into a dense model by removing all routed experts and router layers, retaining only the shared expert. This results in a dense feedforward model initialized from the pre-trained shared expert weights. No additional pre-training is applied to Llama Guard 4. The post-training data consists of multi-image training data up to 5 images and human-annotated multilingual data, previously used to train Llama Guard 3 models. The training data consists of 3:1 text-only to multimodal data.

Below you can find the performance of Llama Guard 4 compared against Llama Guard 3, the previous iteration of the safety model.

Industry observers note that the Llama Prompt Guard 2 series introduces two fresh classifiers with 86M and 22M parameters, focused on detecting prompt injections and jailbreaks. Compared to its predecessor, Llama Prompt Guard 1, this new version offers improved performance, a faster and more compact 22M model, tokenization resistant to adversarial attacks, and simplified binary classification (benign vs. malicious).

To use Llama Guard 4 and Prompt Guard 2, make sure you have hf_xet and the preview release of transformers for Llama Guard installed.

This works because the chat template generates a system prompt that does not mention the excluded categories as part of the list of categories to watch for.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.
  • According to recent reports, targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SR-1 Freedom gets a shorter boom and larger antennas, with roughly two years to finish design, construction, and testing.

NASA has settled key design choices for its planned nuclear-fission-powered spacecraft, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, following a mission review in October.

According to recent reports, targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit. It is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver a capsule carrying three helicopters to Mars.

There have been some changes since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman indicated off the concept [PDF] at the agency's Ignition event in March. Improved shielding and spacecraft design will allow a shorter boom between the reactor and the spacecraft's main body, protecting its electronics and the SkyFall payload. The shorter boom will, according to NASA, "reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.".

The revised design also includes larger X-band antenna dishes to transmit data to Earth.

Decisions are still pending on how many radiator panels the vehicle needs, the output power levels of the nuclear power module, and how long the reactor will operate.

It has been revealed that presently, the mission calls for the spacecraft to start its reactor once it has left Earth orbit and gradually ramp up power. After a period during which performance data will be sent back to Earth, the reactor will be shut down until after the SkyFall capsule, containing a trio of Mars Ingenuity-class helicopters, is delivered to Martian orbit.

Sources indicate that solar arrays will power the spacecraft during its cruise to Mars. The fission reactor will then be reactivated to let engineers collect more data on its performance in deep space.

NASA also awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the nuclear power module.

"Further maturation of the spacecraft aims will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule," the agency remarked.

Sources indicate that the latter part regarding the schedule is certainly a challenge. Meeting the late-2028 launch target leaves roughly two years to finish designing, building, and testing the spacecraft.

In a recent development, ESA is also targeting late 2028 for its long-delayed Rosalind Franklin rover. Missing the intended Mars departure opportunity could push SR-1 into a later launch window, although NASA has not specified a fallback schedule. ®.

The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

📅 21 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blainehansen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis.
  • Sources indicate that something has to change.
  • Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens latest window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Sources indicate that something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens fresh window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier noted than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens latest window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:.

Sources indicate that proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

According to recent reports, this is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a latest formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific initiative was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

Industry observers note that I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):.

Industry observers note that so now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:.

Recent findings suggest that this design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens fresh window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

According to recent reports, I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens latest window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

In a recent development, and you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens upcoming window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a boring Jinja snippet tells us about the new Qwen-3 model.

According to recent reports, the new Qwen-3 model by Qwen ships with a much more sophisticated chat template than its predecessors Qwen-2.5 and QwQ. By taking a look at the differences in the Jinja template, we can find interesting insights into the new model.

Recent findings suggest that A chat template defines how conversations between users and models are structured and formatted. The template acts as a translator, converting a human-readable conversation:.

You can easily view the chat template for a given model on the Hugging Face model page.

Chat Template for Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B.

Let's dive into the Qwen-3 chat template and see what we can learn!

and you can make it optional via a simple prefill...

Qwen-3 is unique in its ability to toggle reasoning via the enable_thinking flag. When set to false, the template inserts an empty pair, telling the model to skip step‑by‑step thoughts. Earlier models baked the tag into every generation, forcing chain‑of‑thought whether you wanted it or not.

QwQ for example, forces reasoning in every conversation.

If the enable_thinking is true, the model is able to decide whether to think or not.

You can test test out the template with the following code:.

In a recent development, qwen-3 utilizes a rolling checkpoint system, intelligently preserving or pruning reasoning blocks to maintain relevant context. Older models discarded reasoning prematurely to save tokens.

According to recent reports, qwen-3 introduces a "rolling checkpoint" by traversing the message list in reverse to find the latest user turn that wasn’t a tool call. For any assistant replies after that index it keeps the full blocks; everything earlier is stripped out.

Here's an example of chain-of-thought preservation through tool calls with Qwen-3 and QwQ.

Check out @huggingface/jinja for testing out the chat templates.

Before, every tool_call.arguments field was piped through | tojson, even if it was already a JSON‑encoded string—risking double‑escaping. Qwen‑3 checks the type first and only serializes when necessary.

Like many models, the Qwen‑2.5 series has a default system prompt.

In a recent development, you are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.

This is pretty common as it helps models respond to user questions like "Who are you?".

Qwen-3 and QwQ ship without this default system prompt. Despite this, the model can still accurately identify its creator if you ask it.

Sources indicate that qwen-3 shows us that through the chat_template we can provide better flexibility, smarter context handling, and improved tool interaction. These improvements not only improve capabilities, but also make agentic workflows more reliable and efficent.

Is there any explanation for why this template sometimes uses bra and ket symbols like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, but then other times uses XML notation like and instead of <|think_start|> and <|think_end|>?

It strikes me as being inconsistent.

Recent findings suggest that the identifiers using bra and ket symbols are tokens, i.e. they are actually recognised and converted to a single "special" token by the tokenizer. For example, <|im_end|> is used as the EOS_TOKEN. (And, as an aside, you need to know this if you want to try fine-tuning these Qwen models, because you need to explicitly set eos_token='<|im_end|>' in your fine-tuning configuration.).

According to recent reports, the XML-style identifiers are placeholders that define sections of the generated output. They are tokenized in the same manner as for any other text (i.e. they are probably converted to multiple tokens, but that depends on the vocabulary), they have no predetermined special meaning, and their use is learned by the model during training.

That stated, the specific placeholders and are pretty standard across reasoning models.

#173687. AI made self-hosting fun again

AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Janlukas ↗ Open Full Page

AI made self-hosting fun again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 155 min read (31028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Janlukas

⏱️ ~155 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been self-hosting things for many years.
  • In a recent development, I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with fresh things.
  • Sources indicate that over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out upcoming software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.
