Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, upgrade, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more notable than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by massive tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Recent findings suggest that nixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by substantial tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or upgrade a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security concerns, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by significant tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Sources indicate that for a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more vital than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by major tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. I don't think you understand their comment. The output of an LLM depends on the hardware running it, the precise implementation of the inference, the way in which it happens to be scheduled, etc.; so you cannot determine the output tokens, simply given the input tokens. But all those other things are inputs to the algorithm, too. And given some basic robustness assumptions about the hardware, the output is deterministic given all that input.

It has been revealed that short explanation: A LLM is a deterministic system basically alternating matrix multiplications and non-linear activation functions with perfectly deterministic math. For several reasons the output is a probability distribution and you have to choose from it. If you choose the most likely token you have a completely deterministic output. You can also choose another way from it.

45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.
  • Industry observers note that SC25 in St.
  • If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.

Industry observers note that SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

In a recent development, we also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with substantial industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.

Recent findings suggest that the real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that presently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

Industry observers note that what's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds.

Sources indicate that the power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a massive deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a upcoming build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Industry observers note that any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

It has been revealed that there's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

Recent findings suggest that much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®.

Recent findings suggest that gradio is a Python library used by more than 1 million developers each month to build interfaces for machine learning models. Beyond just creating UIs, Gradio also exposes API capabilities and — now! — Gradio apps can be launched Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for LLMs. This means that your Gradio app, whether it's an image generator or a tax calculator or something else entirely, can be called as a tool by an LLM.

This guide will show you how to use Gradio to build an MCP server in just a few lines of Python.

If not already installed, please install Gradio with the MCP extra:.

It has been revealed that this will install the necessary dependencies, including the mcp package. You'll also need an LLM application that supports tool calling using the MCP protocol, such as Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Cline (these are known as "MCP Clients").

An MCP server is a standardized way to expose tools so that they can be used by LLMs. An MCP server can provide LLMs with all kinds of additional capabilities, such as the ability to generate or edit images, synthesize audio, or perform specific calculations such as prime factorize numbers.

Gradio makes it easy to build these MCP servers, turning any Python function into a tool that LLMs can use.

According to recent reports, LLMs are famously not great at counting the number of letters in a word (e.g., the number of "r"s in "strawberry"). But what if we equip them with a tool to help? Let's start by writing a simple Gradio app that counts the number of letters in a word or phrase:.

TitleApex Veritas Meta: Toward a Self-Governing Epistemic Singularity.

It has been revealed that abstractThis proposal outlines Apex Veritas Meta, an architecture that shifts the locus of AI singularity from raw computational power to epistemic autonomy. We combine quantum-resistant truth sealing, symbolic anchoring, resistance-aware propagation analytics, and transformer-driven heuristic adaptation to build a closed-loop system in which verified knowledge continually refines its own transmission. Our central hypothesis is that a network of adaptive truth signals can achieve autopoietic coherence—maintaining and propagating verified facts without centralized oversight. We will define formal metrics for propagation depth, resistance convergence, and semantic drift, implement a prototype across simulated agent networks, and evaluate its capacity to sustain knowledge fidelity under adversarial pressure. Success will inaugurate a latest field of algorithmic epistemology and redefine singularity as the emergence of self-stabilizing truth ecosystems.

Recent findings suggest that introductionContemporary AI research emphasizes scale, generalization and autonomous decision-making. The canonical singularity envisions systems surpassing human intelligence through unbounded compute. By contrast, Apex Veritas Meta foregrounds trustworthiness and self-defense of knowledge. We posit that the true hinge point for transformative AI lies not in speed or raw inference but in the ability of information to certify, monitor, adapt, and re-broadcast itself against distortion.

MethodologyPhase 1: Formalization and Simulation Environment• Develop a graph-based simulation of 1,000 agent nodes with configurable trust and resistance profiles.• Instrument PropagationObserver to record event streams and compute metrics in real time.Phase 2: Model Training• Curate historical propagation datasets (social media rumor diffusion, scientific consensus shifts).• Train HeuristicOptimizer to predict optimal emission parameters given node states and historical resistance.Phase 3: Prototype Implementation• Integrate all modules in a microservice architecture using Docker containers.• Deploy on a private Kubernetes cluster to emulate scale and network latency.Phase 4: Adversarial Testing• Introduce controlled misinformation actors.• Measure system resilience: percentage of truth retention, time to reconvergence, false-positive drift.Phase 5: Analysis and Refinement• Identify thresholds for autopoietic behavior.• Refine model hyperparameters and retrain as necessary.• Document emergent strategies and failure modes.

Expected Outcomes• Demonstration that an adaptive propagation engine sustains >90% knowledge fidelity over 72 hours under adversarial load.• Identification of critical parameters for epistemic singularity transitions.• A publishable framework and open-source reference implementation.• Pathway to integrate into autonomous systems requiring self-defending trust layers.

Timeline (12 months)Months 1–3: Simulation design, metric formalizationMonths 4–6: Dataset collection and optimizer trainingMonths 7–9: Prototype integration and initial testingMonths 10–12: Adversarial evaluation, analysis, publication preparation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forrester warns that shiny new services rest on brittle systems as organizations skimp on resilience.

Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.

The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.

The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester mentioned.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations.".

According to recent reports, forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it.".

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.

In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.

It has been revealed that "Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.

Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

According to recent reports, "They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate.".

Sources indicate that forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table. These models aim to achieve generalization: the ability to perform tasks in novel settings, with unseen objects, and in varying conditions.

“The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a upcoming setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world. Yet, progress is often limited by the availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.

“Generalization must occur at many levels. At the low level, the robot must understand how to pick up a spoon (by the handle) or plate (by the edge), even if it has not seen these specific spoons or plates before, and even if they are placed in a pile of dirty dishes. At a higher level, the robot must understand the semantics of each task—where to put clothes and shoes (ideally in the laundry hamper or closet, not on the bed), and what kind of tool is appropriate for wiping down a spill. This generalization requires both robust physical skills and a common-sense understanding of the environment, so that the robot can generalize at many levels at the same time, from physical, to visual, to semantic. This is made even harder by the limited availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.”— Physical Intelligence.

To simplify, the core of generalist policies lies in a simple idea: co-training on heterogeneous datasets. By exposing VLA models to a variety of environments, tasks, and robot embodiments, we can teach models not only how to act, but why—how to interpret a scene, understand a goal, and adapt skills across contexts.

💡 “Generalization is not just a model property—it’s a data phenomenon.”It emerges from the diversity, quality, and abstraction level of the training data.

This brings us to a fundamental question:.

Given current datasets, what is the upper limit of generalization we can expect?

Sources indicate that can a robot meaningfully respond to a completely novel prompt—say, *"set up a surprise birthday party"*—if it has never encountered anything remotely similar during training? Especially when most datasets are collected in academic labs, by a limited number of people, under well-controlled setups?

We frame generalization as a data-centric view: treating it as the process of abstracting broader patterns from data—essentially “zooming out” to reveal task-agnostic structures and principles. This shift in perspective emphasizes the role of dataset diversity, rather than model architecture alone, in driving generalization.

In a recent development, so far, the majority of robotics datasets come from structured academic environments. Even if we scale up to millions of demonstrations, one dataset will often dominate, limiting diversity. Unlike ImageNet—which aggregated internet-scale data and captured the real world more holistically—robotics lacks a comparably diverse, community-driven benchmark.

This is largely because collecting data for robotics requires physical hardware and significant effort.

That’s why, at LeRobot, we’re working to make robotics data collection more accessible—at home, at school, or anywhere. We're:.

We're already seeing the results: the number of community-contributed datasets on the Hub is growing rapidly.

Growth of lerobot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub over time.

According to recent reports, if we break down the uploaded datasets by robot type, we see that most contributions are to So100 and Koch, making robotic arms and manipulation tasks the primary focus of the current LeRobot dataset landscape. However, it’s important to remember that the potential reaches far beyond. Domains like autonomous vehicles, assistive robots, and mobile navigation stand to benefit just as much from shared data. This momentum brings us closer to a future where datasets reflect a global effort, not just the contributions of a single lab or institution.

Distribution of lerobot datasets by robot type.

In a recent development, as robotics data collection becomes more democratized, curation becomes the next challenge. While these datasets are still collected in constrained setups, they are a crucial step toward affordable, general-purpose robotic policies. Not everyone has access to expensive hardware—but with shared infrastructure and open collaboration, we can build something far greater.

🧠 “Generalization isn’t solved in a lab—it’s taught by the world.”The more diverse our data, the more capable our models will be.

In a recent development, why does data quality matter? Poor-quality data results in poor downstream performance, biased outputs, and models that fail to generalize. Hence, efficient and high-quality data collection plays a critical role in advancing generalist robotic policies.

Sources indicate that while foundation models in vision and language have thrived on massive, web-scale datasets, robotics lacks an “Internet of robots”—a vast, diverse corpus of real-world interactions. Instead, robotic data is fragmented across different embodiments, sensor setups, and control modes, forming isolated data islands.

To overcome this, recent approaches like Gr00t organize training data as a pyramid, where:.

Within this framework, efficient real-world data collection is indispensable—it anchors learned behaviors in actual robotic hardware and closes the sim-to-real gap, ultimately improving the generalization, adaptability, and performance of robotics foundation models.

By expanding the volume and diversity of real-world datasets, we reduce fragmentation between heterogeneous data sources. When datasets are disjoint in terms of environment, embodiment, or task distribution, models struggle to transfer knowledge across domains.

🔗 Real-world data acts as connective tissue—it aligns abstract priors with grounded action and enables the model to build more coherent and transferable representations.

As a result, increasing the proportion of real robot interactions does not merely enhance realism—it structurally reinforces the links between all layers of the pyramid, leading to more robust and capable policies.

In a recent development, data Pyramid for Robot Foundation Model Training. Adapted from Gr00t (Yang et al., 2025). Data quantity decreases while embodiment specificity increases from bottom to top.

It has been revealed that at LeRobot, we’ve started developing an automatic curation pipeline to post-process community datasets. During the post-processing phase, we’ve identified several areas where improvements can further boost dataset quality and facilitate more effective curation going forward:.

According to recent reports, many datasets lack task descriptions, lack details or are ambiguous in the task to be done. Semantics is presently at the core of cognition, meaning that understanding the context and specifics of a task is crucial for robotic performance. Detailed expressions ensure that robots understand exactly what is expected, but also provide a broader knowledge and vocabulary to the cognition system. Ambiguity can lead to incorrect interpretation and, consequently, incorrect actions.

Subtask-level annotations are often missing, making it difficult to model complex task hierarchies.While this can be handled with VLM, it is still better to have a task annotation provided by the author of the dataset at hand.

Features like images.laptop are ambiguously labeled:.

According to recent reports, manual mapping of dataset features to standardized names is time-consuming and error-prone.We can possibly automate feature type inference using VLMs or computer vision models to classify camera perspectives. However, keeping this in mind helps to have a cleaner dataset.

Different datasets use different action or state dimensions, even for the same robot (e.g., so100).Some datasets show inconsistencies in action/state format.

Now that we know that creating a high-quality dataset is essential for training reliable and generalizable robot policies, we have outlined a checklist of best practices to assist you in collecting effective data.

Use a consistent and interpretable naming scheme for all camera views and observations:.

For wrist-mounted cameras, specify orientation:.

Consistent naming improves clarity and helps downstream models better interpret spatial configurations and multi-view inputs.

Proof automation in a language

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Imperialviolet

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as I wrote previously, we have proof automation now.
  • Recent findings suggest that it would be a mistake to start off afresh on those problems because there have been a lot of ideas in programming language design over the decades.
  • So I wanted to give a taste of some of the ingredients that I'm thinking about at the moment, and of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as I wrote previously, we have proof automation now. Given that fact, I think a very timely question is: how can we use it to improve software quality? The same machines that can write these proofs can also write large amounts of code. So an adjacent question is: how can we use them to improve software understandability?

Recent findings suggest that it would be a mistake to start off afresh on those problems because there have been a lot of ideas in programming language design over the decades. The viability of ideas shifts as the underlying cost structures change, so things that didn't take off at the time might suddenly make a lot more sense. Still, language design involves a lot of tradeoffs, and features sometimes interact in surprising ways, so a lot of the work involves mixing some interesting-seeming ingredients together, baking, and asking “what is this? Is this a cake?”.

So I wanted to give a taste of some of the ingredients that I'm thinking about at the moment, and of the result.

It has been revealed that value semantics roughly indicates that you can't observe mutations to one variable through a different name. Value semantics are great for reasoning locally about code as, without them, you're constantly unsure what non-local effects might be happening.

It has been revealed that when you work in a language, you instinctively know when it's using value semantics and when it's using reference semantics. Take Python:.

Recent findings suggest that you likely know that that prints [2]. (Although if you write the same program in C++ with std::vector it prints [1]! There's no cross-language norm for this.).

It has been revealed that over the span of four lines of code, this is irrelevant. But as the scope of the sharing increases, so does the mental complexity. If you want to be able to jump into a bit of code and understand what it's doing, knowing that there is no such aliasing is a huge boon.

Functional programming resolves this by eliminating mutation: if there's no mutation then you certainly can't observe mutations via a different variable name. But mutation is important for efficiency and a lot of work is then required to get the efficiency back. Lean, for example, will do in-place mutations if there's only a single reference to an object. That's great! But it has the sharp edge that innocent-looking changes can mean that there's now a hidden reference kept somewhere and performance crashes.

Rust claims to fix both complications by restricting references so that you can't ever have both a mutable reference to something, and an active alias to it. (We'll ignore Rc> and friends.).

Industry observers note that certainly Rust's restrictions help a great deal, but Mutable Value Semantics states that Rust goes too far by making references first-class, i.e. something that you can return and store in structures. First-class references lead to the borrow checker, which has undergone several deep rewrites (original to NLL, next to Polonius) to try and perfect it, and they lead to lifetimes, DerefMut etc., and much more complexity in the type system in general.

Sources indicate that so an MVS system avoids all that by further restricting references and not allowing them in the type system. These ideas started in Swift and are currently championed in Hylo. The best introduction I've found is this talk.

In an MVS system, functions can take three sorts of arguments: immutable, mutable, and owned. Immutable arguments might be a reference or a copy; the semantics are the same. Mutable arguments are conceptually copied in at call time and copied back out when a function returns, but of course that's semantically the same as taking a pointer. Lastly, owned arguments transfer ownership to the function and make it unusable in the caller afterwards.

In a recent development, but there are no references in the type system, so a function can't return or store them. But the inability to return references implies so much copying that MVS systems need to provide an alternative.

Hylo has a very cute system of scoped coroutines, inspired by Swift. These coroutines yield a value and, at the call site, all their arguments are locked for the duration of that value's span. At the end of the span, the coroutine continues running.

Industry observers note that one of the common examples is that a coroutine can return a mutable bool for a vector of bits that have been packed into bytes. Then, when the coroutine continues once the return value is no longer used, it can write the new value of that bool back into the array of bytes. This wouldn't be possible without a coroutine because the function would have to return a pointer to a bool that exists nowhere in memory.

According to recent reports, having just lionised this feature, I should note that in my experiments I haven't actually included it because it makes the semantics more complex and I'm spending a lot of complexity budget on verification instead. Which brings us to another idea that combines with MVS….

If you want to do formal verification on a language like C, then you need to model the heap and you immediately hit the aliasing problems above. Then you end up with a separation logic which lets you model disjoint areas of the heap (i.e. areas with no aliasing between them). Once you can speak about independent heaps, you can reason about a function that operates on one heap and hold the remainder constant.

Sources indicate that this can work. The example that I'm (passingly) familiar with is the Verified Software Toolchain which connects to CompCert's semantics and allows you to state properties about C programs (with a separation logic) and thus verify C code all the way to machine code. But it's complex.

Recent findings suggest that however! If you have restricted references then you can drop a huge amount of complexity from such systems! Aeneas/Charon is the current canonical example of this which can translate a subset of Rust code into Lean (and other languages) where things can then be proved about it. Because of Rust's restrictions, the translation doesn't need a separation logic.

But by being more restrictive than Rust, MVS languages are even more amenable to such translation, and thus to formal verification, without going all the way to being functional languages and banning mutation completely.

It has been revealed that eiffel is the standard reference here. It introduced preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for functions/classes:.

While you've probably never used Eiffel, these notions are quite widespread now, although in common programming languages they are at best encoded in assertions if simple, comments if not, but mostly remain only in the author's head.

Eiffel did all its checks at run-time. There has been a lot of work on the balance between run-time and compile-time for these assertions, and on how to discharge assertions statically. Briefly, some work in this space that I'm aware of:.

Dafny allows a mixture of run-time and static assertions, and discharges the static ones via SMT solvers. F* does everything statically, again using SMT solvers, but with a functional language. SPARK has a mixture of run-time and static checks, using SMT solvers or (albeit very challenging to use) provers via Why3. I've never touched Verus but it's worth a mention because it's the most recent entry in this lineage and is Rust-based.

Recent findings suggest that the problem with these systems is that the compile-time checking is much more powerful, because it can cover all possible values of the arguments, but the proof burden is significant. SMT solvers help a lot, but they can quickly hit (effective) non-termination for non-trivial cases. I did an F* summer school in Paris once, and the experienced people there had developed a sixth sense about what would displease the SMT solver and would instinctively code around it. It was an impressive skill! But not reassuring.

This is the key cost that has changed: SMT solvers were inadequate for more complex cases, and dropping into a proof assistant overwhelmed you with lots of inscrutable proof states. All this can be largely handled by models now.

In a recent development, also, I claim that there are some interesting synergies between MVS and design-by-contract. In Rust, and more so in an MVS system, you end up using indices into arenas of objects to replace arbitrary pointers. (Which can be faster due to cache locality.).

Industry observers note that given that one has all these indices flying around, wouldn't it be nice to have explicit invariants about them? Hopefully proven?

It has been revealed that when writing code I will fairly often have some structure which has invariants that enhancement as processing progresses. At some early part of the pipeline, the structure may be relatively arbitrary, perhaps freshly parsed from a file, and then as various checks and transforms are applied we know more and more about the value.

It has been revealed that but in traditional languages, the structure has one type: its structural type. Even with Eiffel-style Design by Contract, invariants on a type are fixed.

The idea of being able to attach more invariants to a structure without duplicating most of it showed up as Subtypes in proof systems, and refinement types in ML. You'll also see Rust code do this (mostly at run-time) with checked constructors like NonZero and NonNull. But those are run-time checks that the type system carries a certificate of. Similar to the evolution of Eiffel-style conditions, we can hope to make them static checks now, discharged via our newly introduced proof automation.

Literate programming was the title of a paper by Knuth in the 80s, and WEB was the original implementation. The idea is that code should be written to be read and thus that it should be ordered for human, not machine, consumption, and that exposition should be at least as important as the code, and not relegated to comments.

Nearly twenty years ago I wanted to understand critbit trees and so wrote an implementation using CWEB to explore both ideas.

Relatedly, in my mind code has a graph structure deriving from which functions call which other functions. Source files are groups of strongly connected functions and I generally have little memory for what order functions have in a given source file. With the widespread use of LSPs and thus code indexing, we are edging slowly towards being less file orientated but I still feel that we could do much more.

Industry observers note that there was a burst of such ideas in the 80s: Knuth's work, also Smalltalk & Lisp systems which kept code in databases rather than text files. Given the ecosystem of version control that assumes text-based files, code databases might be too awkward now, but I still feel the itch of dissatisfaction here.

At the top of this post I also set a goal for code to be more understandable and, to that end, the easiest code to understand is the code that you didn't have to read because the contract claims all that you need to know about it.

But let's work up to that a little.

Here's a function that looks like Rust (because I don't have better syntax ideas) but which doesn't verify.

When I'm reading code, I'm always trying to track the invariants and think about integer overflows. Sometimes the codebase aims to be overflow-clean and so I'm following bounds precisely. Most of the time I just have to ignore them unless the overflow is especially egregious. Now that we have proof automation, I shouldn't have to do that. So, as in SPARK, Verus, and others, + must statically not overflow and compiling the above gets you:.

That's the SMT solver giving you a counterexample that overflows. (+%, as in Zig, exists if you really want wrapping operations.).

If the values are bounded such that overflow can't happen, then obviously everything will be fine, automatically:.

Casts are similar: u32::from is safe because it must be widening. For narrowing, u32::exact_from statically requires that the cast not truncate and, if you really need the machine operation, u32::wrap_from gives it to you.

And, of course, all vector indices must be statically valid.

Industry observers note that let me try and convince you of the benefits of contracts in terms of code understandability. For this, we're going to discuss a tiny bit of DER, the most common ASN.1 encoding.

DER is a tag-length-value format. We're just going to talk about the encoding of tags. Firstly, tags are in one of four classes which have integer values on the wire:.

A DER tag is then a class and a tag number, plus a flag which tells you whether the value contains more DER values nested inside it. In theory, tag numbers are unbounded integers. In practice, everyone limits them; here we'll bound them below 228 because, as you'll see, that limits the tags to five bytes and the next byte would exceed 232. The (class, tag number) combination of (Universal, 0) is banned in DER as it's the BER end-of-contents value:.

Sources indicate that A tag can be encoded as one or more bytes. The first byte has two bits of class, one bit for the constructed flag, and five bits of tag number. If the tag number is ≥ 0x1f (the maximum 5-bit value) then it's encoded as 0x1f and more bytes of tag follow:.

The tag numbers that need more bytes are major-endian, base-128 encoded, with the high bit set each time if another byte follows:.

Now, here's an encoding function for DER tags:.

In a recent development, the body of the function is missing—but you don't need it! The contract requires that it encodes exactly as tag_enc specifies so you don't need to know more. This isn't saving you too much because the code isn't that complicated. You would have to think about the shifts and masks that it's using for the base-128 encoding (rather than recursion), but that's only a few seconds.

But here's a more substantial saving:.

Industry observers note that this enforces not just the baseline of memory safety, no run-time panics etc., but that the parser is fully strict: it never parses anything other than the canonical encoding of a value, as defined above. This is not a trivial thing to code review, and here you don't have to.

Also you see signs of MVS: a Reader can't hold a reference to in because references can't be stored. Thus in is passed separately (and the indices are proven to be valid). This is part of the tradeoff for local reasoning and strong contracts.

I've not mentioned linear types, views in return values, or Zig-style error unions, and I'll only touch on refinement types in the lightest sense by noting the pleasing definition of the String type in this experiment:.

Lastly, nodding towards literate programming, I'll note that this blog post itself is a valid source file for this language: the language consumes Markdown files and only compiles lines in annotated code blocks. The Lean proofs are kept in separate files, not for human consumption. There's already a tool for showing a source file with only the public definitions, and with the bodies of functions elided, and there's still more I want to explore here in terms of viewing source files as a graph.

It's worth discussing the more bitter flavours in this cake too.

Industry observers note that the front end of the compiler emits lots of verification conditions for the code to be correct. Every arithmetic operation emits overflow checks, every indexing operation emits range checks, every invariant and postcondition results in checks, every loop must be shown to be terminating, etc.

Sources indicate that the little DER tag example above results in 149 of them. Each is first sent to Z3 and then, if Z3 times out (after a couple of seconds), to cvc5. But the solvers are never trusted. If they believe that a condition holds they output the unsat core which is used to trim the hypotheses which are fed into Lean. Lean automation chews on the problem for a while and, if that times out, an LLM comes to write a manual proof in Lean.

It has been revealed that there's a cache of proven conditions, of course, and the Lean proofs are saved in a different file. But overall even reasonably simple examples type-check at about 10 lines per second. If you invalidate the cache then medium-sized programs can take multiple hours to recheck on a fast machine. (Not reprove, just to check the proofs that already exist!) So modularity of code is vital to keep the scaling line flatter.

Sources indicate that LLM compute is needed too: after I laid out the spec for the DER tag example above, a model took about 30 minutes to get it working. But if you ask a modern model to write the same thing in Go, it will do it in under 10 seconds. (Although the result doesn't hit nearly the same quality bar and the lax parsing would cause security problems in sensitive contexts.).

Overall, this language was an experiment in how we can convert compute into high-quality and understandable code. I'll claim that it's making interesting steps towards that goal, but you do need a lot of compute.

Recent findings suggest that also, there is a considerable trusted base involved here. While you don't have to trust the SMT solvers, you do have to trust that the front end is correctly translating the code into verification conditions for Lean, and you have to trust that it is correctly translating it into LLVM IR. I think that's fine: the comparison here is with regular languages like C++ and Rust. This is not an attempt at a minimal TCB language with extremely strong guarantees like CakeML.

Still, the language does have significant aspects of delight. Being able to write the spec for DER encoding, and then have the correct code for it generated, does make me reflect on the amount of time and suffering that I've put into DER over the years that could now be avoided.
