Vision Language Models (Better, faster, stronger)

📅 12 May 2025 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town.
  • According to recent reports, since then, so much has changed.
  • According to recent reports, in this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town. In a previous blog post (from April 2024), we talked a lot about VLMs. A major chunk was about LLaVA, the first successful and easily reproducible open-source vision language model, along with tips on how to discover, evaluate, and fine-tune open models.

According to recent reports, since then, so much has changed. Models have become smaller yet more powerful. We've seen the rise of fresh architectures and capabilities (reasoning, agency, long video understanding, etc.). In parallel, entirely new paradigms, such as multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and multimodal agents have taken shape.

According to recent reports, in this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year. You’ll discover key changes, emerging trends, and notable developments.

We highly recommend reading the first blog post if you want a good primer on how vision language models work.

In this section, we will look at the new types of VLMs. While some are absolutely new, others are improved versions of previous research.

Any-to-any models, as the name suggests, are models that can take in any modality and output any modality (image, text, audio). They do it by aligning the modalities, where an input from one modality can be translated to another (e.g. the word “dog” would be associated with an image of a dog, or with the utterance of the word).

These models have multiple encoders (one for each modality) and then fuse the embeddings together to create a shared representation space. The decoders (multiple or single) use the shared latent space as input and decode into the modality of choice. Earliest attempt to build any-to-any models is Chameleon by Meta, which can take in image and text and output image and text. Meta didn’t release the image generation capability in this model, so Alpha-VLLM released Lumina-mGPT, which has built image generation on top of Chameleon.

The latest and most capable any-to-any model, Qwen 2.5 Omni (figure below) is a good example to understand the architecture of an any-to-any model.

Qwen2.5-Omni employs a novel "Thinker-Talker" architecture, where the "Thinker" handles text generation, and the "Talker" produces natural speech responses in a streaming manner. MiniCPM-o 2.6, an 8B parameter multimodal model is capable of understanding and generating content across vision, speech, and language modalities. Janus-Pro-7B, introduced by DeepSeek AI, is a unified multimodal model that excels in both understanding and generating content across modalities. It features a decoupled visual encoding architecture, separating the processes for understanding and generation.

We suspect an uptick in the number of such models in the coming years. It is a well-known intuition that multimodal learning is the only way we can learn deep representations better. We have curated some any-to-any models and demos in this collection.

Recent findings suggest that reasoning models are models that can solve complex problems. We saw them first with large language models, and now vision language models. Until 2025, there was only one open-source multimodal reasoning model, QVQ-72B-preview by Qwen. It was an experimental model that was developed by the Alibaba Qwen team and came with many disclaimers.

It has been revealed that this year there’s another player, Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking by the Moonshot AI team. It consists of MoonViT (SigLIP-so-400M) as the image encoder and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder with 16B total parameters and only 2.8B active parameters. The model is a long chain-of-thought fine-tuned and further aligned (reinforcement learning) version of the Kimi-VL base vision language model. You can try the model here.

The authors also released an instruction fine-tuned version called Kimi-VL-A3B-Instruct.

The model can take in long videos, PDFs, screenshots and more. It has agentic capabilities as well.

It has been revealed that the community used to scale intelligence through the number of parameters, and then high-quality synthetic data. After a certain point, the benchmarks saturated and scaling models had diminishing returns. The community went to shrink larger models through various methods, like distillation. This makes sense because it reduces compute costs, simplifies deployment, and unlocks use cases like local execution, enhancing data privacy.

When we say small vision language models we often refer to models with less than 2B parameters that can be run on consumer GPUs. SmolVLM is a good example model family for smaller vision language models. Instead of shrinking larger models, the authors went all the way and tried to fit models into tiny number of parameters like 256M, 500M and 2.2B. SmolVLM2, for instance, attempted to solve video understanding in these sizes and found 500M to be a good trade-off. At Hugging Face, we have built an iPhone application, HuggingSnap, to demonstrate that these model sizes can achieve video understanding on consumer devices.

Sources indicate that another striking model is gemma3-4b-it by Google DeepMind. It’s particularly exciting as it’s one of the smallest multimodal models to have 128k token context window, and supports 140+ languages. The model comes with the Gemma 3 family of models, with its largest model ranking first on Chatbot Arena at the time. The largest model was then distilled to a 1B variant.

In a recent development, lastly, although not the smallest, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct is worth noting. The model can do various tasks ranging from localization (object detection and pointing), to document understanding, to agentic tasks; with context length up to 32k tokens.

According to recent reports, you can use small models through MLX and Llama.cpp integrations. For MLX, assuming you have it installed, you can get started with SmolVLM-500M-Instruct with this one liner:.

You can get started with using gemma-3-4b-it model in GGUF format with llama.cpp through CLI with this one-liner:.

You can also serve the same model as follows.

We would like to give a shoutout to moondream2 and Florence-2 as they're the earliest attempts for smallest vision language models. In this blog, we are covering primarily newer models (mostly models that came out after April 2024).

Mixture of Expert (MoEs) models offer an alternative to dense architectures by dynamically selecting and activating only the most relevant sub-models, termed "experts", to process a given input data segment. This selective activation (done by a router) mechanism has demonstrated the potential to substantially enhance model performance and operational efficiency while utilizing fewer computational resources.

According to recent reports, moEs are faster at inference than their similar parameter-dense counterparts because of the selective activation of a smaller slice of the network. They also converge swiftly during training. Every good thing comes with a cost, as MoEs need more memory cost due to the entire model being on the GPU, even if a smaller chunk is used.

In the widely adopted Transformer architecture, MoE layers are most commonly integrated by replacing the standard Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers within each Transformer block. Dense networks use the entire model to run an inference, while similarly sized MoE networks selectively activate some experts. This helps in better compute utilization and faster inference.

Industry observers note that vision language models that have mixture-of-experts decoders seem to have enhanced performance. For instance, Kimi-VL as of now is the most advanced open reasoning model that has a mixture-of-experts decoder. Mixture-of-Experts show promising results with MoE-LLaVA's focus on efficiency and hallucination reduction and DeepSeek-VL2's broad multimodal capabilities too. The latest version of Llama (Llama 4) is an MoE with vision capabilities. MoE as a decoder is a promising research area, and we suspect an increase in models like these.

To get a nice understanding of MoEs we recommend reading this fantastic article.

Industry observers note that VLMs are even making their mark in the field of robotics! There, they are known as Vision-language-action models (VLA). But don't be fooled, those are mainly VLMs with a little moustache and hat. VLAs take images and text instructions, and return text indicating actions for the robot to take directly. VLAs extend vision language models by adding action and state tokens to interact with and control physical environments. These extra tokens represent the system’s internal state (how it perceives the environment), actions (what it does based on commands), and time-related information (like the order of steps in a task). These tokens are appended to the vision language input to generate actions or policy.

VLAs are usually fine-tuned on top of a base VLM. Some people extend this definition further and define VLAs as any model interacting visually with a real or digital world. In this definition, VLAs can do UI navigation or be used in agentic workflows. But many people believe those applications fall in the VLM domain.

Great examples of VLAs are π0 and π0-FAST, the first robotics foundation models by Physical Intelligence, ported to Hugging Face’s LeRobot library. These models are trained across 7 robotics platforms and 68 unique tasks. They show strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance on complex, real-world activities such as laundry folding, table bussing, grocery bagging, box assembly, and object retrieval.

According to recent reports, GR00T N1 is NVIDIA’s open VLA foundation model for generalist humanoid robots. It understands images and language, and turns them into actions, like moving its arms or following instructions, thanks to a system that combines smart reasoning with real-time movement control. GR00T N1 also builds on the LeRobot dataset format, the open standard created to simplify sharing and training on robot demonstrations.

Now that we’ve looked at the latest VLM model innovations, let’s explore how more established capabilities have evolved.

In a recent development, as we’ve seen in earlier sections, VLMs enable generalization over traditional computer vision tasks. Models can now take in images and a variety of prompts, such as open-ended text, and output structured text with localization tokens (for detection, segmentation and more).

Last year, PaliGemma was the first model to attempt solving these tasks. The model takes in an image and text, where text is a description of an object of interest, along with a task prefix. The text prompt looks like “segment striped cat” or “detect bird on the roof”.

In a recent development, for detection, the model outputs the bounding box coordinates as tokens. For segmentation, on the other hand, the model outputs detection tokens and segmentation tokens. These segmentation tokens aren’t all the segmented pixel coordinates, but codebook indices that are decoded by a variational autoencoder trained to decode these tokens into valid segmentation masks (as shown in the figure below).

Many models have been introduced to do localization tasks after PaliGemma. Late last year, an upgraded version of PaliGemma, PaliGemma 2, appeared with the same capabilities and better performance. Another model that came later was Molmo by Allen AI, which can point to instances with dots and count object instances.

Qwen2.5-VL can also detect, point to, and count objects, and this includes UI elements as objects too!

According to recent reports, vision language models in production require filtering inputs and outputs to prevent jailbreaks and harmful outputs for compliance. Harmful content varies from inputs with violence to sexually explicit content. That’s where multimodal safety models come in: they are used before and after vision language models to filter their inputs and outputs. They are just like LLM safety models but with additional image input.

In early 2025, Google introduced the first open multimodal safety model, ShieldGemma 2. It is built on ShieldGemma, the text-only safety model. This model takes in images and content policies and returns whether an image is safe for a given policy. Policy refers to a criterion in which the image is inappropriate. ShieldGemma 2 can also be used to filter outputs of image generation models.

Llama Guard 4 by Meta, is a dense multimodal and multilingual safety model. It is densely pruned from Llama 4 Scout (a multimodal mixture-of-experts) with safety fine tuning.

The model can be used for text-only and multimodal inference. The model can also take in vision language model outputs, complete conversations, and filter them before sending them to the user.

Recent findings suggest that now let’s look at how Retrieval Augmented Generation has evolved in the multimodal space. RAG for complex documents, usually formatted in PDF, is processed in three steps:.

A traditional PDF parser consists of multiple elements to preserve the structure and visual elements in the document, such as layout, tables, images, charts, all rendered into a markdown. But this setup can be hard to maintain.

With the rise of vision language models, this issue was addressed: there are now multimodal retrievers and rerankers.

Sources indicate that multimodal retrievers take a stack of PDFs and a query as input and return the most relevant page numbers along with their confidence scores. The scores represent how likely the page contains the answer to the query, or how relevant the query is to the page. This bypasses the brittle parsing step.

The most relevant pages are then fed to the vision language model along with the query, and the VLM generates the answer.

There are two main multimodal retriever architectures:.

Industry observers note that DSE models consist of a text encoder and an image encoder, returning a single vector per query. The returned scores are softmax over the dot products of embeddings. They return a single vector per passage.

According to recent reports, colBERT-like models, like ColPali, are also dual encoder models, with a twist: ColPali has a vision language model as an image encoder, and a large language model as a text encoder. These models are inherently not encoders, but the models output embeddings, which are then passed to a “MaxSim”. The outputs are multiple vectors, one for each token, unlike DSE. In MaxSim, the similarity between each text token embedding and each image patch embedding is calculated, and this approach captures nuances better. Due to this reason, ColBERT-like models are less cost-efficient, have better performance.

Below you can see the indexing latency for ColPali. Since it’s just a single model, it’s also easier to maintain.

On Hugging Face Hub, you can find these models under the task “Visual Document Retrieval”.

According to recent reports, the most popular benchmark for this task is ViDoRe, which consists of documents in English and French, with documents varying from financial reports, scientific figures to administrative documents. Each example of ViDoRe has the document as image, a query and potential answers. The documents matched with the queries help with contrastive pre-training, so the ViDoRe train set is used to train new models.

Vision language models unlock many agentic workflows from chatting with documents to computer use. Here we will cover the latter since it requires more advanced agentic capabilities. Recently, there have been many vision language models releases that understand and operate over UIs. The latest one is UI-TARS-1.5 by ByteDance, which showed great results in operating over browser, computer and phone use. It can also do gameplay with reasoning, and operate in open world games. Another impactful release of this year is MAGMA-8B, it’s a foundation model for both UI navigation and physical interaction with the real world. Moreover, Qwen2.5-VL (especially its 32B variant as it is further trained on agentic tasks) and Kimi-VL reasoning model are good in GUI agentic tasks.

Recent findings suggest that at the beginning of 2025, we introduced smolagents, a fresh lightweight agentic library that implements the ReAct framework. Shortly after, we implemented vision language support for the library. This integration took place on two use cases:.

The library provides building blocks for the people to build their own agentic workflows with image understanding. We provide different scripts and single-line CLI commands to get the users started easily.

Industry observers note that for the first case, assume we want an agent to describe documents (which is not very agentic, but good for minimal use cases). You can initialize the CodeAgent (an agent that writes its own code!) like the following:.

For the latter use case where we need an agent to get screenshots, we can define a callback to be executed at the end of each ActionStep. For your own use case where you need to get images dynamically, modify the callback however you’d like. We will not define it here in detail for simplicity. Optionally, you can read the blog post and the script itself at the end of this blog post. For now, let’s see how we initialize the agent with callbacks and browser control steps.

It has been revealed that you can simply try the whole example by running the following CLI command. It starts an agent with access to control over the web browser, powered by a vision language model to accomplish web automation tasks (please replace with the website you’d like to navigate to).

It has been revealed that smolagents provides different model types, such as local transformers models, open-source models served using Inference Providers, or endpoints closed-source model providers. We encourage the use of open-source models as many agentic workflows currently require reasoning, which benefits from models with a large number of parameters. Qwen 2.5 VL as of April 2025 is a good candidate for agentic workflows, as the model is further trained on agentic tasks.

Most vision language models these days can handle videos, because videos can be represented as a sequence of frames. However, video understanding is tricky because of the temporal relationship between frames and the large amount of frames, so different techniques are used to select a representative set of video frames.

Since last year, the community has weighed on different approaches and tricks to solve this problem.

A good example is the LongVU model by Meta. It downsamples video frames by passing them to DINOv2 to pick the most similar ones to remove them, and then the model further refines frames by picking the most relevant frames according to the text query, where both the text and the frames are projected to the same space and similarity is calculated. Qwen2.5VL can handle long context and is adapted to dynamic FPS rates, as the model is trained with videos with different frame rates. Through extended multimodal RoPE, it understands the absolute time positions of frames, and can handle different rates and still understand the speed of the events happening in real life. Another model is Gemma 3, which can accept video frames interleaved with timestamps in text prompt, e.g. “Frame 00.00: ..”, and is very performant for video understanding tasks.

According to recent reports, preference optimization is an alternative fine-tuning approach for language models that can also be extended to vision language models. Instead of relying on fixed labels, this method focuses on comparing and ranking candidate responses based on preferences. The trl library offers support for direct preference optimization (DPO), including for VLMs.

Below is an example of how a preference dataset for DPO of a VLM fine-tuning is structured. Each entry consists of an image + question pair and two corresponding answers: one chosen and one rejected. The VLM is fine-tuned to generate responses aligned with the preferred (chosen) answer.

In a recent development, an example dataset for this procedure is RLAIF-V, which contains over 83000 annotated samples formatted according to the structure described above. Each entry includes a list of images (usually one), a prompt, a chosen answer, and a rejected answer, just as expected by the DPOTrainer.There is a RLAIF-V formatted dataset, which is already formatted accordingly. Below is an example of a single sample:.

Once the dataset is prepared, you can use the DPOConfig and DPOTrainer classes from the trl library to configure and launch the fine-tuning process.Below is an example configuration using DPOConfig:.

Sources indicate that to train your model using DPOTrainer, you can optionally provide a reference model to compute the reward difference. If you’re using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), you may omit the reference model by setting ref_model=None.

Recent findings suggest that benchmarks have also evolved significantly over the past year. In our previous blog, we described MMMU and MMBench as two emerging benchmarks for evaluating Vision Language Models. With the rapid progress in the field, the models have saturated on these benchmarks, and we need better evaluation tools. To achieve this, we need tools that assess specific capabilities, on top of general purpose benchmarks.

Now, we highlight two general-purpose benchmarks that stand out: MMT-Bench and MMMU-Pro.

MMT-Bench is designed to assess VLMs across a wide range of multimodal tasks that require expert knowledge, precise visual recognition, localization, reasoning, and planning. The benchmark includes 31325 multi-choice visual questions from various multimodal scenarios, with image, text, video, and point cloud modalities. With 32 different meta-tasks with 162 subtasks, it covers a variety of tasks, including OCR, Visual Recognition, or Visual-Language Retrieval.

In a recent development, MMMU-Pro is a better version of the original MMMU benchmark. It also evaluates advanced AI models’ true understanding capabilities across multiple modalities.It is more complex than MMMU, e.g. it has a vision-only input setting and an increase in the number of candidate options from 4 to 10. The benchmark also incorporates real-world simulation, with vision-only questions derived from screenshots or photos captured within a simulated display, featuring varying backgrounds, font styles, and sizes to mimic real-world conditions.

Indie web browser Ladybird enters alpha testing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upstart engine gets downloadable macOS and Linux builds, but no security guarantees.
  • Sources indicate that the independent Ladybird web browser has reached an key milestone: an alpha test version.
  • Industry observers note that earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upstart engine gets downloadable macOS and Linux builds, but no security guarantees.

Sources indicate that the independent Ladybird web browser has reached an key milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Industry observers note that earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha. We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest.

There are downloads available, covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages.

It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the GitHub repository and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project confirmed that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions.

According to recent reports, we first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser. Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the Serenity prayer, recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022.

About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird. Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, we wrote Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI. At one point, developer Andreas Kling used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage demonstrates, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development.

Recent findings suggest that kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size.

It has been revealed that we tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as The Register and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all.

The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage.

The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others.

The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit.

Some day, when the Servo project matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. That's a significant step. ®.

The $10 of assets don't really count here as it's already baked into the value (it's complicated, don't worry about it).

In a publicly traded tech giant, that valuation change means your share price will go up. Shareholders therefore make some paper money until they cash out for actual money. Good for the shareholders. However, the company can issue new shares are the higher price to get money for... more circular financing.

There's a multiplying force if my company grows too. It means I no longer owe you $10, instead I owe you $20 - which is still an asset on your books. In the above example, it could mean your multiplier goes from 10 to 11 or something, which again, bumps your share price up (and around we go all over again).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agentic offensive framework automates familiar attack techniques, with weak defenses potentially breached in minutes.

Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft noted this week.

ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.

The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.

Sources indicate that microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.

Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.

Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.

According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Industry observers note that like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.

It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.

Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor.".

Recent findings suggest that notably, ARTEX does not offer any newly introduced attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers people, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it mentioned the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.

AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

Recent findings suggest that some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®.

Pimalaya goes stable

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pimalaya

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard.
  • Recent findings suggest that most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody.
  • According to recent reports, in Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once, at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list:.

Recent findings suggest that most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about.

According to recent reports, in Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both.

The thing is, every piece is now connected:.

Releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family.

The other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract: the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a latest major.

Few things made this release possible.

Sources indicate that specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head.

One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies.

One unified API, as a union. Before, the commands shared by every backend were the intersection of what the backends could do: if one backend could not do it, nobody could. Now it is the union: each backend registers the capabilities it really serves, with the same observable result as the others, and a command an account cannot serve fails before even connecting, with a clear capability-missing code.

Sources indicate that measured gates for pimdir. Audits always find something, so "no new finding" never ends. Instead, I built a test generator that produces stores, remote states and an oracle from a seed, and ran campaigns of 4,180 jobs against io-pimdir: crashes injected at every step, the search index checked against a full rebuild after each event, the sync engine replayed against scripted servers. The rule was simple: 2 campaigns in a row without any spec break, then freeze. Campaign 1 found one, campaigns 2 and 3 were clean, a late fix restarted the count, then campaigns 4 and 5 were clean. Freeze.

In a recent development, live tests on real providers. Every CLI was tested against real accounts: Google, Microsoft, Fastmail and iCloud, plus few Chinese providers for Himalaya (QQ, 163, 139). A last "live night" just before the release found few bugs that went straight into the libs.

Libs first, apps after. The libs were released between the 13th and the 25th of November, the apps then moved to them without any patch or git pin. Everything you install comes from crates.io.

pimdir is a local-first standard for personal information: mails, contacts, calendars, tasks and files in one portable store, kept as a replica of every source, and searchable with one query language. A store is one SQLite file plus a content-addressed blob directory, the same on every OS and architecture. I already explained why such a standard is needed in Another year with NLnet, and how the Android app became its first full implementation in Pimalaya for Android enters closed alpha.

It comes in 3 parts, versioned separately:.

They are released together because a store holds sync state that follows the sync part, and the query language binds every program that offers search.

What v1 means: schema version 1 never changes, every schema change is a migration, and a minor version only adds test cases. You can implement it in any language that speaks SQLite, use the I/O-free core of io-pimdir (like the Android app does, on the platform SQLite), or use its std client.

Sources indicate that few days before the freeze, I compared it with notmuch, which is the reference in this area. They do not do the same job (notmuch indexes mail files it does not own, pimdir owns the bodies, syncs them and holds other domains), but the search can be compared. On a store of 1 million messages from the Enron corpus, pimdir was ahead of notmuch on 50 of the 51 query measures and tied the last one, imported the million faster, and used a third of the memory. Stemming, regex and per-thread queries are still missing, they are on the list.

Recent findings suggest that one warning for the early adopters: a store written by a draft version is refused, never migrated. Sync it till nothing is pending with the last draft binary, move its directory aside, then let a release create and sync a fresh one.

This is the change many of you will not like, so let me explain it properly.

In a recent development, every CLI had a configuration wizard: you typed your email address, it discovered the servers, asked for the password, stored it in your keyring, and wrote the TOML for you. It is gone, from every CLI.

The direction. The CLIs are now low-level tools: plain text to glance at, JSON for scripts, frontends and agents. Comfort (tables, colours, relative dates, guided setups, rich composition) belongs to frontends. In fact this is not fresh: it is the same split that started the whole project, back when the logic left the Vim plugin. The CLI was always supposed to be the backend a frontend needs. This release just goes all the way.

Recent findings suggest that I know some of you used the wizard to get started, and that copying a sample feels like a step back. If the welcome or the samples are not clear enough, it is a bug: please open an issue, I would rather fix the docs than bring back a second setup system per CLI.

Himalaya is now a low-level CLI over a unified mail API: the same commands on every backend, the protocol-specific ones next to them, plain text for a glance and --json for the rest.

Backends: IMAP, SMTP, ManageSieve, JMAP, the Gmail API, Microsoft Graph, Maildir (with a new maildir++ layout for Dovecot and Courier stores), mbox, and pimdir. The README has recipes for Proton Mail (through Bridge), Fastmail, Gmail, Outlook, Posteo and iCloud.

It has been revealed that what is gone: the wizard, the m2dir backend (superseded by pimdir), the table and colour options, HIMALAYA_CONFIG. Unknown configuration keys are now refused, JSON keys are camelCase, and the v2 search syntax needs to be rewritten. The migration guide lists everything, with a full table for the queries.

Neverest is rebuilt around the pimdir store: every account syncs into one shared store, which the other CLIs read, search and queue their writes into. It syncs mails, contacts and calendars over IMAP, Gmail, Microsoft Graph, Google Calendar, Google People, CalDAV and CardDAV.

JMAP sources are not supported yet (it is a draft), so Fastmail syncs over IMAP, CardDAV and CalDAV for now. Coming from v0.x? Your configuration and state are not carried over: start from the config.sample.toml, then run neverest sync --init.

The first stable release of Cardamum: a low-level CLI over a unified contacts API, with the same commands on CardDAV, JMAP, Microsoft Graph, Google People, vdir and pimdir.

According to recent reports, card search speaks the pimdir query language on every backend, account capability reveals what an account serves without connecting, and you get the REPL and the MCP server like the others. Editing a card is left to a composer such as tcard. The wizard and the discover route are gone.

Same story for calendars: the same commands on CalDAV, JMAP (fresh), Google Calendar, Microsoft Graph, vdir and pimdir.

In a recent development, newly introduced: event search, recurrence expansion, attendees and alarms, online meetings (--online-meeting), invitation replies through pimdir, and an agenda that draws a month or a year like cal(1) does. Editing an event is left to a composer such as tcal. The wizard, the tables and colours, and the todo and journal commands are gone: tasks and journals will move to dedicated tools (Unfog and Journal), not released yet.

Carillon is a local watcher that fires hooks on what changes in your mailboxes, address books and calendars, over IMAP, JMAP, Maildir, CalDAV, CardDAV, Microsoft Graph, the Google APIs and the pimdir store. It uses push where the server offers it (IMAP IDLE, the JMAP event stream) and polls elsewhere. A hook runs a command, highlights a desktop notification, or both.

Latest in v1: a pimdir backend, on-alarm-trigger for the alarms of events and tasks, on-birthday-trigger for birthdays and anniversaries, a per-hook timeout, and a report of what moved while an IMAP or Gmail session was lost. Hooks now take the same shape as Comodoro's.

Ortie manages OAuth tokens for the other tools. v3 aligns it on the rest of the family: ready-made Google, Microsoft and Fastmail accounts to paste, token revocation, an auth listen to catch a redirection handed off from another machine, account checks, a REPL, and an MCP server that never hands the token to the agent. The wizard and the hooks are gone (the storage write command does what a hook did).

Sources indicate that comodoro manages timers: one server owns a timer, any number of clients drive it, over a local socket or TCP. v3 joins the same standard: comodoro watch feeds a status bar without polling, hooks get the cycle name and duration, plus the welcome, account checks, a REPL and an MCP server. Comodoro is now a binary only: the library is gone, and the open JSON-RPC protocol is the contract for third parties.

None of the above would exist without the libs below, all released in November on crates.io:.

They are all I/O-free, as usual: feel free to build your own tools at the top of them.

Industry observers note that each README lists the ways to install: prebuilt binaries from the GitHub releases (or the install.sh script), cargo install --locked, Nix, and the APT, DNF and Homebrew repositories at pkg.pimalaya.org. The packages are landing there over the coming days, and the nixpkgs and home-manager updates are on their way.

It has been revealed that special thanks to the NLnet foundation and the European Commission's NGI initiative, for the financial support through NGI Zero Core and now the NGI Zero Commons Fund. This kind of slow, deep work is only possible thanks to them.

Industry observers note that and thank you to everyone who reported bugs, tested betas, or simply waited patiently while everything was being rebuilt. Any feedback is welcomed, on GitHub, on Matrix or on Mastodon. Let me know how it goes!

  • In a recent development, through this release, we would like to make Inference Endpoints more community-centric and allow anyone to come and contribute to create incredible inference deployments on the Hugging Face Platform.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are happy to introduce a newly introduced blazing fast OpenAI Whisper deployment option on Inference Endpoints. It provides up to 8x performance improvements compared to the previous version, and makes everyone one click away from deploying dedicated, powerful transcription models in a cost-effective way, leveraging the amazing work done by the AI community.

In a recent development, through this release, we would like to make Inference Endpoints more community-centric and allow anyone to come and contribute to create incredible inference deployments on the Hugging Face Platform. Along with the community, we would like to propose optimized deployments for a wide range of tasks through the use of awesome and available open-source technologies.

The unique position of Hugging Face, at the heart of the Open-Source AI Community, working hand-in-hand with individuals, institutions and industrial partners, makes it the most heterogeneous platform when it comes to deploying AI models for inference on a wide variety of hardware and software.

Recent findings suggest that the new Whisper endpoint leverages amazing open-source community projects. Inference is powered by the vLLM project, which provides efficient ways of running AI models on various hardware families – especially, but not limited to, NVIDIA GPUs. We use the vLLM implementation of OpenAI's Whisper model, allowing us to enable further, lower-level optimizations down the software stack.

In this initial release, we are targeting NVIDIA GPUs with compute capabilities 8.9 or better (Ada Lovelace), like L4 & L40s, which unlocks a wide range of software optimizations:.

Recent findings suggest that CUDA graphs record the flow of sequential operations, or kernels, happening on the GPU, and attempts to group them as bigger chunks of work units to execute on the GPU. This grouping operation reduces data movements, synchronizations, and GPU scheduling overhead by executing a single, much larger work unit, rather than multiple smaller ones.

Industry observers note that last but not least, we are dynamically quantizing activations to reduce the memory requirement incurred by the KV cache(s). The computations are done in half precision, bfloat16 in this case, and the outputs are being stored in reduced precision (1 byte for float8 vs 2 bytes for bfloat16) which allows us to store more elements in the KV cache, increasing the cache hit rate.

There are many ways to continue pushing this and we are gearing up to work hand in hand with the community to improve it!

Whisper Large V3 shows a nearly 8x improvement in RTFx, enabling much faster inference with no loss in transcription quality.

We evaluated the transcription quality and runtime efficiency of several Whisper-based models—Whisper Large V3, Whisper Large V3-Turbo, and Distil-Whisper Large V3.5—and compared them against their implementations on the Transformers library to assess both accuracy and decoding speed under identical conditions.

In a recent development, we computed Word Error Rate (WER) across 8 standard datasets from the Open ASR Leaderboard, including AMI, GigaSpeech, LibriSpeech (Clean and Other), SPGISpeech, Tedlium, VoxPopuli, and Earnings22. These datasets span diverse domains and recording conditions, ensuring a robust evaluation of generalization and real-world transcription quality. WER measures transcription accuracy by calculating the percentage of words that are incorrectly predicted (via insertions, deletions, or substitutions); lower WER indicates better performance. All three Whisper variants maintain WER performance comparable to their Transformer baselines.

To assess inference efficiency, we sampled from the rev16 long-form dataset, which contains audio segments over 45 minutes in length—representative of real transcription workloads such as meetings, podcasts, or interviews. We measured the Real-Time Factor (RTFx), defined as the ratio of audio duration to transcription time, and averaged it across samples. All models were evaluated in bfloat16 on a single L4 GPU, using consistent decoding settings (language, beam size, and batch size).

According to recent reports, you can deploy your own ASR inference pipeline via Hugging Face Endpoints. Endpoints allows anyone willing to deploy AI models into production ready environments to do so by filling in a few parameters. It also features the most complete fleet of AI hardware available on the market to suit your need for cost and performance. All of this directly from where the AI community is being built. To get started, nothing easier, simply choose the model you want to deploy:.

Running inference on the deployed model endpoint can be done in just a few lines of code in Python, you can also use the same structure in Javascript or any other language you're comfortable with.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million newly introduced millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

According to recent reports, but here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

According to recent reports, this matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:.

In a recent development, the discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

Sources indicate that for FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both upcoming wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% said anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Sources indicate that approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

It has been revealed that overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement aims (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

According to recent reports, the average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

According to recent reports, yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

According to recent reports, $1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently reveals they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

Improving Hugging Face Model Access for Kaggle Consumers

📅 14 May 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community.
  • Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.
  • You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community. That’s why we’re excited to announce our intends to bring our platforms and communities closer to better serve AI developers everywhere.

Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.

You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa. Start by visiting a Hugging Face model page like Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. To use it in a Kaggle Notebook, you can click on “Use this model” and select “Kaggle” to open up a Kaggle notebook with a pre-populated code snippet to load the model. You can do the same from a Hugging Face model page on Kaggle by clicking the “Code” button.

Sources indicate that when you run a notebook on Kaggle that references a model hosted on Hugging Face Hub, we will automatically generate a Hugging Face model page if one doesn’t exist already. You don’t need to make any special changes to your code. Additionally, when you make your notebook public, it will automatically show on the “Code” tab of the Kaggle model page.

Industry observers note that discover Hugging Face models and explore all the community examples in public notebooks in one place on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/models. As more Hugging Face models are used on Kaggle, the number of models and associated code examples you can explore for inspiration will grow.

Recent findings suggest that when browsing Hugging Face models on Kaggle, we want to make it easy for you to navigate back to Hugging Face to explore additional details, metadata, community usage in Hugging Face Spaces, discussion, and more. Simply click “Open in Hugging Face” on the Kaggle model page.

According to recent reports, if you use a private Hugging Face model in your Kaggle notebook, authenticate via your Hugging Face account as normal (add your HF_TOKEN in the “Add-ons > Secrets” menu in the notebook editor). A Hugging Face model page won’t be generated on Kaggle.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to access a consent-gated model in your Kaggle notebook, you’ll need to request access to it using a Hugging Face account and follow the prompts on your browser's Hugging Face model page as normal. Hugging Face has documentation to guide you through this process. Otherwise, the integration will work the same as for non-gated models.

According to recent reports, we’re actively working on a solution to seamlessly use Hugging Face models in Kaggle competitions that require offline notebook submissions. While this will take a few more months to complete, we believe the wait will be worth it.

You can read Kaggle’s position on “AI Competitions as the gold standard for empirical rigor for GenAI evaluation” to understand why it’s so key for us to get this part of the integration right! But tl;dr – Kaggle is highly sensitive to data leakage and its impact on model contamination. Our goal is to design this integration to preserve the integrity of our competitions and their vital role in the industry, while enabling seamless access for Kaggle competitors to build with the best models from Hugging Face!

We’d love to hear your feedback in the meantime - share your thoughts and ideas here!

The token factory never sleeps

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job.
  • Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure.
  • Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job. Here's what it takes to keep the tokens flowing in the datacenter you already have.

Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI quickly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly vital. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It declared two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.

Recent findings suggest that agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

Industry observers note that while training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

In a recent development, running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many customers, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.

It has been revealed that enterprises are moving ahead promptly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

Sources indicate that enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

Recent findings suggest that in token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.

The other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Sources indicate that production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real glitch here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

The more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also says it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.

Sources indicate that as boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

There are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, says the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.

Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.

Recent findings suggest that the ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS notes this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.

So that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any new equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

According to recent reports, ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

Inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS claims. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.

Industry observers note that the other issue for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

Industry observers note that on the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS says the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.

Services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so crucial.

In a recent development, ASUS states its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).

Industry observers note that so, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.

Find out more about the liquid-cooled ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System.

Tech Report: The Transformers Library: standardizing model definitions

📅 15 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.
  • Recent findings suggest that transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model.
  • In a recent development, transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model. Since then, we've continuously aimed to add state-of-the-art architectures, initially focused on NLP, then growing to Audio and computer vision. Today, transformers is the default library for LLMs and VLMs in the Python ecosystem.

In a recent development, transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week. We have aimed for these architectures to be released in a timely manner; having day-0 support for the most sought-after architectures (Llamas, Qwens, GLMs, etc.).

Over time, Transformers has become a central component in the ML ecosystem, becoming one of the most complete toolkits in terms of model diversity; it's integrated in all popular training frameworks such as Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, TRL, Nanotron, etc.

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...) for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

As an example, here is how you would work with the transformers backend in vLLM:.

That's all it takes for a new model to enjoy super-fast and production-grade serving with vLLM!

Read more about it in the vLLM documentation.

Sources indicate that we've also been working very closely with llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

We are super proud that the transformers format is being adopted by the community, bringing a lot of interoperability we all benefit from. Train a model with Unsloth, deploy it with SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp to run locally! We aim to keep supporting the community going forward.

To make it easier for the community to use transformers as a reference for model definitions, we strive to significantly reduce the barrier to model contributions. We have been doing this effort for a few years, but we'll accelerate significantly over the next few weeks:.

As a model user, in the future you should see even more interoperability in the tools that you use.

This does not mean that we intend to lock you in using transformers in your experiments; rather, it means that thanks to this modeling standardization, you can expect the tools that you use for training, for inference, and for production, to efficiently work together.

Sources indicate that as a model creator, this means that a single contribution will get your model available in all downstream libraries that have integrated that modeling implementation. We have seen this many times over the years: releasing a model is stressful and integrating in all key libraries is often a significant time-sink.

By standardizing the model implementation in a community-driven manner, we hope to lower the barrier of contributions to the field across libraries.

Recent findings suggest that we firmly believe this renewed direction will help standardize an ecosystem which is often at risk of fragmentation. We'd love to hear your feedback on the direction the team has decided to take; and of changes we could do to get there. Please come and see us over at the transformers-community support tab on the Hub!

Awesome news! Transformers being the default access point for as many models on day 0 as well as in being able to use the inference engine of choice is an epic goal!

if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

Industry observers note that it's interesting, but it seems regardless of the TLDR, Llama.CPP maintains its own implementation and so won't benefit from any "day-0 support" for latest architectures in Transfomers. I was kind of hoping Llama would get straight Transformer compatibility for a moment.

It's not clear what, if anything, is changing there.

You're entirely correct that llama.cpp maintains its own implementation; we've been working hand-in-hand with the team to get better intercompatibility however: export between frameworks on both sides (from transformers to llama.cpp, and vice-versa).

Additionally, with the frequent VLM releases happening recently, we've been working directly with @ngxson to have the implementations day-0 (or week-0) in llama.cpp when the implementation already exists in transformers.

We won't have "automatic day-0 support" as the two libs have different backends; but we can still try by making the two more compatible, reducing the time needed to get there.

Thanks @lysandre . Apologies if I sounded overly negative at all, it's a very good goal.

Since I doubt Llama.cpp would implement Transformers directly as VLM did (although that would be nice), perhaps an in-between project is possible using the low-level C bindings Llama provides. I believe that's how llama-cpp-python and similar work.

Then again I'm not sure how much benefit there is, but food for thought.
