📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.

In a recent development, drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an fresh pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants. This comprehensive approach produces a non-BitNet model in bfloat16 format, the native BitNet model, and a pre-quantized BitNet variant specifically engineered for effortless fine-tuning, enabling owners and developers to precisely tailor these models to their specific applications and needs.

Available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models. Discover the Falcon-Edge series on our dedicated Hugging Face collection.

In a recent development, large Language Models (LLMs), by design, are inherently large and resource-intensive. As demand grows to deploy these models efficiently on edge devices, research into model compression has accelerated. Recent efforts, such as those by DeepSeek and Llama 4, explore training with reduced precision formats—down to FP8—to improve deployment scalability. On the other hand, many state-of-the-art methods emphasize post-training quantization. In contrast to these approaches, BitNet introduces a fundamentally different paradigm: unlike reduced-precision training which still relies on floating-point formats, and post-training quantization which adjusts weights after full-precision training, BitNet operates with the lowest possible precision — ternary weights ({-1, 0, 1}) — directly during training, enabling an end-to-end ultra-efficient model design.

These ternary weights are paving the way for a “matmul-free” LLM design that is notably faster and remarkably memory-efficient in practice. The primary challenge of this innovative approach is the necessity for pre-training BitNet models, which can be computationally demanding and costly for typical owners.

It has been revealed that leveraging the learnings from pre-training data strategies from our center, we pre-train our model on an internal data mixture for approximately 1.5 Tera Tokens. We use the classic WSD learning rate scheduler for pre-training.

We evaluate our models (base and instruct versions) on the former Hugging Face leaderboard v2 benchmark and report the normalized results below in comparison with other models of similar size:.

Additional results (leaderboard v1) on comparing our instructed models with Microsoft’s upcoming BitNet model:.

Falcon-Edge demonstrates on-par and better performances than models of comparable sizes on the leaderboard v2 tasks, demonstrating that it is possible to train powerful BitNet models on desired domains while being competitive enough on other tasks.

If we look closer at the formula of the BitNet linear layer for inference (in terms of Python code):.

The normalization activation_norm_quant quantizes the activations in int8 format, then the activation is computed back in half precision by diving it by x_scale. Since the model has been trained with fake 8-bit activation quantization, we argue that it is possible to approximate that:.

Therefore, instead of quantizing the model post-training, injecting the weight scale after quantizing the weights should lead to a good enough “approximation” of the non-BitNet version of the model:.

We confirm this by running end-to-end evaluations on the bfloat16 variant of our 1B and 3B base models and below are the results:.

The bfloat16 counterparts of the models can be loaded directly via Hugging Face transformers by passing revision="bfloat16" in the from_pretrained function:.

To the best of our knowledge, except from the most recent release from Microsoft previous BitNet releases only focus on releasing the final quantized model, making it usable only for inference. Similarly to the release from Microsoft, we propose to extend the accessibility of research and application of BitNet models by releasing their pre-quantized weights. That way, users can either perform fine-tuning on their target domain, or do continuous pre-training of the BitNet checkpoint as long as nn.Linear layers are replaced by BitnetLinear layers, and by making sure to quantize the model post training in BitNet format. Since the weights corresponds to the pre-quantized weights, performing text generation without replacing the nn.Linear layers with BitnetLinear layers will produce gibberish output.

The pre-quantized weights can be downloaded via Hugging Face's transformers library by specifying the revision argument to be prequantized:.

This way, we will help fostering an ecosystem around first powerful 1-bit fine-tunes by the community. We provide to community the tools to get easily started and fine-tune their own version of powerful BitNet models by packaging all needed utility methods for performing fine-tuning on the pre-quantized weights on a Python package called onebitllms that we will cover in the next section.

It has been revealed that in this release, we also introduce onebitllms - a lightweight Python package that can be plugged into your favorite LLM fine-tuning tools in order to fine-tune any pre-quantized BitNet model. At this time of writing onebitllms exposes these main functionalities:.

Currently, only full-finetuning is supported through this framework, while in this release the model sizes are relatively small, supporting Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for BitNet models remains an exciting and impactful open question for upcoming BitNet models.

To get started, simply install the package directly through pip or from source, and take a look at examples/ folders inside the source code.

With this package, we hope to accelerate research and development around ternary format LLMs, and hope to see many derivations of Falcon-Edge and other future powerful BitNet models developed by the community.

We believe this release opens up multiple interesting directions - among all the possible follow up directions, we right now think that the following open questions will make BitNet models much more impactful in the near future:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today at the Microsoft Build conference, Satya Nadella declared an expanded collaboration with Hugging Face, to make its wide diversity of open models easy to deploy on Azure secure infrastructure.

Industry observers note that if you head over to Azure AI Foundry today, you will find a vastly expanded collection of 10,000+ Hugging Face models you can deploy in a couple clicks to power AI applications working with text, audio and images. And we’re just getting started!

2 years ago, Microsoft and Hugging Face started a collaboration to make open models more easily accessible on Azure - back then the Hub was home to 200,000 open models.

Industry observers note that with now close to 2 million open models on Hugging Face, covering a wide diversity of tasks, modalities, domains and languages, it was time to take our collaboration to the next level. The fresh collaboration unveiled today creates a framework for mutual success to vastly expand how Azure customers can benefit from Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that "Open source is how AI moves faster—with transparency, choice, and community at its core. This collaboration represents our commitment to that momentum. By combining Hugging Face’s vibrant model ecosystem with Azure’s secure, enterprise-grade infrastructure, we’re giving developers the freedom to pick the best model for the job—and helping organizations innovate safely and at scale.”.

-- Asha Sharma, Corporate Vice President at Microsoft.

Making more open models easily accessible to Azure customers, for secure deployment alongside firm private data, will enable enterprises to build AI applications and agents while being fully in control of their technology and data.

We’re enabling companies to take control of their AI destiny, deploying the best open models securely within their Azure account, to build AI applications they can trust and verify.

-- Clement Delangue, CEO and cofounder at Hugging Face.

In a recent development, let’s head over to Azure AI Foundry, and select the Model Catalog. Here you can now find over 10,000 models under the Hugging Face Collection.

Models in the Collection include the most popular, trending models on Hugging Face for a wide range of tasks to work with text, audio and images - including text generation, feature extraction, fill-mask, translation, identifying sentence similarity, image classification, image segmentation, text to image generation, image to text conversion, automatic speech recognition and audio-classification.

To make the Hugging Face Collection on Azure AI Foundry enterprise-ready, we are only featuring models:.

In addition, Microsoft and Hugging Face will continuously test inference containers for vulnerabilities to maintain and patch them as needed.

Now let’s say you want to deploy for instance the popular Microsoft Phi-4 Reasoning Plus open model.

In a recent development, first, let’s select the model in the Hugging Face Collection in Azure AI Foundry, and click the “Deploy button”. The form allows you to select a VM, instance count and deployment parameters, and start the deployment process with just another click!

Now, if you prefer browsing models on the Hub, you can also start from the model page - the “Deploy on Azure ML” option will take you to the same deployment option within Azure AI Machine Learning Studio.

We are really excited about all the new Hugging Face models and modalities now directly available within Azure AI Foundry, but we’re not going to stop there!

In the weeks and months to come, you can expect a rolling thunder of updates:.

If you’re on Azure, it’s time to build with open models!

And when you're ready to make it your own, you can customize it until it looks and feels exactly the way you think a desktop should.

It all starts with Constellations.

Constellations are COSMICâs all-in-one bundled themes.Â  With a single click you can change the wallpaper, accent colors, icons, and fonts. It's literally a one-click switch for a full aesthetic change of your desktop. Instead of having to go to Desktop > Wallpaper, then Desktop > Appearance, then Desktop Panel, then Desktop Dock, then Desktop Window Management, all you do is go to Settings > Desktop > Appearance, select between dark or light mode, enable or disable automatic mode switching, and then select your theme.

As COSMIC is a rolling release desktop, consumers on 24.04 will have experienced many of these features. For the full 26.04 experience, do a fresh install. Pop 24.04 to Pop 26.04 upgrades will be activated in December.

Taking Email Back

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linux-magazine

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.
  • Industry observers note that deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line.
  • According to recent reports, the software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

Industry observers note that deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

According to recent reports, the software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and intends to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

In a recent development, the collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Industry observers note that email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

According to recent reports, two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for customers of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years.".

Sources indicate that he counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he says, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google launched Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

It has been revealed that ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

According to recent reports, IT departments think about email as servers; “what customers want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch says. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client.".

Dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour says, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers.".

As Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he indicates, requires "really huge trade-offs.".

Reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

Sources indicate that stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client.".

Recent findings suggest that stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

It has been revealed that for people who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a fresh protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

It has been revealed that aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so people can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one substantial server host to give up all his weekends.

The research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

The three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality.

It has been revealed that version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

Latest mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nanoVLM is the simplest way to get started with training your very own Vision Language Model (VLM) using pure PyTorch. It is lightweight toolkit which allows you to launch a VLM training on a free tier colab notebook.

We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, and provide a similar project for the vision domain.

Industry observers note that at its heart, nanoVLM is a toolkit that helps you build and train a model that can understand both images and text, and then generate text based on that. The beauty of nanoVLM lies in its simplicity. The entire codebase is intentionally kept minimal and readable, making it perfect for beginners or anyone who wants to peek under the hood of VLMs without getting overwhelmed.

According to recent reports, in this blog post, we cover the core ideas behind the project and provide a simple way to interact with the repository. We not only go into the details of the project but also encapsulate all of it so that you can rapidly get started.

You can start training a Vision Language Model using our nanoVLM toolkit by following these steps:.

Here is a Colab notebook that will help you launch a training run with no local setup required!

Recent findings suggest that as the name suggests, a Vision Language Model (VLM) is a multi-modal model that processes two modalities: vision and text. These models typically take images and/or text as input and generate text as output.

In a recent development, generating text (output) conditioned on the understanding of images and texts (inputs) is a powerful paradigm. It enables a wide range of applications, from image captioning and object detection to answering questions about visual content (as shown in the table below). One thing to note is that nanoVLM focuses only on Visual Question Answering as the training objective.

If you are interested in learning more about VLMs, we strongly recommend reading our latest blog on the topic: Vision Language Models (Better, Faster, Stronger).

"Talk is cheap, show me the code" - Linus Torvalds.

It has been revealed that in this section, we’ll guide you through the codebase. It’s helpful to keep a tab open for reference as you follow along.

In a recent development, below is the folder structure of our repository. We have removed helper files for brevity.

We model nanoVLM after two well known and widely used architectures. Our vision backbone (models/vision_transformer.py) is the standard vision transformer, more specifically Google’s SigLIP vision encoder. Our language backbone follows the Llama 3 architecture.

The vision and text modalities are aligned using a Modality Projection module. This module takes the image embeddings produced by the vision backbone as input, and transforms them into embeddings compatible with the text embeddings from the embedding layer of the language model. These embeddings are then concatenated and fed into the language decoder. The Modality Projection module consists of a pixel shuffle operation followed by a linear layer.

According to recent reports, pixel shuffle reduces the number of image tokens, which helps reduce computational cost and speeds up training, especially for transformer-based language decoders which are sensitive to input length. The figure below demonstrates the concept.

Industry observers note that all the files are very lightweight and well documented. We highly encourage you to check them out individually to get a better understanding of the implementation details (models/xxx.py).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources.
  • Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?
  • We created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources. Quantization offers a powerful solution, shrinking these models to make them more accessible without drastically compromising performance. But the big question always is: can you actually tell the difference in the final image?

Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?

We created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit). The generated images are then presented to you and your challenge is to identify which ones came from the quantized models.

Often, especially with 8-bit quantization, the differences are subtle and may not be noticeable without close inspection. More aggressive quantization like 4-bit or lower might be more noticeable, but the results can still be good, especially considering the massive memory savings. NF4 often gives the best trade-off though.

According to recent reports, building on our previous post, "Memory-efficient Diffusion Transformers with Quanto and Diffusers", this post explores the diverse quantization backends integrated directly into Hugging Face Diffusers. We'll examine how bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, Quanto and native FP8 support make large and powerful models more accessible, demonstrating their use with Flux.

Recent findings suggest that before diving into the quantization backends, let's introduce the FluxPipeline (using the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev checkpoint) and its components, which we'll be quantizing. Loading the full FLUX.1-dev model in BF16 precision requires approximately 31.447 GB of memory. The main components are:.

bitsandbytes is a popular and user-friendly library for 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, widely used for LLMs and QLoRA fine-tuning. We can use it for transformer-based diffusion and flow models, too.

All benchmarks performed on 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU.

In a recent development, note: When using PipelineQuantizationConfig with bitsandbytes, you need to import DiffusersBitsAndBytesConfig from diffusers and TransformersBitsAndBytesConfig from transformers separately. This is because these components originate from different libraries. If you prefer a simpler setup without managing these distinct imports, you can use an alternative approach for pipeline-level quantization, an example of this method is in the Diffusers documentation on Pipeline-level quantization.

For more information check out the bitsandbytes docs.

Recent findings suggest that torchao is a PyTorch-native library for architecture optimization, offering quantization, sparsity, and custom data types, designed for compatibility with torch.compile and FSDP. Diffusers supports a wide range of torchao's exotic data types, enabling fine-grained control over model optimization.

For more information check out the torchao docs.

Quanto is a quantization library integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem via the optimum library.

In a recent development, note: At the time of writing, for float8 support with Quanto, you'll need optimum-quanto<0.2.5 and use quanto directly. We will be working on fixing this.

For more information check out the Quanto docs.

GGUF is a file format popular in the llama.cpp community for storing quantized models.

For more information check out the GGUF docs.

Recent findings suggest that FP8 Layerwise Casting is a memory optimization technique. It works by storing the model's weights in the compact FP8 (8-bit floating point) format, which uses roughly half the memory of standard FP16 or BF16 precision. Just before a layer performs its calculations, its weights are dynamically cast up to a higher compute precision (like FP16/BF16). Immediately afterward, the weights are cast back down to FP8 for efficient storage. This approach works because the core computations retain high precision, and layers particularly sensitive to quantization (like normalization) are typically skipped. This technique can also be combined with group offloading for further memory savings.

For more information check out the Layerwise casting docs.

Most of these quantization backends can be combined with the memory optimization techniques offered in Diffusers. Let's explore CPU offloading, group offloading, and torch.compile. You can learn more about these techniques in the Diffusers documentation.

Note: At the time of writing, bnb + torch.compile also works if bnb is installed from source and using pytorch nightly or with fullgraph=False.

Model CPU Offloading (enable_model_cpu_offload): This method moves entire model components (like the UNet, text encoders, or VAE) between the CPU and GPU during the inference pipeline. It offers substantial VRAM savings and is generally faster than more granular offloading because it involves fewer, larger data transfers.

bnb + enable_model_cpu_offload:.

Industry observers note that group offloading (enable_group_offload for diffusers components or apply_group_offloading for generic torch.nn.Modules): It moves groups of internal model layers (like torch.nn.ModuleList or torch.nn.Sequential instances) to the CPU. This approach is typically more memory-efficient than full model offloading and faster than sequential offloading.

FP8 layerwise casting + group offloading:.

Note: torch.compile can introduce subtle numerical differences, leading to changes in image output.

According to recent reports, torch.compile: Another complementary approach is to accelerate the execution of your model with PyTorch 2.x’s torch.compile() feature. Compiling the model doesn’t directly lower memory, but it can significantly speed up inference. PyTorch 2.0’s compile (Torch Dynamo) works by tracing and optimizing the model graph ahead-of-time.

Explore some benchmarking results here:.

You can find bitsandbytes and torchao quantized models from this blog post in our Hugging Face collection: link to collection.

Here's a quick guide to choosing a quantization backend:.

According to recent reports, quantization significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using large diffusion models. Experiment with these backends to find the best balance of memory, speed, and quality for your needs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This tutorial reveals you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint.
  • We start from an empty cargo latest.
  • In a recent development, the tutorial is split into 12 chapters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that welcome! This tutorial reveals you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint. We open a window, draw rectangles, circles and lines with the mouse, move them around, pick a color, and export the drawing as an image.

We start from an empty cargo latest. By the end, you have about 800 lines of Rust spread over fifteen or so files, with a single dependency: minifb, which opens the window and gives us the keyboard and the mouse. Everything else we write ourselves: filling pixels, drawing a line, checking whether the mouse is on a circle, converting an HSV color to RGB.

In a recent development, the tutorial is split into 12 chapters. Each one ends with a program that compiles and does something you can see, even if at first it's just an image file with a red square in it.

I'm a developer and I've been doing data science for several years. But in my free time, I've always been drawn to low-level things: bare metal, and how a computer works at the very bottom of the stack.

Industry observers note that I wrote this tutorial with someone in mind who is starting out, or simply curious, and who wonders how a program ends up showing something on the screen. It covers the basics of rasterization, that is, how a rectangle or a circle turns into pixels, starting from nothing and in small pieces you can understand one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that that's mostly what I'd like to show: by moving forward step by step, in a language close to the machine, you end up with something that works and that you wrote entirely yourself. It takes time, but there's nothing magic about it. If this tutorial takes away a bit of that mystery and makes a few beginners want to look further down, it will have done its job.

According to recent reports, this tutorial is a way to learn Rust by building something. I assume you've read the first chapters of the Rust Book (variables, functions, if, loops) but haven't written a real program with it yet. The heavier concepts, like enums, traits, borrowing, modules or error handling, come along chapter by chapter, when we need them.

Industry observers note that you don't need to know anything about graphics. As for math, you need Pythagoras for circles and a projection to tell whether the mouse is on a line. I explain it when we get there.

Each chapter has boxes that explain why Rust does things the way it does. If you already know, skip them. Same for the exercises at the end of each chapter: they're there if you want practice, but nothing that follows depends on them.

I'd still recommend typing the code rather than copy-pasting it. It's slower, but typing is how you make mistakes, and fixing them is how you end up understanding what the compiler is trying to tell you.

Recent findings suggest that let's be upfront: at the end, you won't have GIMP. There's no brush, no layers, no undo. And technically, our app isn't even really a Paint. Paint paints pixels that can't be moved once they're down, whereas we keep a list of shapes that can be selected and moved. We come back to this in chapter 11, and the Going further page has ideas for adding a brush, a paint bucket or undo.

After that, Going further suggests ideas to keep going on your own, from freehand drawing to a version that runs in the browser.

Recent findings suggest that all the code is in the pages, you don't need anything else. But if you prefer, the GitHub repo has one tag per chapter: git checkout ch05-mouse gives you the exact code at the end of chapter 5, and git diff ch04-window ch05-mouse demonstrates everything it adds. It's also handy to start again from a clean state if you get lost. The Following along with git page explains all of this.

If you find a mistake, an unclear explanation or a piece of code that doesn't compile, open an issue on GitHub. It really helps.

If you're ready, start here: chapter 0.

Falcon-Arabic: A Breakthrough in Arabic Language Models

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a new benchmark for Arabic NLP.
  • Sources indicate that falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models.
  • Sources indicate that in recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out our official blogpost (EN, AR).

Recent findings suggest that we are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a new benchmark for Arabic NLP. Built on the Falcon 3 architecture, Falcon-Arabic is a multilingual model that supports Arabic, English, and several other languages. It excels in general knowledge, Arabic grammar, mathematical reasoning, complex problem solving, and understanding the rich diversity of Arabic dialects. Falcon-Arabic supports a context length of 32,000 tokens, allowing it to handle long documents and enabling advanced applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in-depth content creation, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

Sources indicate that falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models. It significantly outperforms other Arabic LLMs in its size category and even models up to four times larger across both Arabic-native models and those adapted from other languages. This makes Falcon-Arabic not only a state-of-the-art model in terms of performance, but also a uniquely efficient and accessible solution for developers and researchers working with the Arabic language.

Sources indicate that in recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more. Yet much of this progress has focused on highly represented languages like English, leaving languages such as Arabic underrepresented. Arabic presents unique challenges it's morphologically rich, diglossic (spanning both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and diverse regional dialects), and used across a vast and culturally varied population. Developing robust Arabic LLMs is essential to ensure Arabic-speaking communities are fully included in the AI revolution.

Recent findings suggest that with this goal in mind, we’re introducing Falcon-Arabic a specialized adaptation of the Falcon 3 model family, developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in the UAE. The Falcon models have earned global recognition for their multilingual strength and open-source approach. Falcon-Arabic builds on this legacy, bringing advanced language understanding and generation to Arabic. By training the model to handle both Modern Standard Arabic and key dialects, Falcon-Arabic fills a critical gap in language technology enabling more natural, intelligent, and inclusive Arabic AI across the Gulf, Middle East, and North Africa.

According to recent reports, building Falcon-Arabic started with a strategic decision: rather than training a model from scratch, we chose to adapt a strong multilingual foundation. In the Arabic LLM landscape, three main approaches exist: training from scratch (e.g., Jais-native), adapting multilingual models (like Allam or Fanar), or using models that natively support Arabic alongside other languages (such as Qwen or LLaMA). Observing the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard, it became clear that adapted and multilingual models consistently outperformed others in both efficiency and capability. To build on that momentum, we selected Falcon 3-7B, a model that strikes a practical balance between performance and resource efficiency within the Falcon 3 family developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).

In a recent development, the core challenge was adapting Falcon 3-7B, which originally lacked Arabic support at the tokenizer and embedding level. We addressed this by extending the tokenizer’s vocabulary with 32,000 Arabic-specific tokens, and applying a novel embedding initialization strategy based on textual similarity. This technique mapped new Arabic tokens to semantically related embeddings from the existing vocabulary, allowing the model to inherit prior knowledge and accelerate learning particularly around sentiment, abstract concepts, and reasoning patterns. This gave Falcon-Arabic a head start in understanding and generating high-quality Arabic text.

With the tokenizer and embeddings in place, we began continuous pretraining on high-quality, 100% native Arabic datasets, avoiding the use of machine-translated content to minimize cultural bias and preserve linguistic authenticity. Training followed a multi-stage curriculum: early stages focused on general knowledge and dialect-rich Arabic content to stabilize the model and reinforce logical capabilities, while later phases emphasized math, code, and reasoning. The result is a model that not only speaks Arabic fluently across dialects, but also retains Falcon’s multilingual and reasoning strengths pushing the boundaries for Arabic-first AI.

It has been revealed that we evaluated Falcon-Arabic on OALL v2, the leading benchmark for Arabic Language Models. It includes six multiple-choice tasks such as Arabic MMLU (native and translated), Arabic Exams, Alghafa, MadinahQA, Aratrust and one generative benchmark, Alrage. Falcon-Arabic outperforms all existing Arabic LLMs in its size range and even surpasses models up to 4× larger. It leads in key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, Exams, MadinahQA, and Aratrust, setting a new standard for Arabic-first Language Models.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base-details.

After finalizing the base model training, we performed a post-training alignment phase to fine-tune Falcon-Arabic’s responses according to human preferences. This phase began with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using a combination of high-quality public datasets and internally collected native Arabic instruction data, covering a range of tasks and conversational scenarios.

To further enhance alignment, we applied Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) a reinforcement learning-based method that tunes the model to prefer outputs that humans rate as more helpful, safe, and relevant. This two-step process ensures that Falcon-Arabic Instruct not only understands Arabic well but responds in a way that aligns with real user expectations.

Industry observers note that as shown in the results plots, Falcon-Arabic Instruct leads the pack, outperforming all other Instruct-aligned Arabic LLMs in its size class and even models significantly larger across multiple benchmarks. The model demonstrates strong performance in both instruction following and open-ended dialogue, setting a new standard for Arabic conversational AI.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct-details.

In a recent development, falcon-Arabic sets a upcoming benchmark for Arabic Language Models. With only 7B parameters, it delivers state-of-the-art performance outperforming models of similar size and even those several times larger across key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, MadinahQA, and Aratrust. It combines fluency in Modern Standard Arabic, strong understanding of regional dialects, and robust reasoning and multilingual capabilities, making it ideal for a wide range of applications: from Arabic-first chatbots and educational tools to content generation, code assistance, and document understanding.

Recent findings suggest that to give you a hands-on feel for what Falcon-Arabic can do, we built a simple demo that showcases its capabilities in machine translation even though the model hasn’t been fine-tuned specifically for that task. The tool runs purely on Falcon-7B-Arabic-Instruct, and the results are surprisingly strong across various translation directions. You can try it yourself through the demo linked just below. In fact, we used the same setup to translate this blog post into Arabic for our Arabic-speaking audience. Check it out here 🚀. And if you're curious to explore more, we also provide access to a live playground where you can interact with Falcon-Arabic Instruct and experience its performance across different tasks ✨.

According to recent reports, like all Large Language Models, Falcon-Arabic inherits some common limitations. These include occasional hallucinations (producing plausible but incorrect outputs), sensitivity to how prompts are phrased, and varying performance across very long contexts. While Falcon-Arabic is designed to reduce these issues especially for Arabic tasks people should still apply critical thinking when interpreting results, particularly in high-stakes or fact-sensitive use cases.

According to recent reports, the gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

Industry observers note that the annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

According to recent reports, this is the single most notable gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

Sources indicate that at the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Sources indicate that crucial sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

According to recent reports, one of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 blueprint 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

According to recent reports, the gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

#173644. Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance

📅 21 May 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1915 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants.
  • In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions.
  • Industry observers note that hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out also our official blogpost.

Today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants. At the core of these models lies a hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of the classical Transformer-based attention mechanism with the State Space Model (SSM), known for its superior long-context memory and computational efficiency. This architectural innovation is further enhanced by fundamental advancements in training dynamics and data utilization, enabling Falcon-H1 models to deliver uncompromised performance that rivals the top Transformer-based models across all covered size tiers.

In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions. All our open-source models are with a permissive license based on Apache 2.0.

Industry observers note that hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block. Importantly, the amount of attention and mamba heads can be adjusted independently, allowing for an optimal attention/SSM ratio. This hybrid design enables faster inference, lower memory usage, and strong generalization across tasks.

Wide Range of Model Sizes: Available in six scales—0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B—with both base and instruction-tuned variants, suitable for everything from edge devices to large-scale deployments.

Multilingual by Design: Supports 18 languages natively, including Arabic (ar), Czech (cs), German (de), English (en), Spanish (es), French (fr), Hindi (hi), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), Dutch (nl), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Swedish (sv), Urdu (ur), and Chinese (zh) — with scalability to 100+ languages, thanks to our multilingual tokenizer trained on diverse language datasets.

Compact Models, Massive Performance: Falcon-H1-0.5B delivers performance on par with typical 7B models from 2024, while Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep rivals many of the current leading 7B–10B models. Each Falcon-H1 model is designed to match or exceed the performance of models at least twice its size, making them ideal for low-resource and edge deployments without compromising on capability.

256K Context Support: Falcon-H1 models support up to 256K context length, enabling applications in long-document processing, multi-turn dialogue, and long-range reasoning.

Exceptional STEM capabilities: Falcon-H1 models deliver strong performance in math and science domains thanks to the focus on high-quality STEM data during training.

Robust Training Strategy: Uses a high-efficiency data strategy and customized Maximal Update Parametrization (μP) to ensure smooth and scalable training across model sizes.

When embarking on the Falcon-H1 series development, we chose to fundamentally rethink the training approach. While the field of LLM development has converged on many established practices that reliably produce strong models, these conventions were primarily validated on classical transformer architectures. The shift from pure attention mechanisms to a hybrid attention-SSM design represents a significant architectural change, making it uncertain whether these standard practices would remain optimal.

Recent findings suggest that given this uncertainty, we conducted an extensive experimentation phase, systematically revisiting nearly every aspect of model design and training methodology before launching our final training runs. While we will provide comprehensive details in our upcoming technical report, we'd like to share the key insights that shaped the Falcon-H1 models.

Sources indicate that the hybrid attention-SSM models have a larger configuration space of all the parameters that define the model architecture. Our goal was to probe each of these configuration parameters to check its impact on model performance and efficiency. As a result, we reveal regions of model configuration space with an increased performance at a mild efficiency cost. We can roughly divide the hybrid model configuration space in the following 4 blocks:.

It has been revealed that capabilities of language models are known to come mainly from the training data, and that stays true for Falcon-H1 series. Besides the raw data prepared for the model, it is crucial how and when this data is shown during training. One such data strategy is commonly called curriculum learning, where simpler data is shown at the beginning of the training while the samples requiring more advanced reasoning are left for the end. Surprisingly, a completely opposite strategy worked best for us. Giving even the most complicated data, an advanced math problem or a long context sample, from the beginning of the training seems to give the model more time to learn features essential for handling the respective complex tasks.

Another key aspect is the scarcity of high-quality data. A common concern when training large models is brute force memorization of the data as opposed to its real understanding. To minimize the risk of such memorization, a common practice is not reusing data samples during training, or doing it at most a few times for the highest quality samples. A by-product of this strategy is data mixture being dominated by web samples that have disproportionally large volume compared to high-quality sources. We have found that the memorization effect might be a bit overestimated, and carefully estimating model's memorization window allows to reuse high-quality samples more often without any harm to model's generalization ability.

Sources indicate that classical μP is a technique heavily rooted in theory of neural networks but with a clear practical application: if one finds optimal training hyperparameters at a single base model size, it can be effortlessly transferred to other, typically bigger, model sizes using Mup scaling rules. We employed Mup hyperparameter transfer for the whole Falcon-H1 series, greatly reducing experimentation time and making it possible to train 6 models in parallel.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that, we made the next step into inner workings behind μP to further boost the model performance. In a nutshell, each component of the model “wants” to train at its own intensity, and that intensity depends on the size of the component. μP scaling rules take into account this dependence through so-called ``μP multipliers'' to enable optimal hyperparameter transfer. However, classical μP uses trivial multipliers of 1 at the base model size, which corresponds to a nasusmption that intensity of all components are already optimal at the base size. We discard this assumption and tune the multipliers at the base model size. Specifically, we have divided model parameters into 35 fine-grained groups and performed a joint optimization of the respective 35 multipliers.

One of our first steps in working on Falcon-H1 series was treating and removing spikes that are known to be a serious matter for SSM-based models. The solution that has worked the best for us is placing dampening μP multipliers at a certain location of the SSM block. In addition to the smooth final model training, the removal of spikes is essential to get clean signals in the subsequent experiments.

Sources indicate that we have observed that many aspects of the training dynamics are linked together under a common theme of noise interpretation and control. This includes learning rate and batch size schedules, scaling of the learning rate with batch size, and the behavior of parameter norms. In particular, we have found the parameter norms to be mostly determined by the training hyperparameters rather than the model fitting the data. To take this into account, we have included weight decay, a hyperparameter that primarily controls parameter norms, into both the training schedule and μP multipliers.

In a recent development, the current Falcon-H1 models were trained without reasoning-specific fine-tuning, yet they already demonstrate strong general instruction-following capabilities. To highlight their performance, we present a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against other top-performing Transformer models of similar or larger scales, including: Qwen3-32B (non-thinking mode), Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Gemma3-27B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and LLaMA3.3-70B. For full evaluation settings and methodology, please refer to the Falcon-H1 GitHub page.

One of the standout features of the Falcon-H1 series is the strong performance of its compact models. Below, we compare 1.5B-scale instruct models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Instruct clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct. Even more notably, it performs on par with—or better than many 7B models, including Falcon3-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

🔎 Note: Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep and Falcon-H1-1.5B were trained using identical settings; the only difference lies in their architectural depth and width.

To give a picture of Falcon-H1 performance across languages, we provide average between Hellaswag and MMLU scores for 30B scale models and for a set of selected languages, including Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Swedish. It also demonstrates on-par performance in the other supported languages.

One of the standout features of Falcon-H1 is its ability to handle long-context inputs, an area where State Space Models (SSMs) offer significant advantages in terms of memory efficiency and computational cost.

To demonstrate these capabilities, we evaluate Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct across a set of long-context benchmarks. We focus on three core task categories drawn from the Helmet benchmark suite - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; Recall tasks: JSON KV, RULER MK Needle, RULER MK UUID, RULER MV; Long Document QA tasks: ∞BENCH QA, ∞BENCH MC. These evaluations highlight Falcon-H1’s strength in scaling to longer sequences while maintaining high performance and efficiency.

In addition, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Falcon-H1 series alongside leading Transformer-based models across 23 benchmarks, covering multiple domains and model scales. You can explore the interactive results below—simply select the benchmarks most relevant to your use case to view the corresponding aggregated performance scores (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

We provide a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Base with other leading base models at the same or larger scale, including Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and Gemma3-27B.

🔎 Note: Qwen3-32B does not currently offer a base model checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that below, we compare 1.5B-scale base models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Base clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Base. Notably, it performs on par with Falcon3-7B, and even exceeds it on math and reasoning tasks, making it an excellent foundation for building small-scale reasoning-focused models.

For the base models, we also provide an interactive plot in our official blogpost showcasing their performance across 14 benchmarks, spanning multiple domains and various model scales (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

It has been revealed that we compare input (prefill) and output (generation) throughput between Falcon-H1 and Qwen2.5-32B in the plots below. While Transformers are slightly faster at shorter context lengths, our hybrid model becomes significantly more efficient as the context grows—achieving up to 4× speedup in input throughput and 8× in output throughput at longer sequence lengths. Benchmarks were run using our Falcon-H1 vLLM implementation and the official vLLM implementation of Qwen2.5-32B.

This performance gain highlights the scalability of the Falcon-H1 architecture. We attribute the throughput gap at small context lengths to the more mature optimizations of attention mechanisms, compared to current State Space Models (SSMs) implementations, in current inference pipelines.

⚙️ We invite the community to contribute to further optimizing SSM implementations — a promising direction for advancing the next generation of efficient LLMs.

🔎 Note: Input throughput measures how fast models process tokens when reading/encoding text. Output throughput measures how fast they generate newly introduced tokens. The ratio line shows Falcon-H1/Qwen2.5 performance comparison.

Industry observers note that in line with our mission to foster AI accessibility and collaboration, Falcon-H1 is released under the Falcon LLM license. We hope the AI community finds these models valuable for research, application development, and further experimentation. Falcon-H1 is a continuation of our efforts to create more capable and efficient foundation models. We welcome feedback and collaboration from the community as we continue to refine and advance the capabilities of these models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications.

Recent findings suggest that the condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the tech giant had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds.

It has been revealed that the disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases.

The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS mentioned the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments.

The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations.

Sources indicate that aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case.

Industry observers note that exporters and foreign data centers are expected to check customers for direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located or headquartered in those destinations, including through an ultimate parent. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide sufficient compliance information is a red flag that must be resolved before proceeding.

Sources indicate that A later change from a permitted end use to a prohibited one can require BIS authorization. Data centers already providing covered compute before publication must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date to continue without facing future export restrictions.

Recent findings suggest that computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end customers that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met.

Sources indicate that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries.

Recent findings suggest that the reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located.

Why optimistic updates are corrosive

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was having an X conversation with @ben_codez, and they asked: why is showing an update as succeeded, before the underlying operation has actually succeeded, corrosive?
  • Recent findings suggest that it's corrosive because it normalizes software that is plainly broken and doesn't respect our people.
  • I made a chart of what I understand to be Ben's position on communicating with their users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was having an X conversation with @ben_codez, and they asked: why is showing an update as succeeded, before the underlying operation has actually succeeded, corrosive?

Recent findings suggest that it's corrosive because it normalizes software that is plainly broken and doesn't respect our people. If a user flips a switch, and sees it flip, and then comes back, and the switch is unflipped, the software is broken. How can you operate software that doesn't do what you request it to do? It erodes trust.

I made a chart of what I understand to be Ben's position on communicating with their users.

"Booking confirmed" shown before the server checks the seat.

No self respect Ben: "No self respecting dev would show the user a booking had succeeded before server verification.".

Your like shows as done before the server notes "ok".

Ben: "liking a post", "(It can retry silently).".

If the user closes the tab before the server has it, their like is lost and the user is never told.

Your post reveals greyed out until the server claims "ok".

Ben: "Right!", to a post shown "greyed out maybe, to indicate it wasn't committed".

But in addition to that, it's actually easier to make software that doesn't lie to your consumers. You can skip all the reconciliation machinery that's required to create UI that communicates to users that the change they thought had gone through had indeed not gone through.

Here's a quick demo of using instant intent to communicate the state toggling a switch e.g. a like button.

When you click the switch, the client demonstrates the button as pressed straight away and sends the click to the server. The switch takes no more clicks while it's pressed, and if there's no answer within half a second, it starts to blink. The client then won't patch until the server answers with the reconciled HTML view, which Datastar morphs in place.

Experiment with different latencies and taking it offline, to see how the interaction feels under different scenarios.

The pressed and blinking look is the same CSS the seats use, on the main page.

Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.

Tiny Agents in Python: a MCP-powered agent in ~70 lines of code

📅 23 May 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UPCOMING: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard.
  • Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.
  • According to recent reports, MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPCOMING: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard. 🥳.

Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

According to recent reports, MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs. Essentially, it removed the need to write custom integrations for each tool, making it simpler to plug upcoming capabilities into your LLMs.

In this blog post, we'll show you how to get started with a tiny Agent in Python connected to MCP servers to unlock powerful tool capabilities. You'll see just how easy it is to spin up your own Agent and start building!

Spoiler : An Agent is essentially a while loop built right on top of an MCP Client!

Industry observers note that this section walks you through how to use existing Tiny Agents. We'll cover the setup and the commands to get an agent running.

First, you need to install the latest version of huggingface_hub with the mcp extra to get all the necessary components.

Now, let's run an agent using the CLI!

The coolest part is that you can load agents directly from the Hugging Face Hub tiny-agents Dataset, or specify a path to your own local agent configuration!

If you don't provide a path to a specific agent configuration, our Tiny Agent will connect by default to the following two MCP servers:.

It has been revealed that the following example indicates a web-browsing agent configured to use the Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and it comes equipped with a playwright MCP server, which lets it use a web browser! The agent config is loaded specifying its path in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents Hugging Face dataset.

Industry observers note that when you run the agent, you'll see it load, listing the tools it has discovered from its connected MCP servers. Then, it's ready for your prompts!

do a Web Search for HF inference providers on Brave Search and open the first result and then give me the list of the inference providers supported on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that you can also use Gradio Spaces as MCP servers! The following example uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and connects to a FLUX.1 [schnell] image generation HF Space as an MCP server. The agent is loaded from its configuration in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

Generate a 1024x1024 image of a tiny astronaut hatching from an egg on the surface of the moon.

Now that you've seen how to run existing Tiny Agents, the following sections will dive deeper into how they work and how to build your own.

Industry observers note that each agent's behavior (its default model, inference provider, which MCP servers to connect to, and its initial system prompt) is defined by an agent.json file. You can also provide a custom PROMPT.md in the same directory for a more detailed system prompt. Here is an example:.

agent.json The model and provider fields specify the LLM and inference provider used by the agent. The servers array defines the MCP servers the agent will connect to. In this example, a "stdio" MCP server is configured. This type of server runs as a local process. The Agent starts it using the specified command and args, and then communicates with it via stdin/stdout to discover and execute available tools.

You can find more details about Hugging Face Inference Providers here.

Modern LLMs are built for function calling (or tool use), which enables users to easily build applications tailored to specific use cases and real-world tasks.

It has been revealed that A function is defined by its schema, which informs the LLM what it does and what input arguments it expects. The LLM decides when to use a tool, the Agent then orchestrates running the tool and feeding the result back.

InferenceClient implements the same tool calling interface as the OpenAI Chat Completions API, which is the established standard for inference providers and the community.

Recent findings suggest that the MCPClient is the heart of our tool-use functionality. It's now part of huggingface_hub and uses the AsyncInferenceClient to communicate with LLMs.

The full MCPClient code is in here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓.

Key responsibilities of the MCPClient:.

​​Here’s a glimpse of how it connects to an MCP server (the add_mcp_server method):.

In a recent development, it supports stdio servers for local tools (like accessing your file system), and http servers for remote tools! It's also compatible with sse, which is the previous standard for remote tools.

According to recent reports, the MCPClient's process_single_turn_with_tools method is where the LLM interaction happens. It sends the conversation history and available tools to the LLM via AsyncInferenceClient.chat.completions.create(..., stream=True).

First, the method determines all tools the LLM should be aware of for the current turn – this includes tools from MCP servers and any special "exit loop" tools for agent control; then, it makes a streaming call to the LLM:.

As chunks arrive from the LLM, the method iterates through them. Each chunk is immediately yielded, then we reconstruct the complete text response and any tool calls.

Once the stream is complete, if the LLM requested any tool calls (now fully reconstructed in final_tool_calls), the method processes each one:.

It first checks if the tool called exits the loop (exit_loop_tool). If not, it finds the correct MCP session responsible for that tool and calls session.call_tool(). The result (or error response) is then formatted, added to the conversation history, and yielded so the Agent is aware of the tool's output.

According to recent reports, with the MCPClient doing all the job for tool interactions, our Agent class becomes wonderfully simple. It inherits from MCPClient and adds the conversation management logic.

The Agent class is tiny and focuses on the conversational loop, the code can be found here.

When an Agent is created, it takes an agent config (model, provider, which MCP servers to use, system prompt) and initializes the conversation history with the system prompt. The load_tools() method then iterates through the server configurations (defined in agent.json) and calls add_mcp_server (from the parent MCPClient) for each one, populating the agent's toolbox.

The Agent.run() method is an asynchronous generator that processes a single user input. It manages the conversation turns, deciding when the agent's current task is complete.

There are a lot of cool ways to explore and expand upon the MCP Client and the Tiny Agent 🔥 Here are some ideas to get you started:.

Sources indicate that pull requests and contributions are welcome! Again, everything here is open source! 💎❤️.
