AI Could Soon Edit Live Videos in Real Time

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context.
  • It has been revealed that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time.
  • Industry observers note that microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered editing could reshape that connection by changing speech before it reaches viewers.

It has been revealed that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time. Such capabilities could support clearer communication, but they also raise questions about whose words audiences actually hear. Understanding the differences between original and AI-edited video can help explain what editable video could mean for viewer trust.

Industry observers note that microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch. Its scope covers both recorded presentations and near-real-time changes to live events. The proposed system could remove filler words, correct mispronunciations and replace other speech, including colloquial expressions or words it identifies as inappropriate. It would also adjust the speaker’s lip movements to match the replacement audio.

Audience profiles could influence those choices. The filing describes profiles containing details such as age, language, cultural background and education level, which could guide speech replacements. Viewers could therefore receive different versions of the same event, with wording tailored to their profiles.

Industry observers note that the proposed process begins with capturing a speaker’s audio and video during a live event. An AI agent identifies words to change, guided by editing settings or audience profiles. Generative AI then creates replacement speech and adjusts the corresponding video frames, including lip movements, to match.

These changes would happen within a short broadcast buffer. The filing describes a roughly one-to-10-second delay, giving the system time to process speech before presenting the modified stream. To keep the result flowing naturally, the system would smooth audio and visual transitions around each replacement. Some implementations could also update captions to reflect the edited speech and retain original recordings for later reference.

Industry observers note that multilingual presentations could let viewers hear speech in their preferred language while seeing lip movements that match the translation. Educational broadcasts and training sessions could use this approach to reach audiences across language barriers. Audience-based adjustments could also help explain unfamiliar terms in language suited to viewers’ knowledge.

It has been revealed that speakers who stutter could choose to use optional editing support during presentations or live broadcasts. That choice should remain with the speaker, including control over which speech patterns the system changes. Removing a hesitation can make speech easier to follow while preserving the message, although pauses sometimes convey uncertainty or emphasis. Meanwhile, replacing a factual claim changes the substance of the statement and requires a different level of scrutiny and speaker approval.

Industry observers note that existing AI tools already offer parts of the proposed system’s capabilities, including translated speech, synchronized lip movements and live voice modification. Their uses and limitations help show how Microsoft’s proposal compares with available products and research demonstrations.

HeyGen’s Video Translation tool works with uploaded footage, translating speech into a selected language and synchronizing the speaker’s lips with the fresh audio. Its Dynamic Duration option lets individual segments stretch or compress by up to 20%, allowing more natural pacing when translations are longer or shorter. This flexibility helps accommodate differences in phrasing between languages.

The workflow processes an existing recording before the creator shares the translated version. Microsoft’s proposed system would instead modify an incoming live broadcast within a short delay, making changes while the event continues.

Krisp’s AI Accent Conversion processes speech during live conversations, adjusting pronunciation to help listeners understand the speaker more easily. It aims to preserve the person’s voice and tone while modifying how words sound. This could support communication in customer service calls and meetings where unfamiliar accents create listening challenges.

According to recent reports, the distinction lies in what changes. Accent conversion focuses on pronunciation while preserving the words and their meanings. Microsoft’s proposed system goes further by allowing word replacements and corresponding video edits, potentially changing the statement itself.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s VASA-1 explores how AI can turn a still portrait into a moving, speaking face using an accompanying audio clip. Beyond matching mouth movements to speech, it generates changes in expression and head position that make the face appear more lifelike. It offers another example of how AI can create convincing footage from limited source material.

Industry observers note that its ability to animate a portrait also creates opportunities for impersonation, particularly when someone pairs a recognizable face with fabricated speech. Those concerns led Microsoft to withhold public access, with no full release planned until it has confidence in its ability to ensure regulation-compliant use. This position reflects the challenge of making useful avatar technology available while limiting applications that could falsely portray someone saying something.

According to recent reports, when AI changes speech while preserving a speaker’s appearance, viewers could attribute the replacement words to that person. A speaker might approve pronunciation corrections without agreeing to changes that reshape an opinion or factual claim. Consent therefore needs to cover the scope of editing, especially when the finished video presents generated words as the speaker’s own.

Generated talking faces and synthetic voices extend this concern beyond alterations to existing footage. They could make someone appear to deliver a statement without participating in the recording. Some people already struggle to recognize sarcasm or identify a skit. When staged content already confuses, the prospect of widespread deepfake misinformation becomes a reasonable concern. Research shows that all age groups are susceptible to digital manipulation.

Convincing impersonations could damage reputations or distort public debate. Their growing plausibility could also give people an excuse to dismiss authentic recordings as AI fabrications, making genuine evidence harder to establish.

Broadcasters and creators should clearly disclose AI edits and provide access to original recordings, especially when changes affect meaning. These steps help audiences understand what changed and give speakers control over statements presented in their name. Independent platforms like C2PA Content Credentials can support transparency by documenting media origins and editing history. They function like a nutrition label for digital content, allowing anyone to inspect the available history using compatible tools.

Recent findings suggest that for consequential clips, viewers should compare the footage with sources and independent reporting. Realistic faces, matching lip movements and familiar voices alone offer limited grounds for trust.

AI video editing could improve cross-language communication and give speakers more control over how they present themselves. Microsoft’s proposed system and research demonstrations represent different stages of development. As audiovisual edits become more convincing, disclosure and verifiable original recordings will become more important for maintaining trust.

  • Industry observers note that solomon also unveiled more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.

Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon unveiled the next phase in Toronto. The expansion adds to the fund’s initial $300 million and is intended to help Canadian organizations develop, test and commercialize AI products by offsetting cloud-compute costs. Eligible work includes model training, inference and fine-tuning.

Industry observers note that solomon also unveiled more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies. Those earlier-phase awards are distinct from the expansion and cover health care, agriculture, manufacturing, finance and transportation projects.

Sources indicate that the updated program guide covers up to 80% of eligible cloud-compute costs from sovereign providers and up to 50% from Canadian-based providers. Sovereign suppliers must operate infrastructure in Canada, process and store data there, be incorporated and registered in Canada, be Canadian-owned, and keep governance and decision-making authority in the country.

Canadian-based providers must meet the infrastructure, data and incorporation requirements. The ownership and governance tests do not apply to that category. Multinational companies with Canadian-registered entities can therefore qualify when the infrastructure and data remain in Canada. The rate structure offers a larger potential subsidy for choosing a provider with Canadian ownership and control without excluding multinational suppliers’ Canadian operations.

Eligible proposals must include $100,000 to $5 million in compute costs and end no later than March 31, 2030. Applicants can be Canadian-registered for-profit companies, nonprofit corporations or charities, including qualifying postsecondary institutions; they generally need fewer than 500 full-time-equivalent employees, Canada-based research and development teams and a commercialization plan. Contributions may be non-repayable, conditionally repayable or repayable, depending on the project’s assessed benefits and risk.

Health and life sciences applicants must submit a statement of interest by 11:59 p.m. ET on December 17, 2026. Those invited to proceed must file full applications by 11:59 p.m. ET on January 4, 2027, with compute contracts, invoices or other documentation in place or in progress. A selected applicant whose agreement is still in progress must finalize it before signing a contribution agreement.

Industry observers note that assessment covers market potential, organizational and financial capacity, technology readiness, expected economic and public benefits, and alignment with government priorities. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada says it will endeavour to make funding decisions within 90 business days after the call closes. The department will also use AI tools to support analysis of application information, conduct risk-related research and assist with program administration, while retaining final authority over recipient selection.

Recent findings suggest that an official recipient backgrounder indicates the range of supported work. Vancouver-based Apera AI is developing 4D vision and simulation-driven models for factory robots, while Toronto-based RetiSpec is working on a non-invasive retinal-imaging tool intended to detect early Alzheimer’s disease. Gotcare, also in Toronto, is building an AI-enabled home-healthcare management system focused on rural and underserved populations.

It has been revealed that the sector calls sit within the government’s AI for All strategy, which names five priority areas: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics. The strategy describes Canada’s sovereign compute capacity as nascent and says most Canadian small and medium-sized businesses lack an affordable domestic option, leaving them reliant on foreign cloud platforms for training, testing and deployment.

Sources indicate that the government is also connecting the renewed fund to its commitment to bring 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute online. The expanded program is intended to create demand for Canadian providers and support investment in domestic AI infrastructure, linking commercialization assistance to a broader infrastructure objective.

That makes the reimbursement gap central to the policy: companies receive the strongest support when their computing is owned, operated and governed in Canada. The open question is whether the demand created by these subsidies can support enough affordable domestic capacity while helping Canadian AI products reach the market.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality.
  • Industry observers note that fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality. We also added support for FSDP and PEFT, making it easier than ever to scale GRPO across multiple GPUs.

Industry observers note that fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning. RL has traditionally been applied to optimize large language models (LLMs) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. This approach, often associated with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), utilizes a separately trained reward model to guide the fine-tuning of the primary model.

Recent findings suggest that however, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results. The success of RLHF also depends on the capability of the reward model to effectively discriminate between desired and un-desired behaviour from our model.

It has been revealed that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has seen significant recent popularity alongside DeepSeek's R1 model. GRPO eschews the pre-trained reward model and value models used in RLHF and instead relies on verifiable reward functions which can check the correctness of a model's output in a closed-form manner without needing an external reward model. This has resulted in massive improvements when using GRPO instead of PPO for fine-tuning on domains which are easily verifiable, such as teaching a model to reason, and perform well on math and coding tasks.

The following diagram shows the GRPO vs PPO training pipeline (ref: Figure 4 of DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models):.

That remarked, RL training still eats up a ton of GPU memory, so there's still plenty of room for optimizations here. In this blog post, we talk about an optimization that we recently added to TRL that cuts peak memory usage by 40% during GRPO Training, and we also dive into how to scale GRPO to multiple GPUs and nodes without losing performance or correctness.

We extended the Liger Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss, which lets us avoid having to store the full logits in memory for every training step. The calculation of logits, which involves the model's output head, is a significant contributor to peak memory usage, especially when dealing with large vocabularies, long sequence lengths, or large batch sizes. We address this by chunking the input to the lm_head across the batch and running the forward pass one chunk at a time.

Sources indicate that but if you just implement it in a straightforward way, you won't actually be able to reduce the peak memory since you'd still need to keep all the logits in GPU memory for the backward pass. To get around that, we calculate the gradients for each loss chunk (with respect to the input chunk and the lm_head weight) during the forward pass, and then accumulate them as we go through each chunk.

Here's the visualization of the optimization (ref: Byron Hsu):.

We recently integrated Liger GRPO with TRL in PR #3184, so now you can use the Liger GRPO loss just by setting use_liger_loss to True in your GRPOConfig and enjoy the memory savings!

Heads up: these features aren't in the latest TRL release yet, so you'll need to install TRL from source for now:.

and then you can use it like this:.

Recent findings suggest that we ran a bunch of GRPO experiments with and without the Liger GRPO Loss to see how things compare. For the policy model, we used Qwen3-0.6B and played around with different batch sizes. All the experiments were run on the gsm8k dataset using its reward functions.

Here's the plots of peak memory usage vs batch size for both FP32 and BF16 training. As expected, the memory savings get better with larger batch sizes since we chunk along the batch dimension. So when the batch size goes up, the Liger chunked loss ends up using a lot less memory, up to 40% less, compared to the regular (non-liger) version.

Quick note: Right now, we only support FP32, but we're working on open-sourcing BF16 support for Liger GRPO in TRL. The BF16 results shown here are from internal patches we've been testing.

We also show that Liger Loss is effectively accurate. As seen in the plot, rewards over training steps stay pretty much the same as what you'd see using the standard TRL implementation.

In a recent development, we also added FSDP and PEFT support to Liger GRPO Loss in PR #3260 and PR #3355, respectively, allowing consumers to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs or nodes. PEFT techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters by only tuning the weights of smaller adapter weights on top of the original model, significantly lowering memory pressure as gradients, activations, and optimizer states for the entire model don't need to be held in memory. Additionally, using PEFT in GRPO allows one to forgo loading a separate reference model during training, as we can obtain the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

Here, we show a multi-GPU GRPO training plot using FSDP and PEFT, where we compare the maximum training batch size possible with and without the Liger Loss across different Qwen3 model sizes. We found that with Liger, we were able to bump up the batch size by around 1.5 to 1.8x!

In a recent development, to accelerate text generation during training, Liger Loss can be effectively combined with TRL's integrated vLLM server. This significantly speeds up the collection of rollout data with minimal overhead and offers a seamless integration experience.

It has been revealed that start the vLLM Server: First, launch the vLLM server. This server will handle the generation requests from your training script. Open a terminal and run:.

Note: We assign CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 to run the vLLM server on a specific GPU (GPU 1 in this case), leaving other GPUs free for training.

Configure and Run Your Training Script: Next, modify your training script to use the vLLM server. The key change is setting use_vllm=True in your GRPOConfig.

Launch the Training: Finally, run your training script using accelerate launch (or python if not using Accelerate for multi-GPU/distributed training). Make sure to target a different GPU for training if your vLLM server is occupying one.

(Assuming your script is named train.py and you want to run training on GPU 0).

By following these steps, you can leverage vLLM for faster generation turnarounds during your GRPO training with Liger Loss.

With the integration of Liger-GRPO into TRL, alongside FSDP and PEFT support, fine-tuning language models with GRPO is now more memory-efficient and scalable than ever. We encourage the community to try out these latest features and share their feedback to help us further improve RL training for LLMs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

In a recent development, doorDash has rebuilt its real-time dispatch platform to handle growing delivery demand, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The redesign delivers 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability during peak periods, while enabling the company to run machine learning and reinforcement learning models within dispatch workflows.

The previous dispatch engine tightly coupled business logic, logistics state management, and computationally intensive routing algorithms. As delivery volume increased, its optimization workload became increasingly difficult to process within the time available for dispatch decisions. The underlying algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and during peak periods, demand approached four times the system's processing capacity. The engine consequently relied on fallback heuristics and sometimes made assignment decisions using incomplete information.

As the DoorDash engineering team explained:.

The fatal bottleneck wasn't just raw machine capacity; it was the speed of reality.

In a recent development, rather than address the bottleneck through conventional horizontal scaling, DoorDash redesigned the execution model around two independently scalable tiers. The engineering team described the motivation:.

To scale into the future, the system didn't just need more capacity; it demanded a fundamentally new execution model.

Recent findings suggest that the latest platform separates execution into two independently scalable tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, maintains global logistics state, and validates business rules. Stateless compute workers handle mathematical optimization, vehicle-routing heuristics, and model inference.

It has been revealed that the coordinator distributes localized portions of logistics data to workers using payload sharding over gRPC. This avoids broadcasting the entire global state to every worker and reduces network overhead. Workers process their assigned optimization tasks independently, while the coordinator manages orchestration and result aggregation.

Evolution from DoorDash's monolithic dispatch engine to its distributed architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

It has been revealed that the redesign addresses computational complexity through hierarchical decomposition. Rather than solving one global optimization problem, the coordinator partitions logistics data into geographic clusters and delivery trajectories. Workers process smaller problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer combines results across partitions.

In a recent development, doorDash used shadow testing before directing live dispatch decisions to the newly introduced platform. Production requests were duplicated, with the legacy engine determining assignments while the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison. Teams evaluated matching quality, delivery times, and resilience under load. After establishing parity, they used controlled switchback experiments and fallback mechanisms during rollout.

Shadow testing compares legacy and new dispatch outputs (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

DoorDash reports a tenfold increase in dispatch throughput, with more than 99.96% of runs completing within 20 seconds. During Super Bowl Sunday, the platform maintained more than 99.99% availability despite a 10% week-over-week increase in peak volume.

Sources indicate that the architecture also introduces a hybrid L1/L2 model serving. Latency-sensitive inference runs locally within compute workers using ONNX Runtime, avoiding remote procedure call overhead. More complex evaluations use isolated remote model-serving clusters, keeping heavier workloads away from the coordinator's state-management path.

Sources indicate that doorDash has also deployed multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust dispatch objective weights based on localized marketplace feedback, including merchant congestion and courier utilization. The agents adapt the trade-off between delivery speed and batching efficiency at individual stores. The approach was evaluated through production switchback experiments and accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback.

  • In a recent development, your career has taken you from handheld computing and wireless technology at Mindtree to IoT, enterprise software, and now AI-driven application development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that vikram Srivats is Chief Commercial Officer and Head of Product Experience at WaveMaker. His career spans handheld computing, wireless technology, IoT, and enterprise software. He focuses on the architectural and organizational requirements that turn emerging technologies into maintainable applications at enterprise scale, with an emphasis on code ownership, design consistency, and engineering discipline.

Recent findings suggest that waveMaker provides an agentic application-generation platform for enterprise development teams. Its two-pass approach separates AI-assisted interpretation of design intent from deterministic code generation, using a structured intermediate representation. The platform combines agent, visual, and code-editor workflows with reusable components and integrations designed to fit existing development practices.

In a recent development, your career has taken you from handheld computing and wireless technology at Mindtree to IoT, enterprise software, and now AI-driven application development. How has that progression shaped your view of what it takes for an emerging technology to become genuinely useful at enterprise scale?

According to recent reports, every wave I’ve watched from up close — handheld computing, wireless, IoT, cloud applications — seems to follow the same pattern. The technology does something impressive in a controlled setting. Then it hits enterprise scale, and the gap becomes visible: what it does in a pilot versus what it does reliably in production at a massive user scale, under stringent security audit, integrated with systems built a decade ago, and maintained by engineers who weren’t associated with the tech development itself.

The companies who survive (and thrive) solve the hard architectural problems, not just the interesting, shiny ones. Enterprise scale punishes pure optimism and speed, and rewards discipline and rigor. A technology earns the right to be called enterprise-grade when it performs consistently, survives review, and can be changed by someone who didn’t build it.

According to recent reports, AI coding tools can generate functional applications remarkably quickly. Where do you see the biggest gap today between code that works in a demo and software that is actually ready for production?

Recent findings suggest that the gap is structural. Watching an AI tool generate a working UI in thirty seconds, you’re seeing the easy part: assembling recognizable patterns into something that renders. You’re not seeing consistent adherence to your design system, correct authentication and authorization flows, proper error handling across edge cases, clean integration with your existing APIs, code your security team can audit, or output another developer can modify six months from now without the original author present.

The data backs this up. CodeRabbit’s analysis of production pull requests found AI-generated code introduces 1.7 times more problems than human-written code. Veracode’s testing found security vulnerabilities in roughly 45% of AI-generated output. Google’s DORA research highlighted a 7.2% drop in delivery stability among teams using AI coding tools. The fix is the right architecture around AI that can actually guarantee quality and cost with speed.

According to recent reports, prompt-driven development has made software creation much faster and more accessible. What are the limitations of relying primarily on prompts once applications become larger, more complex, and business-critical?

Prompt-driven development is single-pass: describe intent, the model generates output, you hope it matches requirements. That works for self-contained tasks. It breaks down as complexity grows.

According to recent reports, the core problem is that prompts carry no persistent context about your organization’s standards. An LLM has no memory of the architectural decision your team made many sprints ago — every prompt starts fresh. You get stylistic inconsistency across components, duplicated logic, security configurations that drift from established patterns, and a codebase that gets harder to reason about with each addition. Enterprise applications are living systems built on years of accumulated decisions. Prompts generate for the moment, not the long term, and that mismatch leads to architectural drift or worse, no architecture at all. If you were building a skyscraper, would you skip architecture and planning?

Industry observers note that generative AI is inherently non-deterministic, while enterprises generally want predictable and repeatable software. How significant is that tension, and what approaches can development teams use to control it?

The tension is real. Non-determinism in a creative tool is a feature. In a compiler, it is almost a fatal flaw. Applying LLM-based generation directly to production code treats a creative tool as a compiler, and the results are predictably unpredictable.

The architectural fixes: give the model a narrower, well-defined output space instead of letting it generate arbitrary code. Use an intermediate representation that validates intent before code gets emitted. Build guardrails that encode your organization’s standards so the model operates inside them. Non-determinism is valuable in the reasoning phase, figuring out what to build, and destructive in the generation phase, actually building it. Separating those two phases matters.

It has been revealed that waveMaker uses an intermediate representation and a two-pass approach rather than generating production code directly from prompts. Why do you believe separating AI reasoning from deterministic code generation can produce more reliable applications?

According to recent reports, the two-pass compiler is one of the foundational breakthroughs in software engineering. Early compilers were single-pass: read source, emit machine code, hope for the best. They were fast but fragile. They couldn’t reason about the whole program before committing to output. The move to two-pass — separating analysis from synthesis — is what gave us the reliability and optimization that made modern software possible.

Industry observers note that AI code generation repeated the single-pass mistake. WaveMaker applies the same historical fix. In the first pass, AI agents constrained by a Model Context Protocol (MCP, trained on a decade of production application patterns) convert design intent and natural language into WaveMaker Markup Language (WML): a compact, structured, language-agnostic intermediate representation that captures what the application should do without committing to how it gets implemented. In the second pass, a deterministic, template-based code generator converts WML into production-ready Angular, React or React Native code. Same WML in, same code out, every time. No hallucinations, no phantom dependencies.

It has been revealed that the AI does what it does well: understand intent. The deterministic engine does what it does well: execute reliably. Neither phase carries the full burden of correctness alone. InfoWorld’s published analysis of this lays out the full technical case.

How should AI-generated applications incorporate an organization’s existing design systems, architectural standards, APIs, and reusable components rather than creating something fresh with every prompt?

Every time a tool generates a slightly different button style, skips your established component library, or builds a newly introduced API integration pattern instead of reusing an existing one, it adds technical debt that takes engineers months to reconcile.

The fix is encoding organizational standards as hard constraints, not prompt suggestions. WaveMaker’s component library propagates design tokens from Figma directly, so your design system isn’t something you describe to the AI: it’s actually the space the AI operates in. API integrations via OpenAPI and Swagger get registered once and reused consistently. Security configurations — RBAC, SSO, OAuth, MFA — are set once and applied deterministically across every generated application. Your standards become the rails the system runs on.

In a recent development, security, testing, version control, and CI/CD are already deeply embedded in enterprise development. How should AI application-generation tools fit into these workflows without creating an entirely separate development process?

They shouldn’t create a parallel workflow. The moment an AI tool requires a separate repository, a separate deployment pipeline, or a separate security review process, it adds complexity instead of removing it. Enterprise teams have spent years building the practices around Git, CI/CD, and security scanning that make delivery reliable. Any AI layer that disrupts those workflows gets rejected, correctly.

Industry observers note that instead, AI generated code should live in your Git repository, run through your existing CI/CD pipelines, and get reviewed by your security teams using the tools they already use. There should be no proprietary runtime, no vendor-managed deployment, no lock-in that requires staying on the platform to keep applications running. The generated code should be yours: readable, auditable, maintainable by any engineer who knows the open standards framework.

Industry observers note that one concern with AI-generated software is the technical debt that may emerge months or years later. What needs to happen at the generation stage to ensure that developers can understand, modify, and maintain the resulting code over time?

In a recent development, yes, technical debt from AI generation doesn’t surface immediately. This can be in the form of inconsistent patterns, undocumented assumptions, duplicated logic with subtle variations, and dependencies nobody can explain.

It has been revealed that what has to happen at generation time is disciplined structure. Generated code should follow consistent, recognizable patterns, because consistency is what lets someone who wasn’t there at creation understand it. It should use your established components. And if you have an intermediate representation, that itself is a readable artifact that an engineer who needs to understand why an application behaves a certain way can inspect and trace the reasoning back to the original design intent. That traceability is what separates maintainable generated code from a black box.

Most AI coding assistants have initially focused on making individual developers more productive. What changes when AI development systems are designed for entire engineering teams, including architects, designers, security teams, and developers?

Recent findings suggest that almost everything changes. Individual productivity tools optimize for one loop: one developer, one task, fast feedback. Team-scale systems solve a different problem. How do you maintain consistency across dozens of developers working in parallel? How do an architect’s decisions propagate to every component, not just the ones they personally touch? How do designers get a voice in the output without writing code? How do security teams set standards once and have them enforced automatically across everything generated?

That change from tools that assist to platforms that constrain productively, is the real design challenge. Architects, designers, developers, and security teams need different interfaces to the same underlying system. Architects define structural patterns. Designers watch their design tokens carry through every generated component. Security teams configure authentication once. Developers move between agent mode, visual mode, and code editor mode depending on the task. Everyone operates in the same system, on the same codebase, with the same standards enforced. Scale only happens because the platform was designed for teams, not individuals.

As agentic development matures, which parts of the software development lifecycle do you expect AI agents to take greater ownership of, and which decisions will continue to require human engineering judgment?

According to recent reports, agents will take increasing ownership of the translation layer: converting human intent into structured artifacts. Figma designs into component specifications. Business requirements into data models. API contracts into integration stubs. These are tasks where the input is well-defined, the output space is constrained, and correctness can be verified. Agents will also get better at producing a starting point that’s 80% correct and needs human refinement — faster and better than a blank page.

What will remain with human engineers is anything involving competing values. Should this feature prioritize accessibility or performance when you can’t have both? Should this architecture optimize for extensibility or simplicity given where the product is likely to go? Should this security trade-off get made given the organization’s risk appetite? Agents can inform those decisions. They can’t make them. The most dangerous outcome of agentic AI is assuming that because an agent can make a decision, it should. The best engineering organizations will use AI to move faster on what can be specified, and preserve human judgment for what requires it.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore an AI-powered platform for building and modernizing enterprise applications should visit WaveMaker.

In a recent development, as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

The State of Allocators in 2026 - Finally Stabilised

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's only been a couple of months since the last article, and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised!
  • So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it?
  • In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's only been a couple of months since the last article, and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised! While it feels like the never type did steal a bit of thunder, rust 1.100 was nonetheless a monumental release. Congratulations on the team that shepherded this through.

So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it? What does it get us besides closer feature parity with other system languages like C++ & Zig?

In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit.

Sources indicate that this was one of the leading cases for custom allocation. Dropping in rust is not free. There has been prior art in actually moving memory to a dedicated thread to Drop highly nested structures. This is actually only half a solution. You're still paying for the deallocation call costs, just it's not in the hot path anymore.

Instead, what if we knew that we would have a period of time in our code, where we're going to allocate a lot of stuff, do something with it, and then free everything? A good example of this is a web request, or a database query.

A request comes in, fills in some data structures, and then when the request finishes, the memory isn't needed anymore so it's dropped. This sort of "burst" pattern of allocation, where you allocate a lot up front, and then tear things down all at once at the end, is quite common.

According to recent reports, for this we can use a bump allocator: reserve a big block of memory, and allocate from that, rather than paying the cost of talking to the system allocator for every allocation. Think of it like the BufReader and BufWriter of std io, rather than make repeated syscalls to fetch data, we can buffer that data in a big block, so that we can reduce the overhead considerably.

You want more memory? Just check if the size fits in our block, return that slice, increment our counter (bump!), and we're done. We can add more blocks as well, if we run out. This makes allocations very cheap, we don't need to keep much state around besides from a counter.

The downsides of this approach is when we come to deallocate memory. We don't keep track around where individual allocations are made. However, this actually solves our drop takes a long time problem, since we can just deallocate everything all at once.

Essentially if the impl of the bump allocator is:.

Sources indicate that there are a few tradeoffs for doing things like this in a bump allocator, and not every allocation is going to benefit. Hence why it's crucial to be able to adjust our allocation strategy locally rather than just globally. However, an astute reader might notice that, if we are bumping large swathes of memory, this is going to possibly cause our memory usage to increase considerably. Well, that brings us to our next section: memory accounting.

In a recent development, the next challenge that can be solved by custom allocators is knowing how much memory particular sections of code is being used. I.e, memory accounting. The key here is that, we can use existing allocators, and sprinkle in some extra bookkeeping to keep a pretty accurate ledger.

There are a number of use cases that accounting can shape the behaviour of code. Say you have a cache of objects, and you want to set a threshold above which, we start evicting entries. Or say you want to do an external sort, but you don't know how major your data structures are at the start, but you want to use up as much memory as possible. Or maybe you are wanting to place a limit on a code sandbox, because it's sharing resources with other sandboxes.

What you can do is wrap an allocator, with a custom accounting layer, and use this to drive your decisions. I.e, here is a very trivial example:.

Then we can wrap the global allocator, and see how much our cache is using:.

Now, a single atomic, while is great for an example, does have some perf overhead. So, one of the crates that I have created, while keeping in mind performance, is thresher: an accounting allocator with a callback on threshold. It uses a combined "local" task/thread and "global" counter to avoid atomic contention, feeding back in every 64KiB of allocation.

thresher gets its name from the cutest shark: the Thresher Shark.

Now, what you can do with thresher is, use it to trigger callbacks when allocations are hit:.

This prints out what you'd expect:.

Industry observers note that one production use case, is that we're using thresher on logfire to provide us heap profiles of our rust services when memory hits a configured threshold. I did a deep dive into heap profiles and why they are extremely useful in an older blog: a tale of two lengths. In thresher you can find a jemalloc example where you can instrument this yourself!

OK so we can control memory when it is dropped, we can use memory accounting to know how much memory we're using, what's left? How about where it goes?

It has been revealed that this is probably the more esoteric of the 3 examples I wanted to give. There are some situations where you actually need to control where the memory lives, and sometimes by doing some allocation tricks you can get better performance out.

One example would be what smallvec and friends do. Instead of going straight to the heap to allocate things, they have a small amount that lives on the stack, and only if allocations go above a certain size, then do they write to the heap.

While smallvec is more battle tested, here is some example code about how you could do this with the allocator API:.

Then we can use our toy stack first allocator:.

Et voila! We have smaller allocations on the stack and then push to the heap as needed. This can give some good performance boosts.

Industry observers note that normally when you align memory allocations, this is based upon the thing that is being allocated for. I.e, is it a u64? align to 8 bytes or a u32? align to 4. If it's not correctly aligned, this can cause undefined behaviour and all sorts. You notice in both the bump and small stack example I had to do some shenanigans to find the next appropriately aligned address. However, there is some scenarios where the alignment of memory is external to what is being allocated.

In linux, when you read anything from disk via standard syscalls, you are usually reading from the kernel's page cache. I.e, the spare memory the kernel has around to make things transparently fast. Most of the time that is fine, but there are some times when you want to bypass it.

I.e, there is a long standing bug in kubernetes that can cause pod eviction if you are using the page cache. Or: if you are doing your own caching layer, sometimes it doesn't make sense to double up on memory devoted to caching files.

So, there is a bailout provided, in the guise of O_DIRECT that allows you to directly access files from the file system. However: one of the requirements of using this flag is that you are reading or writing into memory that is aligned to the device's logical block size. This is usually a multiple of 512, but can be less or more depending on the hardware.

The implementation of a block aligned allocator is pretty simple, here's one where we just hardset it to 4096:.

With this, we can now write simple code to read directly using O_DIRECT:.

Here, the read_exact call can fail on some devices if we're not using block size aligned allocations.

Like with the stack first allocation, there are libraries that allow you do this already, such as the aligned-vec crate, with their own data types to work nicely.

But here's the rub: say you had an application where you wanted to blend and mix in different allocation strategies: some vecs you want to be block aligned, some you want allocated on the stack, but you want to be able to use shared methods for both. Do we want to use smallvec and aligned-vec in order to deal with a data structure that is essentially the same thing, just allocated differently?

std allocators allows you to be generic over the collections, regardless of allocator used:.

And I think that's pretty powerful.

Sources indicate that it's going to take a bit of time for the ecosystem to catch up to custom allocators. A lot of popular crates have an MSRV policy that precludes them from using even fresh standard features, and some existing crates, which I would think are a shoe in for the new allocator API, as of writing do not yet have support.

In a recent development, the libs team isn't done yet. This is the MVP of allocators, and, like I mentiond in the the last article, this is the beginning of custom allocator support. There is still work to go to support other collection types like maps etc.. so much to be done. I think that what we have is useful enough to start using it now, and also to start adapting and allowing library consumers the ability to provide their own allocators with their API.

I'm excited to see what people build, and what other use cases are unlocked with it!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation.
  • Figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames).
  • AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation. Our findings show that forcing CodeAgents to generate both thoughts and code in a structured JSON format can significantly outperform traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames). Error bars represent 95% Confidence Intervals.

AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems. How agents express these actions has evolved through several paradigms:.

Traditional JSON Agent: Agents generate structured JSON to call tools.

Sources indicate that these agents operate by selecting from a list of predefined tools and generating JSON-formatted calls. This method for calling tools has been popularized by OpenAI's function calling API, and has since then been the most widely used method to call tools.

It is reliable, but limited by:.

Code Agents: Agents make use of their innate coding ability and write executable Python code directly.

This shift, first presented as CodeAct in the paper “Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” gave AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling.

The key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each action!

However, parsing code from markdown can be error-prone which leads us to a proposition: why not use structured generation to generate code actions?

With Structured outputs, you can force the LLM to generate explicit thoughts and code as a JSON blob:.

The key difference is that the generation is enforced: basically, now instead of just being prompted to output thoughts, then code, the usage of structured outputs forces it to respect the structure.

This approach adds the reliability of structured generation to the flexibility of code execution, thus getting the best of both worlds.

We compared these three paradigms across multiple benchmarks including GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames. The results show a clear pattern: Code actions + structured generation consistently improves performance for capable models.

Across most capable models, the structured approach consistently outperformed the regular CodeAgent approach by 2-7 percentage points on average.

Our implementation of CodeAgent in smolagents extracts Python code from the LLM output, which can fail when:.

Structured generation eliminates these problems with reliable JSON parsing.

To understand why structured generation matters, we analyzed 15,724 agent traces across our benchmarks. The results are striking:.

Agent traces without parsing errors succeed 21.3% more often than those with parsing errors.

According to recent reports, this isn't just about convenience - parsing errors create a cascade of failures that significantly impact overall agent performance. When an agent can't execute its first action due to malformed code, it often struggles to recover, leading to suboptimal problem-solving paths.

Figure 2: Parsing errors in the first step reduce success rates of the agent by 21.3% and increase average steps taken from 3.18 to 4.63.

Additionally: Enforced Reasoning Process.

The use of structured generation and explicit thoughts not just prompts, but forces agents to articulate their reasoning before acting. This leads to:.

Our results also reveal a clear capability threshold: models need sufficient instruction-following ability and JSON coverage in their pre-training data to benefit from structured generation. This suggests that structured approaches work best with:.

Here's what happens when a smaller model (e.g mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) tries to generate structured code - the cognitive load becomes too much:.

Industry observers note that the model generates syntactically broken Python code: web_search(query="Eiffel Tower height")", - notice the malformed string with an extra quote and comma. This leads to an immediate SyntaxError and execution failure.

This illustrates the "structure tax": smaller models struggle to simultaneously handle JSON formatting, Python syntax, and the actual problem-solving logic. The cognitive overhead of structured generation can overwhelm models that would otherwise perform reasonably well with simpler markdown-based code generation.

The LLM will generate something like this:.

Then the "code" part gets executed by the agent as usual : this is the standard CodeAgent, but now it has 100% parsing reliability!

Recent findings suggest that this research suggests we're moving toward a more nuanced understanding of agent architectures. It's not just about "what can the agent do?" but "how should the agent think about what it's doing?".

Maybe making the reasoning process more explicit helps the model stay on track. Or maybe it's just easier to parse. Either way, it’s a win.

Industry observers note that but this is just the beginning. There are so many questions left to explore:.

Recent findings suggest that for now, if you're using smolagents (or building your own CodeAgent system), consider giving structured output a try. Your parsing errors will thank you, and you might just see a nice increase in performance!

Did you try YAML block scalars or Python triple-quoted strings? These require less escaping, so they might mitigate the "structure tax".

Its platform combines access risk analysis, compliant provisioning, access certification, segregation-of-duties controls, and continuous monitoring to help organizations govern human and non-human identities and maintain audit readiness.

You spent nearly 17 years at SAP leading governance, risk, compliance, and identity initiatives before joining Pathlock. How has your view of access governance evolved as enterprises move from managing human consumers to managing AI agents that can independently interact with critical business systems?

My time at SAP was about mastering a known problem of humans interacting with applications, requesting access, getting provisioned, and managers periodically reviewing whether that access still made sense. It was complex, but the actors were predictable.

AI agents break that model and expose upcoming risks for organizations. They’re the fastest-growing class of non-human identities, and they don’t request access the way a person does. They’re granted broad, standing access and then act on it hundreds or thousands of times faster than any human could. That changes the core question of governance. For decades, we focused on controlling who could get into a system. With agents, the harder problem is understanding what happened after access was granted because an agent can execute an entire chain of transactions before anyone notices something’s off.

Pathlock research backs this up. More than half of organizations (52%) can’t fully verify what their AI agents are doing across business systems, and roughly half (48%) can’t trace agent activity end-to-end. That’s a governance gap is tolerable with machines because you had time to catch a bad decision. However, it’s not tolerable at machine speed.

Recent findings suggest that traditional identity governance was largely designed around employees, contractors, and administrators. What fundamentally changes when the “identity” requesting or exercising access is an autonomous AI agent?

Everything about the trust model changes. Traditional identity governance assumed a person behind every request. Someone with a job function, a manager, a reason to need access, and a limited number of actions they could physically take in a day. You could build controls around that, such as role-based access, periodic reviews, segregation of duties, all calibrated to human speed and human judgment.

Recent findings suggest that an autonomous agent doesn’t fit that model. It’s not requesting access the way an employee does. It’s often granted broad, standing permissions up front so it can do its job across systems. And once it has that access, it can act far faster than any person could, executing chains of transactions, modifying records, approving workflows, all without a human in the loop at each step.

According to recent reports, that breaks several assumptions governance was built on. First, who is requesting access stops being the interesting question. An agent’s identity doesn’t always map cleanly to a single person or role, and the same agent might act on behalf of different business processes at different times. Second, and more notable, oversight shifts from access to action. It’s no longer enough to know an agent is authorized to touch the finance system. You need to know what it did there, whether that was appropriate, and whether you’d be able to reconstruct that trail after the fact. Furthermore, AI agents that act on behalf of the user are even harder to detect, since the activity appears as if the human user was behind the UI.

It has been revealed that pathlock research highlights most organizations aren’t there yet. 79% have no dedicated AI governance team, and roughly half can’t fully verify or trace what their agents are doing across systems. That gap is really the core of the challenge. Governance built for human speed and human judgment simply hasn’t caught up to identities that act on their own, continuously.

AI agents may need broad access across ERP, finance, HR, procurement, and other enterprise systems to complete complex workflows. How can organizations give agents enough authority to be useful without creating excessive privileges or latest security vulnerabilities?

This is really a least privilege problem at machine scale, and it’s the tension every organization deploying agents will run into. The instinct is to over-provision and give the agent broad access up front, so it never hits a wall mid-workflow. That’s exactly how you end up with an agent that can approve a vendor payment, alter that vendor’s banking details, and close out the transaction, when it only ever needed to do one of those things.

It has been revealed that the fix is fundamentally similar to what we’ve always preached in access governance. Segregation of duties, least privilege, entitlements scoped to the task and the moment rather than standing indefinitely, but it must be automated and enforced continuously, because no human team can review permissions at the speed agents operate. An agent handling invoice matching doesn’t need open access to the general ledger, it needs exactly what that workflow requires, for exactly as long as it’s running. And the same SoD principles that apply to people apply here too. An agent that can both initiate and approve a transaction has recreated a classic violation, just faster.

None of that matters without traceability. Visibility into what an agent did has to be a first-class requirement, not something bolted on after an incident. Done well, tightly scoped, well-governed access makes an agent more useful, because its output can be trusted without someone double-checking everything behind it. The organizations getting this right are building governance into the deployment from day one.

Sources indicate that segregation of duties has traditionally prevented a single person from controlling conflicting parts of a business process. How should companies rethink segregation-of-duties policies when AI agents can execute multiple steps of a workflow autonomously?

Recent findings suggest that traditional SoD assumed one person, one role, and a workflow slow enough that a second person would naturally check the first person’s work at the next step. Agents dissolve that assumption. A single agent can be built to handle requisition, approval, and payment in one continuous run, which means the conflict controls we relied on for decades can simply be automated away, not by intent, but by convenience.

The rethink starts with applying the same logic to agents that we’ve always applied to people. No single identity, human or machine, should control both sides of a transaction that’s meant to have independent checks. In practice that means mapping SoD rules at the task level rather than the role level, so an agent that initiates a payment is structurally barred from also approving it, even if both actions technically fall under one automated workflow. It also means treating agent-to-agent handoffs as seriously as human handoffs. If one agent approves what another agent submitted, you need assurance that’s a genuine, independent check and not two instances of the same logic rubber-stamping each other.

Sources indicate that the harder shift is monitoring. With people, SoD violations usually surface in periodic access reviews. With agents acting continuously, you need conflict detection running in real time, evaluating what an agent is doing across a workflow as it happens. Companies that only think about SoD at the point of granting access are already behind. The conflicts that matter now show up in execution.

Should enterprises treat AI agents, bots, and other non-human identities differently from human users when it comes to provisioning, access certification, monitoring, and revoking privileges, or should essentially the same governance framework apply?

Industry observers note that the underlying principles should be the same. Least privilege, segregation of duties, certification, and the ability to revoke access on demand. What must change is how those principles get implemented, because agents don’t behave like people.

Provisioning must be scoped to the task and granted in the moment. Certification can’t stay a quarterly checkbox either. A person’s role changes slowly; an agent’s effective access can shift with every task, so certification needs to be closer to continuous. Monitoring is the biggest gap today. We built audit trails around human behavior, and those baselines don’t hold for something executing thousands of actions an hour. Revocation must be instant and complete, since an agent with even a day of residual access at machine speed is a very different exposure than a slow offboarding for a person.

So, it’s less about a separate framework for agents and more about applying the same one with a much higher bar for speed and precision, since gaps close in on you far faster than they did with human identities.

Recent findings suggest that permissions tell security teams what an identity can do, but AI agents introduce a greater need to understand what they actually did. How vital will continuous behavioral and transaction-level monitoring become as agentic AI adoption grows?

It’s going to become the center of gravity for governance. Permissions were always the easier half of the problem. They’re static, auditable, and change infrequently. What an identity does with those permissions was the harder half even with humans, and we mostly got away with lighter monitoring there because people move at human speed and leave a paper trail as they go.

Agents remove that cushion. An agent can be perfectly entitled and still cause damage, not by exceeding its permissions, but by using them in a way nobody anticipated, executing a sequence of legitimate actions that adds up to a bad outcome. That’s why the question must shift from “was this authorized” to “was this appropriate,” and you can only answer that by watching behavior and transactions as they happen.

Recent findings suggest that this is also where the traceability gap we’re already seeing becomes dangerous. Today, close to half of organizations can’t trace agent activity end-to-end, which means if something does go wrong, they’re reconstructing it after the fact rather than catching it in progress. As agentic adoption grows, that’s not a sustainable position. Continuous, transaction-level monitoring is what turns an agent from a black box you hope is behaving into a system you can stand behind, with a real record of what it did and why.

Sources indicate that cloud migrations and moves to platforms such as SAP S/4HANA can significantly reshape roles, integrations, and permissions. Where do you see access risks most commonly emerging during these transformations, and how can organizations prevent legacy access problems from being carried into the upcoming environment?

The biggest risk is siloed governance during the migration itself. In a legacy environment like ECC, GRC often sits separately from the technical teams running the migration, and when that happens, organizations carry years of accumulated roles and risk straight into the newly introduced system rather than redesigning them. Our 2025 Digital Transformation & Access Risk Report found that 52% of organizations don’t blueprint GRC controls early in the migration project. That’s the root cause of most of what goes wrong.

Sources indicate that people tend to treat a move to S/4HANA as a technical upgrade, when it’s really a full business transformation. Roles get restructured, integrations multiply, and new transaction codes get introduced, so this is the moment to redesign access from scratch. Once bloated roles and stale SoD conflicts get carried into the new environment, they become far harder to unwind, because now they’re embedded in a system everyone assumes was built cleanly.

It has been revealed that preventing that means bringing GRC into the migration from day one. That includes running SoD analysis and access risk assessments in parallel with the technical build and giving teams real-time visibility into access risk throughout the transports moving from development through QA and into production. Organizations that treat governance as part of the transformation itself come out the other side with a system that’s easier to audit and maintain.

Many companies still rely on periodic and often manual user-access reviews. As the number of human and machine identities grows, do you expect access governance to shift toward continuous, automated controls rather than point-in-time certification exercises?

Recent findings suggest that yes, and I’d say it’s less a prediction than something already underway. Periodic, manual user access reviews were built for a world where the number of identities was manageable and roles changed slowly enough that a quarterly or annual checkpoint made sense. Neither of those conditions holds anymore. The sheer volume of human and machine identities has outgrown what any team can meaningfully review by hand, and a lot of organizations are still running that process through spreadsheets and email approvals, which was already a strain before agents entered the picture.

Sources indicate that point-in-time certification also tells you someone’s access was appropriate on the day it was reviewed but notes nothing about the 90 days in between. With the pace at which access changes now, especially with machine identities that pick up new entitlements as workflows demand them, that gap is where real risk accumulates undetected.

It has been revealed that continuous, automated controls close that gap by evaluating access and usage as conditions change. That means the review becomes exception-based rather than exhaustive, with automation surfacing what’s changed or looks anomalous so people can focus their judgment where it’s needed instead of rubber-stamping thousands of unchanged entitlements. Organizations still doing this manually are working harder than they need to and are most likely to miss the access risk that matters.

Boards and senior executives increasingly have oversight responsibility for cybersecurity and compliance, but identity risk can be highly technical. What metrics should leadership teams track to understand whether access to critical enterprise systems is actually creating material business risk?

Industry observers note that boards don’t need technical details, just metrics translated into business risk. A few matter most. Open segregation-of-duties violations in finance, procurement, and payroll since those map directly to fraud risk. The percentage of identities, human and machine, covered by certification and monitoring, since ungoverned access is a blind spot regardless of how strong other controls are. And time-to-revoke, which indicates how long exposure windows stay open after someone leaves or a role changes.

I’d also add visibility into AI agent activity specifically, since roughly half of organizations still can’t fully verify or trace what their agents are doing. Together, these tell leadership whether access is genuinely governed or just assumed to be.

Looking ahead several years, as autonomous agents become capable of initiating transactions and making operational decisions across enterprise applications, what will a mature governance model for AI agents need to look like?

According to recent reports, A mature model must treat agents as full participants in governance. That means every agent has a clear identity, a defined purpose, and entitlements scoped to that purpose rather than broad standing access granted for convenience.

Access must be dynamic, expanding and contracting with the task rather than sitting as a permanent grant, and segregation of duties must be enforced structurally, so no single agent can both initiate and approve consequential actions. None of that works without continuous, transaction-level monitoring, since permissions only tell you what an agent can do, not what it did, and that distinction becomes the whole ballgame once agents are making operational decisions on their own.

Accountability also must be built in from the start. Every action needs to be traceable to the agent that took it, the data it acted on, and ideally the reasoning behind the decision, so organizations can explain outcomes after the fact rather than reconstruct them under pressure. And governance can’t sit solely with security teams anymore. It has to be a shared responsibility across business, risk, and compliance functions, with board-level visibility into how much operational authority agents hold.

  • After Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php1, ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their new gTLD program site2.
  • The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting":3.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php1, ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their new gTLD program site2. They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private tech giant effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project.

The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting":3.

WordPress contributor Jamie VanRaalte objected on the grounds of "Part of a pattern - .php should not go to one company" and also remarked the .wordpress application was a similarly inappropriate power grab of another open-source project:4.

Web developer Ryan Maietta highlighted the "File Extension Confusion and Security Risks" of using an established filetype as a TLD and the risk of people confusing websites using this domain as being officially endorsed by the PHP project:5.

Forensic analyst Herbert Bärschneider also objected simply on the grounds of confusing the TLD with the filetype:6.

And finally, the ICANN-affiliated Mark William Datysgeld described .php as being "Not viable from a technical perspective"7 highlighting that he has already had challenges creating the page for it on the PHP-based ICANN Wiki site, causing it to return a 404 error response8:.
