No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper.
  • This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck.
  • Before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

Before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:.

In online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

Recent findings suggest that the main issue was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

This approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

Industry observers note that unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is introduced and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially important in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

The shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below reveals the difference:.

It has been revealed that in the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:.

During training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

In contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:.

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now introduces vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:.

According to recent reports, co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:.

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:.

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:.

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the new co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

To ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

In a recent development, when training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's crucial to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that when using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

Recent findings suggest that the sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:.

Level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

Level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a big difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

ZeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:.

Recent findings suggest that this is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

As recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:.

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:.

In a recent development, we evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned important lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

According to recent reports, tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Issue #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

It has been revealed that level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This matter was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading latest weights.

It has been revealed that segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open matter with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

It has been revealed that co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

It has been revealed that vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

Sources indicate that colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be launched and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

In a recent development, traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

Industry observers note that while challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

Your AI Can Stay in the Country and Still Cross the Wrong Border

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that consider a US bank that has approved an AI agent to help staff review customer disputes.
  • During one review, the agent needs to extract information from an attached document.
  • This is becoming a significant concern as enterprises give AI agents access to business systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that consider a US bank that has approved an AI agent to help staff review customer disputes. The bank has chosen an AI model hosted in a US data center and checked that its deployment meets the processing-location commitments made to customers.

During one review, the agent needs to extract information from an attached document. It calls a third-party tool that sends the document to an overseas service. The AI model stayed in the US, but the customer’s information crossed a border the bank never intended it to, and the agent may have done exactly what the employee asked. The problem lies in how the agent completed the task and whether anyone checked where the information would go.

This is becoming a significant concern as enterprises give AI agents access to business systems. An agent can retrieve records and call external services while completing a task, introducing processing locations that may not have been included in the original AI deployment assessment. NIST’s research on tool use in agent systems highlights how tool permissions and their ability to access external resources affect the risks of using them.

For CIOs, this means ensuring that every service an AI agent uses complies with the business’s data sovereignty requirements, even when an outage forces traffic to be rerouted.

Industry observers note that A bank may have agreed to keep some customers’ information in the US while allowing other records to be processed in approved overseas locations. Its own security policies may impose tighter restrictions. Those commitments must be reflected in the AI systems employees use, so engineers need to know which models and external tools can receive each customer’s information.

It has been revealed that AWS addresses this in its October 2026 Digital Sovereignty Lens announcement. Its guidance examines the infrastructure companies use, the third-party services they depend on, and where they store and process data.

Once the agent retrieves a customer’s records, it may pass a document to another service for processing. That creates a separate decision about who receives the information and where it goes. The employee’s permission to access the account does not necessarily extend to sharing its contents with an external provider.

Recent findings suggest that the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications identifies tool misuse and identity-related abuse among the risks that organizations need to address when agents take actions on their behalf. These risks require controls where the action occurs. Agents should have defined permissions for the tools they can use, and outgoing requests need appropriate checks before sensitive information is transmitted.

It has been revealed that an AI gateway may govern requests sent to models, while an agent calls other services through separate connections. If those connections aren’t covered by the relevant controls, governing the model’s traffic will leave a gap.

You shouldn’t trust a service simply because it operates on an approved network. NIST’s zero-trust guidance for multi-cloud applications recommends checking the identity of the application or service requesting access and whether that access is permitted.

Sovereign AI adds another limitation to the supply-and-demand problem that AI infrastructure already manages. A organization might have several AI providers to choose from, but the best option for a request depends on what each provider can offer at the time. A cheaper model may be too slow, while another may already be struggling to handle demand.

For the bank, a fast, inexpensive model is no use if it processes customer information in a country the contract doesn’t allow. The bank also needs to know that whichever provider receives the request is authorized to handle those records.

In a recent development, smarter routing applies those restrictions to each request. A destination that falls outside the customer’s approved options is excluded, leaving the system to weigh cost, performance, and available capacity among the eligible providers.

The underlying policies still need to come from the business, and their enforcement must extend to the relevant model and tool traffic. Routing cannot protect a connection it never sees or compensate for permissions that were incorrectly granted.

I expect more enterprises and service providers to build these policy-aware routing capabilities into their AI control planes as AI traffic spreads across more applications and infrastructure.

According to recent reports, the bank’s primary AI service goes down. Another provider in Canada could handle the requests, and under normal circumstances, switching over would make sense. But if the bank has promised that the affected customer information will be processed only in the US, that Canadian service is not an acceptable recovery destination.

Sources indicate that AWS’s Digital Sovereignty Lens documentation recognizes this trade-off. Strict residency requirements can limit recovery options, creating a direct relationship between sovereignty and continuity planning.

Industry observers note that the bank could prepare for this by arranging backup capacity with another approved provider or spreading its workloads across US locations. It could also have a different model ready to handle essential work if its usual service goes down, as long as the applications can use it.

When conditions change, the system can redirect requests to those approved alternatives without compromising the customer’s restrictions.

There will still be situations where no compliant alternative is available. The business then needs an agreed response. Some requests may have to wait, while certain workflows could continue with reduced functionality or an approved manual process. For a critical service that cannot tolerate those interruptions, the business must invest in additional compliant capacity in advance.

Service providers will need to give customers reliable information about where workloads run and what happens when traffic moves between their facilities. Enterprises will need ways to express their own restrictions and apply them across the AI services they use.

Neither can assume that a model’s advertised hosting location tells the complete story. A request’s actual path may involve other services, and compliance records should reflect those interactions.

That requires the AI control plane to coordinate routing with access policies and information about available destinations. Teams should also record decisions so they can understand why a particular service was selected and whether applicable restrictions were met.

Recent findings suggest that I would encourage CIOs to test this using an actual agent workflow. Follow the request through the model and every tool the agent calls, checking which services receive customer information and where they process it. Then see what happens when the primary inference destination becomes unavailable.

Does the system use another approved service, or does it send the request somewhere the customer never authorized? If the team cannot answer that confidently, it needs to revisit the design before an outage puts everyone under pressure to get the service running again.

In a recent development, david Wang is VP of Product at Tetrate, which builds infrastructure for routing and governing AI traffic across enterprise and service-provider environments. Founded by creators of Istio and Envoy, Tetrate has deep roots in open-source application networking, service mesh and distributed systems. Its engineers contribute to Istio and Envoy, and the manufacturer co-created Envoy AI Gateway with Bloomberg, the project now known as Agent Router under the Agentic AI Foundation. David previously held vice president roles at MuleSoft and Databricks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR after Three-Year Migration.
  • Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.
  • GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR after Three-Year Migration.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

Written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style update costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

It has been revealed that for every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all consumers. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 sx prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional @primer/styled-react package let sx keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:.

Recent findings suggest that A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

On Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not big enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

GitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

The Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that what's your FI number?
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Recent findings suggest that forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as rapidly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

According to recent reports, side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Firm). Here is the honest comparison.

According to recent reports, A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Sources indicate that self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

In a recent development, the 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

Sources indicate that the decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

Sources indicate that the most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

In a recent development, most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Recent findings suggest that businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

According to recent reports, dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.

Over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text. However, in real-world robotics, advancements have been much slower. Robots still struggle to generalize across diverse objects, environments, and tasks. This limited progress stems from a lack of high-quality, diverse data and the absence of models that can reason and act like humans in the physical world.

It has been revealed that in response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture. VLAs typically take as input raw visual observations and natural language instructions, and output corresponding robot actions. While promising, much of the recent progress in VLAs remains locked behind proprietary models trained on large-scale private datasets, often requiring costly hardware setups and extensive engineering resources. As a result, the broader robotics research community faces significant barriers in reproducing and building upon these models.

According to recent reports, smolVLA addresses this gap by offering an open-source, compact, and efficient VLA model that can be trained on consumer-grade hardware using only publicly available datasets. By releasing not only model weights but also using very affordable open-source hardware, SmolVLA aims to democratize access to vision-language-action models and accelerate research toward generalist robotic agents.

Architecturally, it combines Transformers with flow-matching decoders, and is optimized for speed and low-latency inference with the following design choices:.

Despite using fewer than 30k training episodes—an order of magnitude less than other VLAs—SmolVLA matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, both in simulation and the real world.

In a recent development, to make real-time robotics easier to use, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack. This technology separates how robots perform actions from how they understand what they see and hear. Because of this separation, robots can respond more quickly in fast-changing environments.

SmolVLA is not only a lightweight yet capable model, but also a method for training and evaluating generalist robotics policies. In this section, we introduce the model architecture behind SmolVLA and the asynchronous inference setup used for evaluation, which has proven to be more adaptable and capable of faster recovery.

SmolVLA consists of two core components: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes multimodal inputs and an action expert that outputs robot control commands. Below, we share the details of the main components of SmolVLA architecture and the Asynchronous Inference. More details can be found in our technical report.

We use SmolVLM2 as our VLM backbone. It’s optimized for multi-image inputs and consists of a SigLIP vision encoder and a SmolLM2 language decoder.

The decoder layers process concatenated image, language, and state tokens. The resulting features are then passed to the action expert.

SmolVLA’s action expert is a compact transformer (~100M parameters) that generates action chunks, i.e. sequences of future robot actions, conditioned on the VLM’s outputs. It is trained using a flow matching objective, which teaches the model to guide noisy samples back to the ground truth. In contrast, while discrete action representations (e.g., via tokenization) are powerful, they often require autoregressive decoding, which is slow and inefficient at inference time. While flow matching allows direct, non-autoregressive prediction of continuous actions, enabling real-time control with high precision.

According to recent reports, more intuitively, during training, we add random noise to the robot’s real action sequences and ask the model to predict the “correction vector” that brings them back to the correct trajectory. This forms a smooth vector field over the action space, helping the model learn accurate and stable control policies.

We implement this using a transformer architecture with interleaved attention blocks (see the figure 2), and reduce its hidden size to 75% of the VLM’s, keeping the model lightweight for deployment.

While combining a vision-language model with an action prediction module is a common design pattern in recent VLA systems—such as Pi0, GR00T, Diffusion Policy — we identified several architectural choices that significantly enhance the robustness and performance. In SmolVLA, we apply three key techniques: reducing the number of visual tokens, skipping upper layers in the VLM, and interleaving cross- and self-attention layers in the action expert.

According to recent reports, high-resolution images improve perception but can significantly slow down inference. To strike a balance, SmolVLA limits the number of visual tokens to 64 per frame during both training and inference. For example, a 512×512 image is compressed into just 64 tokens, instead of 1024, using PixelShuffle as an efficient shuffling technique. While the underlying Vision-Language Model (VLM) was originally pretrained using image tiling for broader coverage, SmolVLA uses only the global image at runtime to keep inference lightweight and fast.

Industry observers note that rather than always relying on the final layer of the VLM—which can be expensive and sometimes suboptimal—we use features from intermediate layers. Prior work has shown that early layers often provide better representations for downstream tasks. In SmolVLA, the action expert only attends to VLM features up to a configurable layer NN during training, set to half the total layers. This halves the compute cost of both the VLM and the action expert, significantly speeding up inference with minimal performance loss.

Inside the action expert, attention layers alternate between:.

We found that this interleaved design is both lighter and more effective than using full attention blocks. Models that rely only on CA or only on SA tend to sacrifice either smoothness or grounding.

In SmolVLA, CA ensures that actions are well-conditioned on perception and instructions, while SA improves temporal smoothness—especially critical for real-world control, where jittery predictions can result in unsafe or unstable behavior.

We are really excited about releasing asynchronous inference because it guarantees greater adaptability and improved performance without changing the model. In short, async inference keeps the robot responsive by overlapping execution and remote prediction.

Industry observers note that while vision and language models thrive on web-scale datasets like LAION, ImageNet, and Common Crawl, robotics lacks a comparable resource. There’s no “Internet of robots.” Instead, data is fragmented across robot types, sensors, control schemes, and formats—forming disconnected "data islands". In our previous post, we explored how this fragmentation could be resolved through open, collaborative efforts. Just as ImageNet catalyzed breakthroughs in computer vision by providing a large, diverse benchmark, we believe that community-driven robotics datasets can play the same foundational role for generalist robot policies.

According to recent reports, smolVLA is our first step toward that vision: It is pretrained on a curated mix of publicly available, community-contributed datasets designed to reflect real-world variation. Rather than optimizing for dataset size alone, we focus on diversity: a range of behaviors, camera viewpoints, and embodiments that promote transfer and generalization.

All training data used in SmolVLA comes from LeRobot Community Datasets , robotics datasets shared on the Hugging Face Hub under the lerobot tag. Collected in diverse settings, from labs to living rooms, these datasets represent an open, decentralized effort to scale real-world robot data.

In a recent development, figure 4. A glimpse of the community dataset. Special thanks to Ville Kuosmanen for creating the visualization. Unlike academic benchmarks, community datasets naturally capture messy, realistic interactions: varied lighting, suboptimal demonstrations, unconventional objects, and heterogeneous control schemes. This kind of diversity will be very useful for learning robust, general-purpose representations.

We used a customfiltering tool created by Alexandre Chapin and Ville Kuosmanen to select datasets based on frame count, visual quality, and task coverage. After a meticulous manual review (special thanks to Marina Barannikov), we curated a collection of 487 high-quality datasets focused on the SO100 robotic arm, standardized at 30 FPS. This yielded around 10 million frames—at least one order of magnitude smaller than other popular benchmark datasets, yet significantly more diverse.

It has been revealed that A common issue across community datasets was noisy or missing task descriptions. Many episodes lacked annotations or included vague labels like “task desc” or “Move”, “Pick”. To improve quality and standardize the textual input across datasets, we used Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct to generate concise, action-oriented descriptions.

Given sample frames and the original label, the model was prompted to rewrite the instruction in under 30 characters, starting with an action verb (e.g., “Pick,” “Place,” “Open”).

It has been revealed that another challenge was inconsistent camera naming. Some datasets used clear names like top or wrist.right, while others used ambiguous labels like images.laptop, which varied in meaning. To fix this, we manually went through the datasets and mapped each camera view to a standardized scheme: OBS_IMAGE_1: Top-down view OBS_IMAGE_2: Wrist-mounted view OBS_IMAGE_3+: Additional viewpoints.

We further isolate the contributions of community dataset pretraining and multitask finetuning. Without pretraining on the LeRobot community datasets, SmolVLA initially achieves 51.7% success on SO100. After pretraining on community-collected data, performance jumps to 78.3%, a +26.6% absolute improvement. Multitask finetuning further boosts performance, showing strong task transfer capabilities even in low-data regimes.

Table 1. Impact of Pretraining on Community Datasets and Multitask Finetuning.

Despite being compact, It consistently outperforms or matches the performance of significantly larger models and policies pretrained on higher-scale robotics data.

Finally, we evaluate SmolVLA under synchronous and asynchronous inference modes. Async inference decouples action execution from model inference, allowing the policy to react while the robot is moving.

This results in more responsive and robust real-world performance, especially in dynamic environments with shifting objects or external disturbances.

SmolVLA is our contribution to building robotics foundation models that are open, efficient, and reproducible. Despite its small size, it matches or outperforms larger, proprietary models across a range of real-world and simulated tasks. By relying solely on community-contributed datasets and affordable hardware, SmolVLA lowers the barrier to entry for researchers, educators, and hobbyists alike. But this is just the beginning. SmolVLA is more than just a model — it's part of a growing open-source movement toward scalable, collaborative robotics.

Sources indicate that together, we can make real-world robotics more capable, more affordable, and more open. ✨.

Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ktz

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday.
  • But current hardware pricing is totally screwed.
  • Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.

But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It indicates just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).

Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).

October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive.

Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty rapidly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

In a recent development, maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion.

It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.

It has been revealed that three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.

As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings.

Industry observers note that the jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.

In a recent development, if I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the newly introduced normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

Work, Workflows and Workforce: The Three-Part Approach to Evaluating AI ROI

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, CFOs need to explain what the business is getting from its AI spending.
  • In a recent development, I think about AI transformation in three categories: work, workflows and workforce.
  • Sources indicate that each category requires financial discipline, but the timing and measures of return will differ.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CFOs need to explain what the business is getting from its AI spending. That becomes difficult when the same conversation covers an employee using AI to prepare for a meeting and a multimillion-dollar effort to redesign customer support. Those investments have different purposes, and evaluating them against identical expectations can produce poor decisions.

In a recent development, I think about AI transformation in three categories: work, workflows and workforce. Work is how individuals do their jobs. Workflows are the broader business processes leadership must redesign. Workforce is how teams, roles and responsibilities must be structured to support those redesigned workflows.

Sources indicate that each category requires financial discipline, but the timing and measures of return will differ. CFOs should encourage learning where capabilities are still developing, demand measurable outcomes for major process investments and fund the workforce needed to deliver them.

Industry observers note that work starts with individuals figuring out how AI can improve their daily responsibilities. Someone in accounting might automate a recurring analysis. A marketer might use AI to prepare a campaign brief. These improvements develop from employees learning the tools and recognizing opportunities in their own jobs.

Spreadsheets are a useful comparison. Employees across departments learned to use them without relying on IT to build every calculation. AI requires a similar expansion of skills. Employees need enough knowledge to use models, build simple agents where appropriate and question manual tasks they have accepted for years.

Recent findings suggest that putting a precise ROI requirement on every interaction would make that learning harder. An employee may prepare for a meeting more effectively, but assigning a defensible financial return to that improvement is difficult. Early in adoption, finance should give employees room to learn and experiment.

Recent findings suggest that that still requires cost controls. CFOs can establish budgets, set individual usage caps and monitor consumption. Managers should track repeat usage, practical applications and whether employees are developing useful skills. User groups can help effective approaches spread across departments.

It has been revealed that as usage matures, finance can identify underused licenses and compare the cost of tools performing similar tasks. Trying to maximize adoption and minimize every dollar of spending simultaneously can stall progress before employees know what the tools can do.

In a recent development, the largest returns come from rethinking how an entire business process operates. Giving developers AI coding tools may help them complete individual tasks faster. Redesigning software delivery requires leadership to examine how code is written, reviewed, tested and deployed, including where work slows down between those steps.

Recent findings suggest that that is an executive responsibility. The leader running the function must define how the process should change and partner with AI and IT teams on the technology required. Individual experiments alone are unlikely to produce that coordinated redesign.

For CFOs, these initiatives should carry the same expectations as other major software investments. Before committing capital, establish how the process performs today, the outcome management expects, the cost of achieving it and the period over which returns will be measured. The executive sponsoring the initiative should commit to those results upfront.

It has been revealed that customer support provides a practical example. Finance could measure cost per resolved case, resolution time and escalation rates, while checking that customer experience remains acceptable. In product development, relevant measures could include release velocity, defects and engineering capacity. The business case should connect those operational changes to the function’s existing priorities.

It has been revealed that that connection requires care. Hours saved create capacity, but the financial benefit depends on what happens next. Does the team handle more volume without additional hiring? Does it avoid outside spending? Can it deliver valuable products sooner? Faster output may create substantial value without reducing current payroll.

Recent findings suggest that finance and the sponsoring executive should agree on these assumptions before deployment and review them as the initiative scales. They also need conditions for modifying or stopping an investment that fails to deliver. Measuring ROI after a major rollout leaves too much room for shifting expectations.

Recent findings suggest that as AI changes how work gets done, leaders need to reconsider how teams are organized. Responsibilities, reporting relationships and handoffs designed around manual processes may no longer fit. Workforce transformation means adjusting those structures so teams can deliver the outcomes promised by redesigned workflows.

Recent findings suggest that consider customer support. As AI handles more routine requests, leaders may need to shift people toward complex cases, oversight of automated responses and improvements to the support process. In engineering, faster code generation may require a different balance between writing code and reviewing, testing and deploying it.

Sources indicate that these changes should be planned alongside the workflow redesign. Leaders need to decide who owns the process, where human judgment is required and how teams will coordinate as responsibilities shift. Automating tasks while retaining every existing handoff can leave the broader process slow and expensive.

Industry observers note that CFOs should test whether the proposed team structure supports the investment case. If AI creates capacity in one part of a process, can another team absorb the additional volume? Will employees move into higher-value work, or will capacity sit unused? The financial return depends on how effectively leaders reorganize work around that capacity.

According to recent reports, hiring and upskilling should support the roles those workflows require. Finance should include training and transition costs in the investment blueprint, then assess whether the fresh structure improves throughput, service quality or cost per outcome. That connects workforce decisions directly to the returns expected from AI.

Recent findings suggest that the framework also helps CFOs evaluate where AI capabilities should come from. Start with functionality already available in existing software. If that cannot meet the need, assess other products built for the task. Custom development should follow a clear assessment of whether available solutions can deliver the required outcome.

In a recent development, building a replacement for an established system can introduce maintenance obligations and technical debt alongside the initial development expense. Finance should compare total ownership costs, including integration, model consumption, security, human oversight and ongoing support. The objective is to improve the process at a sustainable cost.

Sources indicate that AI belongs within the overall software investment discussion. Finance has long weighed the cost of technology against the people and resources required to perform the work. Variable charges tied to model usage or agent activity make it especially notable to understand how costs change as adoption and transaction volumes grow.

Boards should see that distinction in reporting. Everyday tools warrant a view of adoption, learning and spending controls. Major workflow investments need a view of operational outcomes and financial returns against commitments. Workforce investments need evidence that the skills and organizational changes required for those returns are taking hold.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a tech giant that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me.".

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain noted the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been.".

Recent findings suggest that A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain stated, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

It has been revealed that to replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

According to recent reports, jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

In a recent development, he closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthcare has been treating AI readiness and value-based care (VBC) readiness as separate journeys, but they are the same one.
  • Many healthcare organizations have been on a multi-year shift away from a system where profits are tied to care volume to one where incentives align with outcomes.
  • According to recent reports, AI promises better care, lower costs, and improved outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthcare has been treating AI readiness and value-based care (VBC) readiness as separate journeys, but they are the same one. The data foundation, governance, and cross-organization collaboration necessary to succeed in VBC are exactly what AI needs to deliver results, and the organizations that recognize this will move faster than those that do not.

Many healthcare organizations have been on a multi-year shift away from a system where profits are tied to care volume to one where incentives align with outcomes. In 2024, 45% of all U.S. healthcare payments flowed through an alternative payment model (APM) contract, and nearly 30% were part of a downside risk contract. This shift will continue to accelerate as cost pressures mount and technology offers more opportunities to provide higher-quality care at a lower cost.

According to recent reports, AI promises better care, lower costs, and improved outcomes. The global AI in healthcare market is valued at $36.7 billion in 2025 and projected to grow to $505.6 billion in 2033, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of nearly 40%. Yet most organizations are struggling to scale it. They are running into obstacles that make broad adoption difficult, and the same challenges showing up in their AI strategy have complicated the industry’s transition to VBC, namely:.

But there is also good news, because organizations that have already built capabilities to support VBC are uniquely positioned to realize meaningful results and ROI on their AI initiatives.

Recent findings suggest that AI holds promise to improve U.S. healthcare in multiple ways, from streamlining manual workflows and repeatable tasks to recommending appropriate treatment pathways based on unique patient needs. But not all the things these new technologies can provide will require the same capabilities. Administrative AI tools can dramatically improve efficiency and produce measurable benefits within an organization, with capabilities like summarizing and managing data, automating processes like prior authorizations, and assisting in simple or repeatable tasks (for example, IT support or notetaking during patient encounters).

Outcome-focused tools—the ones essential for VBC success—need more advanced capabilities to predict outcomes, intervene earlier to reduce preventable clinical encounters or expenses, anticipate and stratify risk in patient populations, and improve both clinical and financial results. This type of AI requires an ecosystem built to support data sharing, interoperability, and collaboration. While many healthcare organizations have made significant progress in areas of interoperability and collaboration, 2023 data from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) reveals that less than half (42%) of hospitals report clinicians routinely using clinical information from outside providers when treating patients, despite more than 70% having access to that information. Progress toward full interoperability remains disjointed and slow.

While many payers and providers have launched AI pilot programs, evaluated vendors, and explored point solutions and large language models, there is still only limited enterprise-scale deployment among organizations.

At the IndustryDive AI in Healthcare virtual event, Mutaz Shegwei, Senior Research Director, shared findings from IDC’s Worldwide Healthcare Provider AI and IT Investment Survey (September 2026) showing that only 12.6% of healthcare organizations describe their AI strategy as fully scaled. Nearly half remain in ad-hoc or emerging stages of adoption, particularly when it comes to measuring success. Three capabilities consistently emerged as notable to the ability to scale AI in the future: a comprehensive data platform, enterprise-wide governance, and formal measurement of outcomes.

In a recent development, the IDC research found that 43.4% of providers either have or are planning comprehensive data platforms that integrate internal and external information, while a similar percentage have established or intend to establish AI governance councils. Fewer than one in four organizations (22.7%) measure AI’s impact through a formal enterprise-wide program, and without measurement there is no “proof of value” for these initiatives. The gap isn’t in ambition or technology—it’s in the foundation.

Sources indicate that historically, healthcare organizations have treated AI transformation and value-based care initiatives as separate and parallel efforts, with different budgets, leadership structures, and objectives. That approach is now holding both efforts back. By aligning AI and VBC data readiness efforts, payers and providers will have the foundation necessary to optimize organizational efficiency, clinical care delivery, and patient outcomes.

A recent survey of payer executives found that 66% do not have the data infrastructure and technology in place to support AI-driven decision making. Additionally, 92% said that not having a single, connected data source is a major barrier to scaling AI in VBC initiatives.

In a recent development, healthcare organizations often possess vast amounts of information, including claims, pharmacy, laboratory, eligibility, financial, and provider data. The challenge is not data availability but transforming that information into a trusted, usable asset. Rather than fixing these complications, AI systems amplify underlying data strengths and weaknesses. If datasets are incomplete, inconsistent, delayed, or fragmented, AI models bring out those shortcomings rather than resolve them.

This dynamic closely mirrors the requirements of value-based care, where success depends on the ability to track quality, cost, utilization, and risk through data. Organizations that have already invested in population health analytics, provider performance measurement, longitudinal patient records, and care management already have much of the foundation to support advanced AI applications.

An intertwined strategic approach to AI and VBC also improves specific operational workflows. Care coordination, risk stratification, and prior authorization are all areas where both providers and payers are actively deploying AI capabilities. Outcomes in these domains depend heavily on shared information and aligned incentives between organizations—the ability to collaborate and share clean, enriched data from a single source of truth.

Stop funding AI and VBC as separate programs. Align planning, governance, and budget under one strategy.

Recent findings suggest that if the goal of deploying AI is simply to comb through volumes of data and interpret it in a report, healthcare organizations may have dozens of options from which to choose. Many AI tools can successfully identify patterns in a dataset. But for organizations that want their AI to take the next step toward identifying risks and opportunities, and suggesting options for intervention, the AI must have appropriate context.

A broad understanding of organizational goals, program incentives, population health and risks, and operational realities will ensure that an organization gets appropriate outputs from its AI. For example, if two separate employers are examining their diabetes-related risk and looking at interventions for their employees that will help meet VBC goals, it’s critical that the AI they use understands factors unique to their organization.

An employer with a highly transient workforce would be more interested in diabetes interventions that produce measurable short-term results, while a second employer with a long-tenured workforce may benefit from diabetes programs that take longer but produce better long-term health results. Organizations that are already optimizing for VBC—accounting for variables like patient populations, provider relationships, and incentive structures—would understand these contextual nuances and could apply a similar structure to their AI. The same model, deployed without context, gives both employers the wrong answer.

Administrative efficiency is a critical part of improving U.S. healthcare, but the true promise for AI in the industry lies in its ability to anticipate disease, mitigate preventable utilization, predict risk, and provide a path forward to improve patient health while reducing costs. That’s also the central premise for pursuing VBC programs and contracts. AI and VBC programs both require a strategic approach to ensure appropriate human oversight that can optimize outcomes, monitor results, and improve performance. Rather than choosing between an AI or a VBC roadmap, or pursuing them as separate strategic priorities, leaders can start by:.

The healthcare organizations that can succeed in their AI efforts won’t necessarily be the ones with the most AI pilot programs or the most advanced models and technology. It will be the organizations that align their AI and VBC efforts to ensure both are built around strong governance, interconnected systems, and a trusted data foundation.
