OpenAI Group PBC, io Products, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan filed counterclaims against Apple on November 27, 2026, in California federal court, alleging that Apple misappropriated confidential hardware designs and manufacturing records. The accompanying answer denies Apple’s trade-secret and contract claims, while the counterclaims contain 12 causes of action.

Apple began the underlying case in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on July 10, 2026, alleging trade-secret misappropriation and breaches of Intellectual Property Agreements. The defendants admit Liu’s and Tan’s employment histories and current OpenAI roles but deny stealing Apple’s trade secrets.

According to recent reports, the central new allegation concerns an operations employee identified only as Employee X, who OpenAI says joined from Apple on December 2, 2025. He initially handled camera and optics quality before his responsibilities expanded to enclosures, finishing, inspection and manufacturing quality; his last day at OpenAI was June 2, 2026.

Industry observers note that the counterclaims describe transfers to personal email accounts and phone numbers, including a 76-page supplier measurement and inspection procedure sent on February 5, 2026. The materials allegedly included design geometry, manufacturing measurements, finishing criteria, supplier-performance results and inspection software. On June 1, 2026, Employee X sent six archives to a personal Singapore number, including structure.zip and CPK_GRR.zip, containing unreleased-device geometry, enclosure measurements, process-capability records and gauge analyses.

Sources indicate that openAI alleges that Employee X rejoined Apple and, on information and belief, briefed senior Apple Asia-Pacific Operations personnel in July 2026 on its confidential hardware work and unreleased-product roadmap at Apple’s request. OpenAI sent Apple a cease-and-desist letter on October 9, 2026, requesting an investigation, preservation, containment and an accounting.

It has been revealed that openAI notes the records’ value comes from specific engineering and production work rather than ordinary supplier identities: access to designs, test results and failure analyses could let a competitor avoid unsuccessful trials, qualify manufacturing methods sooner and anticipate production problems. The federal claim targets Apple’s alleged knowing acquisition, use or disclosure of that information through Employee X.

Sources indicate that the filing separately alleges that Apple’s supply-management personnel pressured shared vendors to identify OpenAI projects and the names, locations and assignments of workers with Apple experience. Suppliers feared losing Apple allocations if they supported OpenAI. For many specialized functions, OpenAI has only one or two qualified suppliers, making interrupted capacity difficult to replace promptly.

It has been revealed that one finishing supplier allegedly moved OpenAI’s work on a general-purpose anodizing line, a shared metal-finishing process, to a separate overnight shift after Apple objected to OpenAI devices being processed in the same area or at the same time as Apple work. The change increased costs for the supplier and OpenAI. A second manufacturer allegedly withdrew from planned work because of threats from Apple, forcing OpenAI to revamp operations, staffing and contracting. The interference claim concerns actual disruption of existing purchasing and manufacturing commitments, rather than merely lost future orders.

Sources indicate that the counterclaims also challenge Apple’s broad contractual definition of proprietary information and a one-year restriction on soliciting Apple employees or contractors after departure. Liu and Tan argue that California’s protection against contracts restraining lawful work prevents those terms from reaching general skills, public information or lawful recruiting.

OpenAI indicates 400 Apple employees have left for OpenAI and that Apple’s account and enforcement practices deter further hiring. Tan, who worked at Apple for approximately 24 years and is now OpenAI’s Chief Hardware Officer for Consumer Products, seeks declarations that his agreement cannot bar use of public information, general skills or lawful recruiting.

Liu alleges that Apple encouraged employees to mix work files and communications with personal iCloud and iMessage accounts, then used the resulting access after departures. After leaving Apple on January 22, 2026, he allowed his personal iCloud account to remain signed in on a returned Apple device solely so his former manager could retrieve Apple work files. His permission did not extend to review of his personal data.

The filing says Apple and forensic consultant Charles River Associates reviewed Liu’s personal iMessages and other materials, including post-employment communications with non-Apple third parties. Those allegations support an invasion-of-privacy claim and claims under federal and California computer-access laws. They also underpin OpenAI’s unfair-competition claim that the prospect of post-departure monitoring deters engineers from moving to a competitor.

Industry observers note that the counterclaim plaintiffs request compensatory damages where permitted, reasonable royalties or statutory relief for trade-secret misappropriation, restitution, attorneys’ fees and narrowly tailored injunctions against established ongoing or threatened unlawful conduct. They also demand a jury trial.

Industry observers note that the counterclaims broaden the case beyond files retained during employee departures. They put the infrastructure behind OpenAI’s unreleased hardware effort—supplier capacity, recruiting and the boundary between work and personal accounts—into the same judicial examination of whether either firm unlawfully obtained the other’s information.

KV Cache from scratch in nanoVLM

📅 04 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • Recent findings suggest that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Recent findings suggest that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

This repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

Recent findings suggest that in autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Recent findings suggest that most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental revision.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Recent findings suggest that previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{new}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

Sources indicate that in the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

Recent findings suggest that KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

Industry News: ScreenSuite - The most comprehensive evaluation suite for GUI Agents!

📅 06 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate.
  • We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!
  • It has been revealed that in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

It has been revealed that in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

In particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

It has been revealed that this means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

In a recent development, A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

Industry observers note that the literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

Sources indicate that if you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a new option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

According to recent reports, we’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

It has been revealed that unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

– All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to swiftly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

Today at GTC Paris, we are excited to announce Training Cluster as a Service in collaboration with NVIDIA, to make large GPU clusters more easily accessible for research organizations all over the world, so they can train the foundational models of tomorrow in every domain.

It has been revealed that many Gigawatt-size GPU supercluster projects are being built to train the next gen of AI models. This can make it seem that the compute gap between the “GPU poor” and the “GPU rich” is promptly widening. But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

Recent findings suggest that how do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster.

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:.

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

Sources indicate that the Telethon Institute of Genomics and Medicine - TIGEM for short - is a research center dedicated to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind rare genetic diseases and developing novel treatments. Training new AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

According to recent reports, AI offers new ways to research the causes of rare genetic diseases and to develop treatments, but our domain requires training new models. Training Cluster as a Service made it easy to procure the GPU capacity we needed, at the right time.

-- Diego di Bernardo, Coordinator of the Genomic Medicine program at TIGEM.

Numina is a non-profit organization building open-source, open-dataset AI for reasoning in math - and won the 2024 AIMO progress prize.

It has been revealed that we are tracking well on our objective to build open alternatives to the best closed-source models, such as Deepmind's AlphaProof. Computing resources is our bottleneck today - with Training Cluster as a Service we will be able to reach our goal!

-- Yann Fleureau, cofounder of Project Numina.

Mirror Physics is a startup creating frontier AI systems for chemistry and materials science.

Together with the MACE team, we're working to push the limits of AI for chemistry. With Training Cluster as a Service, we're producing high-fidelity chemical models at unprecedented scale. This is going to be a significant step forward for the field.

-- Sam Walton Norwood, CEO and founder at Mirror.

Training Cluster as a Service is a fresh collaboration between Hugging Face and NVIDIA to make AI compute more readily available to the global community of AI researchers.

Access to large-scale, high-performance compute is essential for building the next generation of AI models across every domain and language. Training Cluster as a Service will remove barriers for researchers and companies, unlocking the ability to train the most advanced models and push the boundaries of what’s possible in AI.

-- Clément Delangue, cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that integrating DGX Cloud Lepton with Hugging Face’s Training Cluster as a Service gives developers and researchers a seamless way to access high-performance NVIDIA GPUs across a broad network of cloud providers. This collaboration makes it easier for AI researchers and organizations to scale their AI training workloads while using familiar tools on Hugging Face.

-- Alexis Bjorlin, vice president of DGX Cloud at NVIDIA.

We are excited to collaborate with NVIDIA to offer Training Cluster as a Service to Hugging Face organizations - you can get started today at hf.co/training-cluster.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Sources indicate that here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

It has been revealed that compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:.

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:.

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165.

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

It has been revealed that the Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

Sources indicate that at a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The following table highlights how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

Industry observers note that the 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Industry observers note that consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

In a recent development, investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

Put the math to work starting today.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

In a recent development, the historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

Recent findings suggest that when you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Sources indicate that market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and upcoming highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Sources indicate that pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

It has been revealed that simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

Sources indicate that more frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Industry observers note that yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Recent findings suggest that compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

  • NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.
  • In a recent development, today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major patch to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

In a recent development, today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major patch to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

Industry observers note that users can fine-tune GROOT N1.5 with any LeRobot dataset. For this tutorial, we will be using the table cleanup task as an example for fine-tuning.

According to recent reports, it's important to note that datasets for the SO-100 or SO-101 are not in GR00T N1.5's initial pre-training. As a result of this, we will be training it as a new_embodiment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Newly introduced York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • It has been revealed that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Newly introduced York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

It has been revealed that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

In a recent development, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

Sources indicate that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in May 1986 for $1m.

It has been revealed that gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Latest York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Newly introduced York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

Sources indicate that french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

In a recent development, picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

The Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Recent findings suggest that willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in Latest York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Recent findings suggest that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s Upcoming York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” noted Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown.
  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the upcoming attribution.
  • Recent findings suggest that the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, Upcoming York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the upcoming attribution.

Recent findings suggest that the framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano indicates the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

According to recent reports, the early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano states that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

In a recent development, julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s fresh chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day indicates.

Recent findings suggest that llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s newly introduced conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

In a recent development, the process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she indicates. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

In a recent development, day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

#173591. Latest Update: How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1001 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation.
  • Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests.
  • Sources indicate that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of fresh as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable matter, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

Sources indicate that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".).

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

Industry observers note that A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

Recent findings suggest that in one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

Sources indicate that of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:.

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:.

According to recent reports, separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

Disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Industry observers note that another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are presently lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the organization was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the organization was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

Sources indicate that “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the tech giant’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

It has been revealed that the indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim organization and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

In a recent development, the government mentioned Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim firm that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their organization and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the organization could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

Industry observers note that but Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

Industry observers note that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

Sources indicate that “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme noted. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

It has been revealed that the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

According to recent reports, “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

It has been revealed that “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

In a recent development, ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the tech giant’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

According to recent reports, “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme stated. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

In a recent development, the case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Industry observers note that around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

It has been revealed that in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

How Containers Work: Building a Container Runtime in Go

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when we run docker run alpine sh, it feels like we just booted a tiny virtual machine.
  • But there's no virtual machine here.
  • Sources indicate that in this article, we will build our own container runtime using those system calls in about 250 lines of Go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when we run docker run alpine sh, it feels like we just booted a tiny virtual machine. We get a newly introduced hostname, a new filesystem, our shell is PID 1, and the rest of the system seems to have disappeared.

But there's no virtual machine here. The shell is just a regular process on the host, started with a few Linux kernel features that limit what it can see and how much it can use. Docker, containerd, and runc are all tooling built around those features, and underneath it all, it's just a handful of system calls.

Sources indicate that in this article, we will build our own container runtime using those system calls in about 250 lines of Go. Along the way, we'll look at namespaces, pivot_root, overlay filesystems, cgroups, and what Docker adds on top.

From the host's point of view, a container is a process like any other. If we start one with our runtime and look at it from the outside:.

Recent findings suggest that process 40 is the "container". The host sees it, can signal it, and can read everything about it in /proc/40. What makes it a container is what the process itself sees, and three kernel features control that:.

Namespaces give the process its own view of a global resource: its own process IDs, hostname, mounts, and network interfaces.

A different root filesystem makes / inside the process point at a directory of files we chose, usually an image.

Control groups (cgroups) cap how much memory, CPU, and how many processes it can use.

Everything else in a container runtime is plumbing around these three.

Let's call our runtime box. It takes a directory to use as the root filesystem and a command to run:.

It works in two stages. The parent process, box run, prepares everything that has to happen outside the container: a writable filesystem layer and a cgroup with limits. It then starts a copy of itself, box child, inside new namespaces. The child finishes the setup that has to happen inside, switches to the new root filesystem, and replaces itself with the user's command.

Here's our entry point, which dispatches between the two:.

Note: Everything here needs Linux, root, and cgroup v2, which most distributions have used by default for a few years now. On macOS or Windows, we can run it inside a privileged Linux container, which is how I tested it. We'll cover that in Running It.

A namespace wraps a global system resource so that processes inside it see their own isolated copy. Linux has eight kinds:.

Sources indicate that A process gets fresh namespaces when it's created, by passing these flags to the clone system call. In Go, we can set them on exec.Cmd.

Our run function creates the filesystem and the cgroup, then starts the child in five upcoming namespaces:.

The exit code handling copies a shell convention: a process killed by a signal reports 128 plus the signal number. That's why a container killed by the out-of-memory killer exits with 137, which is 128 + 9 for SIGKILL, in Docker and in box alike.

Industry observers note that the run function returns an exit code instead of calling os.Exit itself, so the deferred cleanups always run. A runtime that leaks a mount or a cgroup every time something fails gets messy quickly.

Next, the child sets the hostname, makes its mounts private, switches root, and then replaces itself with the user's command:.

It has been revealed that sethostname only affects the fresh UTS namespace, so the host keeps its own name. The MS_PRIVATE remount keeps the container's mounts to itself. A new mount namespace starts as a copy of the parent's, and on most systems those mounts are shared, meaning mount events propagate between namespaces. Without making them private, the container's /proc mount could show up on the host.

syscall.Exec doesn't start a fresh process. It replaces the current one, so the user's command inherits the child's PID, which is 1 in the new PID namespace. There's no box process left inside the container.

Let's see what that looks like from the inside:.

The shell is PID 1 and sees only its own processes. On the host, the same shell has an ordinary PID like 40. A process in a PID namespace has one ID per namespace it's visible in.

Recent findings suggest that the network namespace starts with a loopback interface that's down and nothing else, so the container has no network at all. Docker's default bridge network is built on top of this, and we'll touch on it in What Docker Adds.

According to recent reports, the child is started as /proc/self/exe child ..., which is a fresh copy of the same binary. It would be simpler to call the namespace system calls directly in the parent, but Go makes that hard.

The Go runtime starts several OS threads before main runs, and some namespace changes only apply to the calling thread. Others, like a newly introduced PID namespace, only apply to processes created afterward. Doing it in a running Go program means fighting the scheduler for control of which thread does what.

Passing the flags to clone sidesteps that: the kernel creates the child already inside the new namespaces, and the child is a brand new Go program that starts up there. runc solves the same problem a different way, with a small piece of C that runs before the Go runtime starts.

Fresh namespaces alone don't change the filesystem. The child can still see the host's entire /. To look like an Alpine container, it needs Alpine's files as its root.

A container image is a directory tree of files plus some metadata. The easiest way to get one is to ask Docker to export a container's filesystem as a tar archive:.

Recent findings suggest that that directory now holds /bin, /etc, /lib, and everything else in Alpine, about 9 MB. box treats it as a read-only image.

Sources indicate that the classic way to change a process's root is chroot, but it's not a security boundary. A process with root privileges inside a chroot can escape it with a few well-known tricks, because the old root is still mounted and reachable.

Sources indicate that container runtimes use pivot_root instead. It moves the old root filesystem to a directory under the newly introduced one, after which the runtime unmounts it entirely:.

Recent findings suggest that the bind mount of the fresh root onto itself looks redundant, but pivot_root refuses to pivot to a directory that isn't a mount point. Once the old root is unmounted, the host's filesystem is gone from this mount namespace. There's no path left to reach it.

In a recent development, this all happens in the child's private mount namespace. The host's mounts are untouched.

Two directories need special handling after the switch.

According to recent reports, /proc is how tools like ps find processes. Mounting a fresh proc filesystem inside the fresh PID namespace makes it list only the container's processes. Without the new mount, ps would either fail or show the host's processes.

Sources indicate that /dev is where device files live, and an exported image has an empty one. If we run the container without fixing it, things break immediately:.

In a recent development, we could just mount the host's /dev, but that would also give the container access to every disk and device on the machine. Instead, Docker mounts a small in-memory filesystem and only creates the basic devices. Let's do the same:.

A device file is just a name pointing at a driver, identified by a major and minor number. /dev/null is character device 1:3 on every Linux system, so creating a file with that number gives the container a working /dev/null without exposing anything else.

If the container used the image directory directly, anything it wrote would change the image for every container after it. Running rm -rf / inside would destroy the image.

Docker avoids this with an overlay filesystem, which stacks directories on top of each other and presents them as one:.

The lower directory is the image, and it's never written to.

The upper directory starts empty and receives every write.

The merged directory is the combined view, and it's what the container uses as its root.

Sources indicate that reading a file returns the upper copy if one exists, otherwise the lower one. Writing a file from the lower layer copies it up first. Deleting one creates a marker in the upper layer that hides it. A real Docker image has many lower layers, one per build step, stacked the same way.

According to recent reports, the work directory is scratch space the kernel needs to make copy-up operations atomic. The cleanup deletes the upper layer, which makes every container start from the clean image, the same as docker run --rm.

Let's create a file and delete another one inside a container to see the layers in action:.

Industry observers note that inside the container, the fresh file exists and the deleted one is gone. In the image on the host, nothing changed, and the next container starts from the original files.

It has been revealed that namespaces control what a container can see. Control groups control how much it can use. On cgroup v2, every cgroup is a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup, and we set its limits by writing to files in it:.

mkdir creates the cgroup, and the kernel fills the directory with control files. cpu.max of 50000 100000 lets the cgroup's processes run for 50 ms in every 100 ms period, which is half a CPU. memory.swap.max of 0 stops the container from escaping its memory limit by swapping.

Industry observers note that the usual way to put a process in a cgroup is to write its PID to the cgroup's cgroup.procs file after it starts. That leaves a window where the process is running without limits. run avoids it with UseCgroupFD, which passes the open cgroup directory to clone, so the kernel creates the child already inside the cgroup. It needs Linux 5.7 or later.

When the container exits, run reads memory.events, where the kernel counts how many times it killed a process in this cgroup for running out of memory:.

Let's see what happens when we hit each limit. First, a loop that starts 30 background processes runs into the limit of 20:.

The process limit is the one that stops fork bombs. Without it, a container can exhaust the host's process table, which takes down everything on the machine.

Next, buffering 200 MB through tail runs into the 64 MiB memory limit, and the kernel kills it:.

Sources indicate that finally, CPU limits don't kill anything, they just slow the container down. Here's the same busy loop of two million iterations, run on the host and then inside box:.

The work costs the same CPU time in both, but inside the container it's spread over twice the wall-clock time, because the kernel pauses the container's processes for the second half of every 100 ms period.

On a Linux machine with cgroup v2, build box and run it as root:.

Sources indicate that on macOS or Windows, Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM, and a privileged container in it can act as the "host". I tested box this way, cross-compiling it with GOOS=linux and mounting the binary into an Alpine container started with --privileged.

There's one extra step needed here, though. cgroup v2 doesn't allow a cgroup to have both its own processes and child cgroups with resource controllers, and the privileged container's processes already live in the cgroup box wants to create children under. Moving them into a leaf cgroup first and then enabling the controllers fixes it, the same trick Docker-in-Docker uses:.

Industry observers note that the same container also can't host an overlay filesystem's upper layer on its own overlay root, so /var/lib/box needs to be a tmpfs mount there. On a regular Linux host, neither step is necessary.

Our box runtime has the core pieces, but it's missing almost everything that makes Docker safe and convenient to use:.

Networking: Docker creates a virtual Ethernet pair for each container, puts one end in the container's network namespace and the other on a bridge on the host, and uses NAT so containers can reach the outside world. box containers have no network at all.

It has been revealed that dropping privileges: the shell in box runs as full root. Docker drops most of root's capabilities, applies a seccomp profile that blocks more than 40 of the 300-plus system calls, and can map container root to an unprivileged host user with a user namespace.

Images: box uses a directory someone else unpacked. Docker pulls layered images from registries, verifies them by content hash, and stacks the layers with overlayfs.

Lifecycle: Docker runs containers in the background, keeps their logs, restarts them, and lets us exec into a running one, which joins its existing namespaces with the setns system call.

Docker's own architecture splits this work into layers. The docker CLI talks to dockerd, which hands containers to containerd, which manages their lifecycle and images. To actually start a container, containerd calls runc, which reads a JSON description of the container defined by the OCI runtime spec and does what box does: clone with namespace flags, pivot_root, mounts, cgroups, and finally exec.

runc is written in Go too, and now that we know these system calls, its source code is a great next read.

In this article, we learned that a container is just a Linux process, and built a small container runtime in Go using namespaces, pivot_root, overlay filesystems, and cgroups.

These pieces also explain a lot of everyday container behavior: why a container's PID 1 needs to handle signals, why exit code 137 means out of memory, why a container can't see host devices, and why changes inside a container disappear when it's removed.

You can also review the resources below to keep learning:.
