Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most vital artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a upcoming dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most key museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a newly introduced institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Industry observers note that raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Industry observers note that produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Industry observers note that working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s upcoming Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Sources indicate that museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

Left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

The Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most important artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

In a recent development, an apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

It has been revealed that comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Industry observers note that schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance.
  • Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them.
  • We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:.

Industry observers note that in our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

We used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:.

Sources indicate that loRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The update to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

Industry observers note that QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

It has been revealed that for instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:.

According to recent reports, gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

For this demonstration, we leveraged an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) to explore its performance. The full training command using accelerate is shown below.

It has been revealed that configuration for RTX 4090: On our RTX 4090, we used a train_batch_size of 1, gradient_accumulation_steps of 4, mixed_precision="bf16", gradient_checkpointing=True, use_8bit_adam=True, a LoRA rank of 4, and resolution of 512x768. Latents were cached with cache_latents=True.

Training Time (RTX 4090): Fine-tuning for 700 steps on the Alphonse Mucha dataset took approximately 41 minutes on the RTX 4090 with train_batch_size of 1 and resolution of 512x768.

It has been revealed that output Quality: The ultimate measure is the generated art. Here are samples from our QLoRA fine-tuned model on the derekl35/alphonse-mucha-style dataset:.

According to recent reports, this table compares the primary bf16 precision results. The goal of the fine-tuning was to teach the model the distinct style of Alphonse Mucha.

The fine-tuned model nicely captured Mucha's iconic art nouveau style, evident in the decorative motifs and distinct color palette. The QLoRA process maintained excellent fidelity while learning the newly introduced style.

The results are nearly identical, showing that QLoRA performs effectively with both fp16 and bf16 mixed precision.

For customers with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

Recent findings suggest that we fine-tuned FLUX.1-dev LoRA on an H100 SXM GPU slightly modifieddiffusers-torchao training scripts. The following command was used:.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for users with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

Sharing your fine-tuned LoRA adapters is a fantastic way to contribute to the open-source community. It allows others to easily try out your styles, build on your work, and helps create a vibrant ecosystem of creative AI tools.

Industry News: 7,600 GitHub Repos Were Poisoned. The Malware Hides in Your Build Config.

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that last week I cloned a repo I had never looked at before, ran the build, and thought nothing of it.
  • According to recent reports, apiiro, the supply chain security company that measured the campaign, put it bluntly: 6,541 of the 7,609 repos, about 86 percent, belong to personal accounts more than a year old, with five or more repos and real activity behind them.
  • I build software for a living, or at least I try to, and the part of this that keeps me up is not the size of the number.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that last week I cloned a repo I had never looked at before, ran the build, and thought nothing of it. That is the whole point of this story. A campaign researchers call PolinRider has now been found in at least 7,609 GitHub repositories, and the people who got hit were not careless beginners downloading random binaries. They were real developers with real accounts, and most of them probably still do not know it happened.

According to recent reports, apiiro, the supply chain security company that measured the campaign, put it bluntly: 6,541 of the 7,609 repos, about 86 percent, belong to personal accounts more than a year old, with five or more repos and real activity behind them. Only 16 owners look like throwaways. The loader was pushed into 2,040 repositories in a ten-day window, October 27 to November 6. The victims named so far include Neutralinojs, InstaWP Connect, and fxhash. These are projects people actually use.

I build software for a living, or at least I try to, and the part of this that keeps me up is not the size of the number. It is how ordinary the infection looks.

The loader itself is 58 lines of Python. It hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py, the kind of file you scroll past a hundred times without reading. When Python imports the file, the loader does something I had never seen before in a supply chain attack: it reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself, decodes the transaction input as JavaScript, and runs it with Node.js.

That wallet is not a secret. Researchers at SafeDep published it: 0x3b1574417524c11a7403c4b232CAcBb320CceBC6. The JavaScript it fetches reads a second wallet to find the command-and-control server, then hands the next stage to a detached interactive Node process.

In a recent development, the trick has a name, NullReceiver, and it is the reason this campaign is hard to kill. The C2 address is encoded in the first eight bytes of a fake destination wallet address. The rest of the address is a marker that always decodes to the ASCII string "helloipbot!!". Every time defenders take down a server, the operators publish one latest blockchain transaction and every infected loader in the world points at the new IP. No redeployment, no new malware, no new commits. Apiiro researcher Shmulik Cohen noted it plainly: taking a server down changes nothing, one transaction moves every loader to the next one.

It has been revealed that the payloads it fetches are called /0x/cls and /0x/ls, served over port 443. The first runs twice, once with eval inside the build process and once as a hidden background process. The second runs only in the background, so it keeps going after the build finishes. Nobody has captured a live copy of either script yet, so the exact contents are still unknown. But an earlier version of the second stage was decoded from Binance Smart Chain, and Cohen says it is most likely a remote-access tool: it skips CI machines, runs the operator's JavaScript and shell commands, reads the clipboard, uploads files, and plants itself in VS Code, Cursor, Discord, and GitHub Desktop so it restarts with them.

In a recent development, polinRider does not start with a repo. It starts with a person. Researchers assess it as a sub-cluster of a long-running campaign called Contagious Interview, and the entry point is exactly what the name suggests: fake recruitment.

Recent findings suggest that the operators run fraudulent hiring portals with names like BlockNovas, AccuraSoftHire, and HuntRole. A developer applies, gets a take-home assessment, and is told to run a project. Other versions of the lure ask candidates to sideload a Chrome extension after enabling Developer mode, or paste a command into the terminal as part of a "standard settings bundle." One site asks for a short verification video, and the camera check always fails until the server marks the candidate as having installed a "driver." That driver is a one-line curl command. On Windows it installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background, and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same thing.

It has been revealed that once the machine is owned, the stolen GitHub token does the rest. The worm rewrites commits the developer already made, keeping the author, the message, and the date, and slips the loader in after hundreds of spaces in a build config. You look at the history and everything checks out. Your name is on the commit. The message is yours. The date is yours. The code is not.

Industry observers note that the most visible edge of this showed up on November 25. Lukasz Gornicki, a maintainer of AsyncAPI Generator, opened heads-up problems in eight open-source projects, including Meshery, Jitsi Meet, Jaeger, stdlib, and PipeCD. A GitHub account named Eternity0207 had pushed an obfuscated malware loader into pull requests across all of them.

According to recent reports, stepSecurity documented what happened next. The account opened more than 200 pull requests targeting projects like AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse, and Open Food Facts, then force-pushed a modified commit containing the loader. Each time, the payload stayed on the branch for 30 to 40 minutes and was then force-pushed away, so the final diff looked clean. One AsyncAPI maintainer noted exactly that: the final diff looked clean.

And the trigger was not running some suspicious script. For AsyncAPI Generator, the loader ran when a developer ran npm run build. For Open Food Facts, it ran when the test configuration loaded. For CircuitVerse, opening the folder in VS Code was enough.

According to recent reports, this is not a newly introduced campaign that just appeared. OpenSourceMalware found a PolinRider attack from May 2025 that targeted nine npm packages, itsa-utils, itsa-jsext, itsa-react-docviewer, and six more, pushed as poisoned versions within 90 minutes using a hijacked maintainer account. Those used an earlier technique called EtherHiding to fetch a downloader called JADESNOW, which delivered a Python backdoor named InvisibleFerret. The blockchain records behind all of it go back to February 2025. The 2025 sample carries the same payload but not the spread behavior, which reveals up in the same maintainer's GitHub repositories in four windows between January and July 2026. Researchers believe the infection simply sat on the maintainer's machine from 2025, because the 2026 pushes ran from it.

In a recent development, that is the part I keep coming back to. The campaign did not need to break into GitHub. It broke into one developer's laptop, waited, and used that person's own credentials and reputation to poison everything they touched.

In a recent development, I am not going to pretend there is a single tool that fixes this. But a few things are cheap, and after this week I am doing all of them.

Industry observers note that first, I review diffs before I run anything, even in repos I trust, and especially in repos I just cloned. git log and git show cost seconds. A commit that only touches a build config or a test file is exactly where this loader lives. If a repo I cloned has a commit I cannot explain, I check it before I build, not after.

It has been revealed that second, I treat build and test files as code that runs, because they are. Running npm run build or opening a folder in VS Code is execution. A conftest.py or a package.json script is not documentation. I do not run a project's build on my main machine the first time I touch it anymore, and if the project is unfamiliar, it goes in a container or a throwaway VM first.

Industry observers note that third, I check my GitHub tokens. Fine-grained tokens with the smallest scope I actually need, short expiry, and a look at the authorized applications and tokens in my settings every month. A stolen classic token with repo scope is the key to this whole worm. If my token ever leaks, the damage is not just my account, it is every repo I have push access to.

Fourth, I do not run take-home assessments on my real machine. If a hiring process asks me to run a project, install a driver, sideload an extension, or paste a command into my terminal, that is the interview ending, not starting. No legitimate employer needs me to run unsigned code to prove I can write code.

And fifth, I keep my secrets out of the places a stealer looks. Environment variables in a password manager or a secrets file outside the project, never committed, never sitting in a shell history file, and browser sessions logged out of anything that matters on a machine I use for random builds.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 put the difference well in a report last month: ordinary cybercrime groups use supply chain worms for opportunistic theft, but North Korean state-sponsored actors use open-source registries as a primary way into corporate environments. Compromising one maintainer account turns into widespread affected cloud environments. That is the threat model now. Not a vulnerability in a library. A person, with a job application and a GitHub token.

According to recent reports, the uncomfortable truth is that open source runs on trust, and trust is exactly what this campaign weaponizes. The commit has your name on it. The repo has a thousand stars. The pull request looks clean. None of that means anything anymore unless someone actually reads the diff.

Sources: The Hacker News (Nov 2026), Apiiro, SafeDep, StepSecurity, OpenSourceMalware, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42. Attribution of PolinRider to North Korean-linked actors is the assessment of the researchers cited, and the contents of the /0x/cls and /0x/ls payloads remain undetermined at the time of writing, as no live copies have been captured.

Breaking: Building Accessible Filter Controls for a Static Directory

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that filters are the busiest controls on a local directory.
  • The fixes are not complicated, and most of them come from using plain HTML elements the way they were designed.
  • Industry observers note that custom toggle chips built from styled divs look nice and are a pain to make accessible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that filters are the busiest controls on a local directory. Someone lands on a city page with forty plumbers and narrows it down to the ones open on weekends that offer emergency service. On a static site those filters are usually a handful of checkboxes and a small script that hides cards that do not match. They are also one of the places where directory sites most often break for keyboard and screen reader consumers.

The fixes are not complicated, and most of them come from using plain HTML elements the way they were designed. This post walks through the markup, the script and the testing for filter controls on a static directory page.

Industry observers note that custom toggle chips built from styled divs look nice and are a pain to make accessible. You have to add roles, states, keyboard handling and focus styles by hand, and something usually gets missed. A native checkbox gives you all of that for free, and you can still style its label to look like a chip.

Industry observers note that group related filters in a fieldset with a legend. Screen readers announce the legend when focus enters the group, so a user hears "Hours, group" before "Open weekends, checkbox, not checked". Without it they hear a list of disconnected options with no context. Give each checkbox a visible label element tied to it, and make the label the click target so the hit area is big enough on a phone.

When a sighted user ticks a filter, they see the list shrink. A screen reader user hears nothing unless you tell them. The standard approach is a status region that updates with the number of matching listings. Mark it with role="status", which behaves as a polite live region, so the announcement waits until the user finishes what they are doing.

Sources indicate that each listing card carries data attributes such as data-weekend="1" set at build time from your Google Maps export. Using the hidden attribute removes non-matching cards from the accessibility tree as well as from view, which a CSS opacity trick would not do.

Sooner or later a combination of filters returns nothing. Do not leave the user with a blank list. Show a short message in the same status region, such as "No plumbers match these filters. Try removing one.", and add a clear-filters button right below it. Make sure the button is reachable with the Tab key and that focus does not jump somewhere unexpected after it runs. Moving focus back to the first checkbox in the group is a reasonable choice.

According to recent reports, static directories have an advantage here. The full list is already in the HTML, so with scripts off a visitor still sees every listing and can scroll. That is a fine fallback. What you want to avoid is filters that look clickable but do nothing when the script fails. One simple fix is to render the filter fieldset with the hidden attribute and remove it from the script once it loads, so the controls only appear when they will work.

These notes on layout and usability for directory websites cover more of the design side, and the planning behind which filters exist at all is covered in this article on planning categories and filters for a fresh local directory. Fewer, well-chosen filters are easier to make accessible than a long row of options nobody uses.

Sources indicate that do not remove the focus outline. If the default outline clashes with your design, replace it with a clearer one using :focus-visible, which demonstrates the ring for keyboard customers without showing it on every mouse click. The checked state should differ by more than color, for example with a check mark or a filled background plus a border, so it reads for users who cannot tell your two brand colors apart.

Keep tap targets comfortable. WCAG 2.2 added a minimum target size criterion at level AA, and chip-style labels with some padding clear it easily.

Recent findings suggest that run through the filters with only the keyboard: Tab into the group, Space to toggle, Tab to the results. Then try a screen reader. VoiceOver on macOS and iOS and NVDA on Windows are free and cover most of what you need to hear. Listen for the legend, the checkbox state and the count patch. Automated checkers like axe catch missing labels, but they cannot tell you whether the experience makes sense.

It helps. Writing the active filters to the query string lets people share or bookmark a filtered view. Read the query string on load and set the checkboxes to match, then run the same filter function.

For a single choice from a long list, such as a county, a native select works well. For several independent yes or no options, checkboxes are clearer and easier to scan.

Recent findings suggest that 1 Click Directory Builder turns a Google Maps export from Outscraper, Apify or any scraper into a complete static directory with search, filters and a map. The patterns above are worth checking on any directory you ship, whichever tool built it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

But once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

Designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

In a recent development, SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:.

Or you can spin a server and send requests:.

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

With the latest transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:.

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

It has been revealed that note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

Any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

In a recent development, kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:.

Performance Improvements: transformer models at the moment lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

How to plan your cash flow when clients pay late

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A late payment stops being a surprise after the first one.
  • Recent findings suggest that your invoice says 30 days.
  • Use the date the money actually reached your account, not the date you asked for it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A late payment stops being a surprise after the first one. If a client has paid you two weeks after the due date for three invoices in a row, that is not bad luck. That is the schedule. Planning cash flow around late payers is mostly the work of writing that schedule down and building the rest of your month around it.

Recent findings suggest that your invoice says 30 days. Your client's finance team pays on the last Friday of the month, after an approval nobody told you about. Those are two different dates, and only one of them belongs in a forecast.

Use the date the money actually reached your account, not the date you asked for it. After six months with a client you have enough history to know the difference without guessing.

Three columns next to every outstanding invoice: the due date, the date you expect to be paid, and what actually happened last time.

With those three lines you can see which invoices will fund this month and which will not.

Recent findings suggest that monthly totals hide the problem. Two invoices due in the same week, both paid late, leave a hole in the middle of the month even when the month ends fine.

A four-week view, with every expected payment sitting in the week you actually expect it, indicates you the hole while you can still do something about it.

Recent findings suggest that not a savings goal, a working rule. If your biggest outstanding invoice is 2,000 and that client always pays three weeks late, then 2,000 is the amount you need available to cover the gap, or the amount you need to avoid spending in advance.

Recent findings suggest that the buffer is not there to feel comfortable. It is there so a late payment does not turn into a decision about which bill to delay.

If two projects both bill their final invoice in the same week, and both clients pay late, you get one bad month and no lever to pull.

Sources indicate that move one final invoice a week earlier when you agree the schedule, or split the last stage into two smaller invoices. Clients rarely object to a billing schedule that was set before the work started.

Industry observers note that A deposit is the cheapest cash flow tool there is. It moves money to the front of a project, while you are doing the work, instead of the end, while you are waiting.

Write the rule before the month where it matters: if an invoice is two weeks late and above a set amount, work on that client's other projects pauses until it clears.

Recent findings suggest that A rule you decided in advance is a policy. The same decision made in the moment, with the client waiting on work, is an argument.

Recent findings suggest that put it in the quote when you agree the terms, not when an invoice is late. One sentence does the work: work pauses on any project where an invoice is more than 14 days past due, and resumes when it is paid.

When you invoke it later you are not introducing a new condition. You are applying the one they already agreed to.

The moment to look at the next four weeks is when you send a latest invoice, because that is when you know what is coming and you can still move a milestone or ask for a deposit.

Reviewing it when a payment is already late is a post-mortem, not a strategy.

Industry observers note that none of this works from memory. You need the list: who owes what, when it was due, when it actually arrived last time, and which invoices land in the next four weeks.

Recent findings suggest that I built Get Paid for that. It is a single HTML file that runs offline in your browser: an invoice list with due dates and balances, notes on what you chased and what was promised, a monthly view of what is outstanding, CSV import and export, and a backup. It does not create invoices, take payments, or send email.

It is a one-time purchase of 49.99 on Whop.

If you would rather keep the forecast in a spreadsheet, the same columns work there: client, amount, due date, expected date, actual date.

#173574. Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1435 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for major works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers noted that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for major works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a newly introduced buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” remarked the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

In a recent development, with India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox mentioned this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that highlighted at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (Latest York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

In a recent development, several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which showed small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

While both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff mentioned she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

Recent findings suggest that the gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff mentioned.

In a recent development, speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery demonstrated a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that the gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

Meanwhile, concerns of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

Industry observers note that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of latest Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gemma 3n was confirmed as a preview during Google I/O.
  • Today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries.
  • This post rapidly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemma 3n was confirmed as a preview during Google I/O. The on-device community got really excited, because this is a model designed from the ground up to run locally on your hardware. On top of that, it’s natively multimodal, supporting image, text, audio, and video inputs 🤯.

Today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries. This includes transformers & timm, MLX, llama.cpp (text inputs), transformers.js, ollama, Google AI Edge, and others.

This post rapidly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.

Here is the Gemma 3n Release Collection.

Two model sizes have been released today, with two variants (base and instruct) each. The model names follow a non-standard nomenclature: they are called gemma-3n-E2B and gemma-3n-E4B. The E preceding the parameter count stands for Effective. Their actual parameter counts are 5B and 8B, respectively, but thanks to improvements in memory efficiency, they manage to only need 2B and 4B in VRAM (GPU memory).

According to recent reports, these models, therefore, behave like 2B and 4B in terms of hardware support, but they punch over 2B/4B in terms of quality. The E2B model can run in as little as 2GB of GPU RAM, while E4B can run with just 3GB of GPU RAM.

It has been revealed that in addition to the language decoder, Gemma 3n uses an audio encoder and a vision encoder. We highlight their main features below, and describe how they have been added to transformers and timm, as they are the reference for other implementations.

Industry observers note that the easiest way to vibe check the model is with the dedicated Hugging Face Space for the model. You can try out different prompts, with different modalities, here.

Install the latest version of timm (for the vision encoder) and transformers to run inference, or if you want to fine tune it.

The easiest way to start using Gemma 3n is by using the pipeline abstraction in transformers:.

Initialize the model and the processor from the Hub, and write the model_generation function that takes care of processing the prompts and running the inference on the model.

Since the model supports all modalities as inputs, here's a brief code explanation of how you can use them via transformers.

Support for videos is done as a collection of frames of images.

Gemma 3n comes with day 0 support for MLX across all 3 modalities. Make sure to upgrade your mlx-vlm installation.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to MLX, Gemma 3n (text only) works out of the box with llama.cpp. Make sure to install llama.cpp/ Ollama from source.

Check out the Installation instruction for llama.cpp here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md.

Finally, we are also releasing ONNX weights for the gemma-3n-E2B-it model variant, enabling flexible deployment across diverse runtimes and platforms. For JavaScript developers, Gemma3n has been integrated into Transformers.js and is available as of version 3.6.0.

For more information on how to run the model with these libraries, check out the usage section in the model card.

Recent findings suggest that given the size of the model, it’s pretty convenient to fine-tune it for specific downstream tasks across modalities. To make it easier for you to fine-tune the model, we’ve created a simple notebook that allows you to experiment on a free Google Colab!

We also provide a dedicated notebook for fine-tuning on audio tasks, so you can easily adapt the model to your speech datasets and benchmarks!

Industry observers note that with this release, we also introduce the Hugging Face Gemma Recipes repository. One will find notebooks and scripts to run the models and fine tune them.

Industry observers note that we would love for you to use the Gemma family of models and add more recipes to it! Feel free to open Complications and create Pull Requests to the repository.

In a recent development, we are always excited to host Google and their Gemma family of models. We hope the community will get together and make the most of these models. Multimodal, small sized, and highly capable, make a great model release!

Recent findings suggest that if you want to discuss the models in more detail, go ahead and start a discussion right below this blog post. We will be more than happy to help!

A huge thanks to Arthur, Cyril, Raushan, Lysandre, and everyone at Hugging Face who took care of the integration and made it available to the community!

#173571. Tech Report: I removed the empty rows from my nonograms. Then my camels got taller.

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (640 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: I removed the empty rows from my nonograms. Then my camels got taller.

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm a junior solo developer from South Korea.
  • According to recent reports, my game is Whale Squares: Nonogram.
  • In a recent development, in my last post, I wrote about making 9,000 of these puzzles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm a junior solo developer from South Korea. I use a translator to help me write in English.

According to recent reports, my game is Whale Squares: Nonogram. In a nonogram, also called Picross, you use the numbers beside the rows and columns to fill in cells and make a picture.

In a recent development, in my last post, I wrote about making 9,000 of these puzzles. This one is about what came after.

Industry observers note that someone testing the app told me there were too many empty rows. If a row or column has a clue of 0, every cell in it is empty. By default my app puts an X in each of those cells before you start.

Recent findings suggest that on some 25×25 puzzles, more than ten rows and columns were already crossed out. I'd picked a substantial board and only had the middle to solve.

The original picture had white space around it. When I put the picture on the grid, I included all that white space too. That's why the picture was so small in the middle.

Industry observers note that I cropped off the white space and made the picture bigger. A wide picture could reach both sides of the board and still leave empty space above and below. I stretched the short side to fill the square.

That brought the empty rows down to about two. I thought that was good enough and shipped the update.

According to recent reports, after it went out, I saw the two camels. They were standing side by side like before, but now they were both tall and thin. The elephants in the circus parade were taller too. A lot of the pictures on the biggest boards looked wrong like that.

The picture is everything in this game, and I'd stretched it out of shape. It felt like there was something wrong with my whole game.

This time I changed the board to fit the picture. I kept the long side at the puzzle size and shortened the other side in steps of five cells. A puzzle in the 25×25 pack could be 25×20 or 25×15, depending on the picture.

The pictures looked right again and there were hardly any empty rows. But more than 2,500 puzzles now had rectangular boards. Near the start of that pack there were more rectangles than squares.

I think a rectangular puzzle once in a while is fun. I don't see them very often, though. Nonograms have been around a long time. To me a square board feels like one of the rules by now. I wanted to respect the old game and stay as close to it as I could.

Recent findings suggest that for the giraffe, I wanted to keep the long neck. The diplodocus is long right down to its tail, and the suspension bridge needs room to stretch across the board. I kept rectangles for pictures like those, where the length is part of what you want to see.

For the rest I used fresh pictures that fit a square. I threw away a lot of pictures.

There are fewer than 300 rectangular boards now. You'll hardly see any near the start of a pack.

Recent findings suggest that when a picture changed, its answer changed too. A cell you filled in correctly before might need to be empty now. For those puzzles, the app clears your half-finished board once. It keeps the record of puzzles you've finished.

It has been revealed that this version is now out on Google Play and the App Store. I only wanted to remove a few empty rows. It turned into changing the board shape and making newly introduced pictures.

Whale Squares: Nonogram on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=kr.binarytech.goraekan&utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=blog_202611.

Whale Squares: Nonogram on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6835263397.

Welcome the NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VLM to Hugging Face Hub

📅 27 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding.
  • Sources indicate that check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL!
  • Llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding. Available on Hugging Face, it excels in extracting and understanding information from complex documents like invoices, receipts, contracts, and more. With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Sources indicate that check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! Users can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

Industry observers note that llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

It has been revealed that this strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

Sources indicate that for the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

Recent findings suggest that in the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

Recent findings suggest that the document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

To ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

According to recent reports, A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

In a recent development, figure 2 below reveals the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Industry observers note that llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

In a recent development, to ensure the output is formatted precisely as you need, we recommend including detailed instructions within your prompts. We've provided some examples below to illustrate how this works for various tasks:.

Industry observers note that OCRBench v2 is an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate OCR models across a diverse range of real-world document types and layouts. It includes over 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs to rigorously assess a model’s capabilities in visual text localization, table parsing, diagram reasoning and key-value extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL outperforms other VLMs on this benchmark and also achieves strong accuracies in benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, making it a compelling option for enterprises aiming to automate document workflows such as:.

Its combination of high accuracy, strong layout aware reasoning, and efficient deployment on a single GPU makes it an ideal choice for large-scale enterprise automation.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for various document processing tasks across multiple industries. Here are some of the key use cases where the model excels:.

Automating the extraction of line items, totals, dates, and other key data points from invoices and receipts. This is crucial for accounting, ERP integration, and expense management.

Extracting structured data from passports, IDs, and tax forms for regulatory compliance and KYC processes.

Automatically identifying key clauses, dates, and obligations in legal documents.

Extracting patient data, claim information, and policy details from medical records and insurance forms.

According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL provides developers with the tools to automate document processing workflows at scale. It is available through the NVIDIA NIM API and for download on Hugging Face, where you can begin building production-ready document understanding applications. Users can also use NVIDIA NeMo to finetune the model on their own dataset.

The tutorial will walk you through:.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a powerful multimodal model designed to meet the demanding needs of intelligent document processing in modern enterprises. Whether you are processing invoices, contracts, or compliance documents, this model provides the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability required for high-performance document understanding.

For a hands-on experience, check out our tutorial on invoice and receipt document intelligence, and start leveraging the full power of Llama Nemotron Nano VL today.
