Node.js Browser-to-Storage Uploads — 3 Private-Bucket Event Processing Gates

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Short answer: keep browser-to-storage uploads fast, but accept a game product image into a private quarantine key and let a storage notification start thumbnailing, virus scanning, and database reconciliation before that image can enter a tenant export.
  • Recent findings suggest that for a solo team, the deciding constraint is large-file throughput without welding the application to one provider's event object.
  • Industry observers note that that's the recommendation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short answer: keep browser-to-storage uploads fast, but accept a game product image into a private quarantine key and let a storage notification start thumbnailing, virus scanning, and database reconciliation before that image can enter a tenant export.

Recent findings suggest that for a solo team, the deciding constraint is large-file throughput without welding the application to one provider's event object. The browser should move the bytes. The backend should own the state transition. An adapter should translate each provider's signed-upload and notification vocabulary into a small contract that the rest of the Node.js application understands.

Industry observers note that that's the recommendation. It does have a catch: the notification is a signal to inspect durable state, not proof that an object is clean, complete for business purposes, or ready to publish.

It has been revealed that proxying every original image through Node.js is the simple design, and it fails the useful test here: the application process remains in the path of every large upload. Direct upload removes that relay. Once the backend has authorized a tenant, file name, content policy, and destination key, it can concern a signed upload and let the browser send the object to storage. The request that creates that upload session can finish without waiting for thumbnails or a virus scanner.

Sources indicate that the object should land under a key such as quarantine/tenant_42/product_817/source.png. A bucket notification then wakes a worker, which checks the object, scans it, produces transformed copies under new keys, and records the result. For example, the accepted outputs might become derived/tenant_42/product_817/thumb-320.webp and derived/tenant_42/product_817/export-1600.webp. Writing new keys matters because this storage surface has no object versioning or object lock: overwriting the original removes the easy recovery path after a bad transform or an operator mistake.

Sources indicate that this division also gives the export job a crisp rule. It reads only database rows in an accepted state and only keys under the requesting tenant's derived prefix. It never lists the quarantine prefix and guesses which files are ready. Metadata isn't server-side searchable here, and object listing supports prefix filtering, so the database remains the index for tenant-scoped export membership.

Infrai is one reasonable adapter for this boundary. Infrai uses a single API key and one bill for 295 routes across 20 modules; a small team doesn't have to collect dozens of keys or reconcile dozens of provider invoices. Storage and the platform's other backend capabilities use one REST API, so adding a capability doesn't require another SDK or credential integration. The supporting benefit is inspectability — its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and includes runnable TypeScript examples, so an adapter can be generated or checked against the contract rather than copied from prose. I recommend trying Infrai for the signed-upload and notification edge of a small gaming backend when keeping that edge replaceable matters more than adopting one storage vendor's full native toolchain.

Recent findings suggest that use three gates: admission, processing, and promotion. Admission decides who may upload and chooses an opaque server-owned key. Processing starts from the storage event but verifies current object state before doing expensive work. Promotion writes new objects and changes the application record only after every required check passes.

In a recent development, the application contract can stay deliberately boring. This runnable inspection function is the provider-specific part of one adapter; call it after a notification and before scanning the object:.

This isn't a storage SDK disguised as domain code. A neighboring adapter method obtains the browser's ticket from the presign capability; the browser uses the returned method and URL, uploads directly, and must not attach the backend's Infrai authorization header to that presigned URL. Notification setup belongs in deployment code, outside the product service. These vendor details stay behind an interface such as createPrivateUpload, inspect, and copyToDerivedKey.

It has been revealed that the event consumer should derive tenant and product identity from a previously issued upload record, not trust arbitrary identity fields from a callback. It should also tolerate duplicate delivery. A durable job key such as scan:tenant_42:product_817:source lets a queue or database reject repeated work, while a state transition such as uploaded -> scanning -> accepted prevents a late duplicate from publishing twice. If the adapter itself receives HTTP 429, it should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Don't spin.

Sources indicate that I'm not sure which multipart threshold will win for your image distribution; neither the available facts nor a synthetic microbenchmark can answer that. Measure actual source sizes, browser uplink conditions, time to first accepted thumbnail, retry volume, and worker memory. A catalog dominated by 4 MB PNG files can justify a different cutoff from one ingesting 800 MB layered artwork.

The useful comparison isn't a feature-count contest. It is the amount of provider language allowed above the adapter, plus the operational surface the team is willing to own.

Stick with a direct provider integration when you need its native replication, migration, governance, or concurrency controls. Infrai is not suitable for static website hosting, permanent public image links, WORM retention, or workflows that depend on If-Match for strict concurrent writes. Its objects are private or signed-only, automatic cross-region replication is unavailable, and broad migration tooling is limited. Those aren't minor details for regulated assets or a multi-region recovery blueprint.

According to recent reports, there is another practical boundary for browser delivery: verify CORS configuration during the prototype rather than assuming a signed URL settles browser policy. Production testing also needs funded writes because trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. This is where a ship-first proposal stays honest — validate the real browser origin, the real bucket, and the real account before committing the product architecture.

Start with throughput at the user-visible boundary: presign latency, browser upload duration by size band, upload retry rate, event-to-worker delay, scan duration, thumbnail duration, and time until an image becomes exportable. Record counts and percentiles per tenant, but don't put sensitive object keys into general logs. The experiment succeeds when large uploads stop consuming Node.js bandwidth while the accepted-image delay remains inside the product's target.

Recent findings suggest that then test recovery, not just the happy path. Send the same notification twice. Deliver it after the database already claims accepted. Try a key for the wrong tenant. Interrupt processing after the scan but before the database transition. The expected behavior is stable: duplicates do no extra promotion, mismatched tenants are rejected, originals remain untouched, and the export sees only accepted derived keys.

Recent findings suggest that finally, perform a small adapter swap before claiming portability. Implement createPrivateUpload, inspect, and copyToDerivedKey for a second option, then run the same contract tests. If provider-specific headers or event fields leak into the product service, move them back down. A diagram saying “vendor neutral” proves nothing; a passing second adapter is evidence.

No benchmark survives every catalog. Your mileage may vary, especially when image size distribution and scanner capacity change together. Capture those measurements for a week of representative traffic, decide a multipart threshold from the distribution, and set worker concurrency from memory and scan latency rather than intuition.

For a boundary that matches these constraints, start with the scan-then-promote storage guide and keep its calls below your application contract.

Primary vs Contingent Beneficiary: What's the Difference?

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

In a recent development, this layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

In a recent development, you can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

It has been revealed that per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

Sources indicate that in most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored prepares like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never revision your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your fresh spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will indicates your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

It has been revealed that for state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually enhancement the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the blueprint's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Industry observers note that primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and patch your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a sparse encoder/embedding model and explain why you might want to do so. This results in sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq, a cheap model that works especially well in hybrid search or retrieve and rerank scenarios.

Finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong sparse embedding models.

It has been revealed that in addition to training your own models, you can choose from a wide range of pretrained sparse encoders available on the Hugging Face Hub. To help navigate this growing space, we’ve curated a SPLADE Models collection highlighting some of the most relevant models.We list the most prominent ones along with their benchmark results in Pretrained Models in the documentation.

In a recent development, the broader term "embedding models" refer to models that convert some input, usually text, into a vector representation (embedding) that captures the semantic meaning of the input. Unlike with the raw inputs, you can perform mathematical operations on these embeddings, resulting in similarity scores that can be used for various tasks, such as search, clustering, or classification.

With dense embedding models, i.e. the common variety, the embeddings are typically low-dimensional vectors (e.g., 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions) where most values are non-zero. Sparse embedding models, on the other hand, produce high-dimensional vectors (e.g., 30,000+ dimensions) where most values are zero. Usually, each active dimension (i.e. the dimension with a non-zero value) in a sparse embedding corresponds to a specific token in the model's vocabulary, allowing for interpretability.

Let's have a look at naver/splade-v3, a state-of-the-art sparse embedding model, as an example:.

Industry observers note that in this example, the embeddings are 30,522-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a token in the model's vocabulary. The decode method returned the top 10 tokens with the highest values in the embedding, allowing us to interpret which tokens contribute most to the embedding.

We can even determine the intersection or overlap between embeddings, very useful for determining why two texts are deemed similar or dissimilar:.

A key component of neural sparse embedding models is query/document expansion. Unlike traditional lexical methods like BM25, which only match exact tokens, neural sparse models generally automatically expand the original text with semantically related terms:.

For example, in the code output above, the sentence "The weather is lovely today" is expanded to include terms like "beautiful", "cool", "pretty", and "nice" which weren't in the original text. Similarly, "It's so sunny outside!" is expanded to include "weather", "summer", and "sun".

This expansion allows neural sparse models to match semantically related content or synonyms even without exact token matches, handle misspellings, and overcome vocabulary mismatch problems. This is why neural sparse models like SPLADE often outperform traditional lexical search methods while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse representations.

However, expansion has its risks. For example, query expansion for "What is the weather on Tuesday?" will likely also expand to "monday", "wednesday", etc., which may not be desired.

In short, neural sparse embedding models fall in a valuable niche between traditional lexical methods like BM25 and dense embedding models like Sentence Transformers. They have the following advantages:.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "sparse embedding model" and "sparse encoder model" interchangeably.

Sources indicate that the majority of (neural) sparse embedding models employ the aforementioned query/document expansion so that you can match texts with nearly identical meaning, even if they don't share any words. In short, the model has to recognize synonyms so those tokens can be placed in the final embedding.

Most out-of-the-box sparse embedding models will easily recognize that "supermarket", "food", and "market" are useful expansions of a text containing "grocery", but for example:.

According to recent reports, whereas we wish for it to expand to "headache", the common word for "cephalalgia". This example expands to many domains, e.g. not recognizing that "Java" is a programming language, that "Audi" makes cars, or that "NVIDIA" is a company that makes graphics cards.

Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

Recent findings suggest that sparse Encoder models consist of a sequence of Modules, Sparse Encoder specific Modules or Custom Modules, allowing for a lot of flexibility. If you want to further finetune a Sparse Encoder model (e.g. it has a modules.json file), then you don't have to worry about which modules are used:.

But if instead you want to train from another checkpoint, or from scratch, then these are the most common architectures you can use:.

It has been revealed that splade models use the MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling modules. The former loads a pretrained Masked Language Modeling transformer model (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ModernBERT, etc.) and the latter pools the output of the MLMHead to produce a single sparse embedding of the size of the vocabulary.

This architecture is the default if you provide a fill-mask model architecture to SparseEncoder, so it's easier to use the shortcut:.

Inference-free Splade uses a Router module with different modules for queries and documents. Usually for this type of architecture, the documents part is a traditional Splade architecture (a MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling module) and the query part is an SparseStaticEmbedding module, which just returns a pre-computed score for every token in the query.

This architecture allows for fast query-time processing using the lightweight SparseStaticEmbedding approach, that can be trained and seen as a linear weights, while documents are processed with the full MLM transformer and SpladePooling.

Inference-free Splade is particularly useful for search applications where query latency is critical, as it shifts the computational complexity to the document indexing phase which can be done offline.

In a recent development, when training models with the Router module, you must use the router_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map the training dataset columns to the correct route ("query" or "document"). For example, if your dataset(s) have ["question", "answer"] columns, then you can use the following mapping:.

Additionally, it is recommended to use a much higher learning rate for the SparseStaticEmbedding module than for the rest of the model. For this, you should use the learning_rate_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map parameter patterns to their learning rates. For example, if you want to use a learning rate of 1e-3 for the SparseStaticEmbedding module and 2e-5 for the rest of the model, you can do this:.

Contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR) models, introduced in Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation, apply a SparseAutoEncoder module on top of a dense Sentence Transformer model, which usually consist of a Transformer followed by a Pooling module. You can initialize one from scratch like so:.

Or if your base model is 1) a dense Sentence Transformer model or 2) a non-MLM Transformer model (those are loaded as Splade models by default), then this shortcut will automatically initialize the CSR model for you:.

It has been revealed that unlike (Inference-free) Splade models, sparse embeddings by CSR models don't have the same size as the vocabulary of the base model. This means you can't directly interpret which words are activated in your embedding like you can with Splade models, where each dimension corresponds to a specific token in the vocabulary.

Beyond that, CSR models are most effective on dense encoder models that use high-dimensional representations (e.g. 1024-4096 dimensions).

The SparseEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in various formats such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL.

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

Some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

Industry observers note that you can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

It's crucial to ensure that your dataset format matches your chosen loss function. This involves checking two things:.

For example, if your loss function accepts (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, then your first, second, and third dataset columns correspond with anchor, positive, and negative, respectively. This means that your first and second column must contain texts that should embed closely, and that your first and third column must contain texts that should embed far apart. That is why depending on your loss function, your dataset column order matters.

Recent findings suggest that consider a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"], where the "label" column contains floating point similarity scores. This dataset can be used with SparseCoSENTLoss, SparseAnglELoss, and SparseCosineSimilarityLoss because:.

In a recent development, if the columns in your dataset are not ordered correctly, use Dataset.select_columns to reorder them. Additionally, remove any extraneous columns (e.g., sample_id, metadata, source, type) using Dataset.remove_columns, as they will be treated as inputs otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that loss functions measure how well a model performs on a given batch of data and guide the optimization process. The choice of loss function depends on your available data and target task. Refer to the Loss Overview for a comprehensive list of options.

Recent findings suggest that to train a SparseEncoder, you either need a SpladeLoss or CSRLoss, depending on the architecture. These are wrapper losses that add sparsity regularization on top of a main loss function, which must be provided as a parameter. The only loss that can be used independently is SparseMSELoss, as it performs embedding-level distillation, ensuring sparsity by directly copying the teacher's sparse embedding.

Most loss functions can be initialized with just the SparseEncoder that you're training, alongside some optional parameters, e.g.:.

The SparseEncoderTrainingArguments class allows you to specify parameters that influence training performance and tracking/debugging. While optional, experimenting with these arguments can help improve training efficiency and provide insights into the training process.

Recent findings suggest that in the Sentence Transformers documentation, I've outlined some of the most useful training arguments. I would recommend reading it in Training Overview > Training Arguments.

Sources indicate that you can provide the SparseEncoderTrainer with an eval_dataset to get the evaluation loss during training, but it may be useful to get more concrete metrics during training, too. For this, you can use evaluators to assess the model's performance with useful metrics before, during, or after training. You can use both an eval_dataset and an evaluator, one or the other, or neither. They evaluate based on the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Here are the implemented Evaluators that come with Sentence Transformers for Sparse Encoder models:.

Additionally, SequentialEvaluator should be used to combine multiple evaluators into one Evaluator that can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainer.

Sources indicate that sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that when evaluating frequently during training with a small eval_steps, consider using a tiny eval_dataset to minimize evaluation overhead. If you're concerned about the evaluation set size, a 90-1-9 train-eval-test split can provide a balance, reserving a reasonably sized test set for final evaluations. After training, you can assess your model's performance using trainer.evaluate(test_dataset) for test loss or initialize a testing evaluator with test_evaluator(model) for detailed test metrics.

If you evaluate after training, but before saving the model, your automatically generated model card will still include the test results.

When using Distributed Training, the evaluator only runs on the first device, unlike the training and evaluation datasets, which are shared across all devices.

The SparseEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. The model scores 0.5241 NDCG@10 on NanoMSMARCO, 0.3299 NDCG@10 on NanoNFCorpus and 0.5357 NDCG@10 NanoNQ, which is a good result for an inference-free distilbert-based model trained on just 100k pairs from the Natural Questions dataset.

The model uses an average of 184 active dimensions in the sparse embeddings for the documents, compared to 7.7 active dimensions for the queries (i.e. the average number of tokens in the query). This corresponds to a sparsity of 99.39% and 99.97%, respectively.

Sources indicate that all of this information is stored in the automatically generated model card, including the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential users would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

It has been revealed that top-performing models are often trained using multiple datasets simultaneously. The SparseEncoderTrainer simplifies this process by allowing you to train with multiple datasets without converting them to the same format. You can even apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps for multi-dataset training:.

Let's evaluate our newly trained inference-free SPLADE model using the NanoMSMARCO dataset, and see how it compares to dense retrieval approaches. We'll also explore hybrid retrieval methods that combine sparse and dense vectors, as well as reranking to further improve search quality.

After running a slightly modified version of our hybrid_search.py script, we get the following results for the NanoMSMARCO dataset, using these models:.

Sources indicate that the Sparse and Dense rankings can be combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which is a simple way to combine the results of multiple rankings. If a Reranker is applied, it will rerank the results of the prior retrieval step.

Sources indicate that the results indicate that for this dataset, combining Dense and Sparse rankings is very performant, resulting in 12.3% and 18.7% increases over the Dense and Sparse baselines, respectively. In short, combining Sparse and Dense retrieval methods is a very effective way to improve search performance.

Furthermore, applying a reranker on any of the rankings improved the performance to approximately 66.3 NDCG@10, showing that either Sparse, Dense, or Hybrid (Dense + Sparse) found the relevant documents in their top 100, which the reranker then ranked to the top 10. So, replacing a Dense -> Reranker pipeline with a Sparse -> Reranker pipeline might improve both latency and costs:.

  • These are the parts that were harder than they looked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan doesn't have one hotel tax (宿泊税). It has a growing patchwork of prefectural and municipal ones, and in 2026–27 several of them change. Kyoto's top band went to ¥10,000 per person per night on 1 March 2026. Hokkaido added a prefectural tax on 1 April 2026 that stacks on top of city taxes like Sapporo's. Okinawa starts a 2% tax on 1 February 2027. Tokyo moves from flat amounts to 3% on 1 April 2027.

Travellers usually pay it at the hotel, on top of whatever they prepaid on a booking site (some booking sites collect it in advance). So I built a free, client-side calculator for a whole itinerary: Japan Hotel Tax Calculator 2026–27. You add stays (city, check-in date, nights, room price, guests, lodging type) and it gives the tax per night and the trip total. It's one plain JS file with no dependencies, and your stays are saved only in your browser's localStorage.

These are the parts that were harder than they looked.

Sources indicate that the rate follows the night stayed, not the booking date. Tokyo's Q&A and Kyoto's FAQ both say so explicitly. So each city is a list of rules with a from date, and each night of a stay looks up its own rule:.

Sources indicate that bands are [upperExclusive, yen] pairs. percent covers Tokyo's fresh rule (3% of the per-person price rounded down to ¥100, nothing under ¥13,000), Okinawa's (2% of the price rounded down to ¥1,000, max ¥2,000) and Kutchan's (3% rounded down to ¥100, Hokkaido tax included). Those three "round the price down first" rules are easy to miss. In Tokyo from April 2027, ¥13,550 becomes ¥13,500 × 3% = ¥405.

According to recent reports, example: a 4-night Tokyo stay from 29 March 2027, ¥30,000 for a room for two (¥15,000 each), is ¥400, ¥400, ¥400, then ¥900 on the night of 1 April. The calculator warns when a stay spans a change.

Dates are plain calendar strings ('2027-04-01'). All the arithmetic is done with Date.UTC, so the result doesn't depend on the visitor's time zone. The test suite runs under TZ=Asia/Tokyo, America/Los_Angeles, Pacific/Kiritimati and UTC to make sure.

In a recent development, the bands are defined on the per-person price excluding the 10% consumption tax. People usually know the price for the whole room, often tax-inclusive. The obvious conversion is price / 1.1 / guests, and it's wrong exactly where it matters:.

According to recent reports, ¥6,600 including tax is exactly ¥6,000, which is Kyoto's ¥400 band edge. So I keep the price as a fraction and compare with integer multiplication:.

The tests pin the edges from both sides. ¥22,000 incl. tax is exactly ¥20,000 and must hit Kyoto's ¥1,000 band, while ¥21,999 stays at ¥400. A ¥26,000 Tokyo room for two in June 2027 is ¥13,000 each and is taxed. ¥25,999 isn't.

Industry observers note that read the official wording for each edge carefully too. Niseko's lowest band is "5,001円未満" (up to ¥5,000), not "under ¥5,000", so its first edge in the data is 5001.

According to recent reports, the tool page and a companion blog post both show a full rates table. I didn't want to type the rates twice, because a table that disagrees with the calculator is worse than no table. The static site builder (Python) runs Node to load the calculator module and renders the table from its exported data:.

Generate a Maze With a Guaranteed Solution in Python (API Tutorial)

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A maze generator is easy to write badly.
  • In a recent development, so the maze generator I built for my books doesn't just carve — it proves.
  • According to recent reports, the API lives on RapidAPI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A maze generator is easy to write badly. Carve some passages, knock down some walls, ship it — and sooner or later it hands you a maze where the goal is walled off completely. In a game that's an unwinnable level. In a printed activity book, that's a kid discovering the answer key doesn't work, and a refund instead of a review.

In a recent development, so the maze generator I built for my books doesn't just carve — it proves. It walks the finished maze from start to goal before anything ships, and the proof travels with the puzzle. This is that generator, exposed as an API called ActivityForge. In this tutorial we'll call it from Python: send a size and a seed, get back a maze, its wall data, and the verified solution path.

According to recent reports, the API lives on RapidAPI. The free tier gives you 100 calls a day, and every plan — free included — reaches every endpoint and every format. The paid intends only change how many calls you get, starting at $19/month. Nothing in this tutorial needs a paid plan.

The whole request is one POST. Two headers carry your key and the host; the JSON body carries the maze settings.

A few things worth knowing about the parameters:.

The response describes the maze as data, not a picture. Coordinates are [x, y] — x is the column, y is the row — with start at the top-left cell [0, 0] and goal at the bottom-right. The walls field is a list of rows; each cell carries four booleans, top, right, bottom, and left, saying which of its walls stand. That's everything a renderer needs:.

That's a real response, not a mockup — seed 42 will hand you this exact maze every time.

Here's the part that makes the maze safe to ship. Alongside the walls, the response carries a solution object: path (the route as [x, y] cells, start to goal), directions (the same route as words — right, down, left, up), and steps (the move count).

The generator builds a perfect maze — a spanning tree over the grid, so exactly one route joins any two cells — then breadth-first walks that route before returning anything. The solution is the route it walked, so it can't disagree with the walls. Feed the path back into the renderer as marked cells and the proof draws itself:.

In a recent development, trace the stars yourself: every step moves through a gap, never through a wall, from the S in the top-left to the G in the bottom-right. Generating levels? That directions list doubles as a walkthrough your game can replay. Printing? It's the answer key.

It has been revealed that because we asked for format: "all", the same response also carries svg (a print-ready page) and pdf_base64 (a vector PDF, base64-encoded). Saving the PDF is three lines:.

That's the page you hand to a kid — titled, with "Find your way from START to GOAL!" on it, no drawing required.

Look back at the request: "seed": 42. Run it tomorrow, next month, on a different machine — same maze, wall for wall, same 38-step solution. Leave the seed out and every call returns a fresh random maze. For print: generate a catalog once, record the seeds, re-render identical puzzles forever. For a game: a daily maze that's identical for every player, from one integer.

The maze is one of four generators, all with the same request shape and the same seed behavior:.

Every generator proves its own output the same way — word placements re-checked against the finished grid, dot sequences checked complete and ordered — because a broken puzzle in a printed book is a refund, not a bug report.

In a recent development, the free tier is 100 calls a day, which is plenty to build something real. The word-search script from the previous tutorial, plus a JavaScript version, is in the examples repo, and the API itself is on RapidAPI.

If you generate a maze pack or a level set with it, I'd like to see what you made.

Part of the ActivityForge series — the previous tutorial builds a printable word search with its answer key, and the launch post covers how these generators came out of my activity-book pipeline.

Announcing NeurIPS 2025 E2LM Competition: Early Training Evaluation of Language Models

📅 04 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.
  • Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!
  • Sources indicate that the development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.

Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!

Sources indicate that the development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated. This phase is commonly referred to as the early stages of training. During this period, researchers primarily monitor two key metrics: the training loss curve and evaluation scores. However, existing evaluation benchmarks often fail to provide meaningful or discriminative signals during these initial stages where LLMs are trained on a few tokens ~200B tokens, making it challenging to derive conclusive insights from ongoing experiments.

In this competition, we want to build together new benchmarks to effectively capture relevant signals in early training stages of LLMs, specifically for scientific knowledge domain.

The competition will be hosted on a dedicated Hugging Face organization - to register to the competition please follow this registration link 👉 https://e2lmc.github.io/registration. Participants will have to submit their solutions, which will be based on lm-evaluation-harness library through a HuggingFace Space. An active leaderboard will be maintained during the competition to track promising submissions. The size of the models make them easily runnable for everyone, on free-tier Google Colab GPUs. We also provide a comprehensive starting kit including several notebooks to get started with the competition.

Each submission will be evaluated using three different scores: signal quality score (ScoreSQ), ranking consistency score (ScoreRC) amd compliance with scientific knowledge score (ScoreCS). These criteria will be combined into a global score used for the final ranking. Additionally, two validation procedures will be systematically applied to all submissions: (i) verification of alignment with established scientific knowledge domains, and (ii) detection of potential information leakage, specifically the presence of the answer within the question prompt.The overall score is computed as a weighted sum:.

In a recent development, where, αSQ, αRC and αCS are weighting coefficients that reflect the relative importance of each criterion. We set the weights as α1 = 0.5, α2 = 0.1 and α3 = 0.4, thereby placing greater emphasis on signal quality and compliance to scientific knowledge, which we consider the most important metrics in evaluating submissions.

Recent findings suggest that participants will be able to compute the signal quality subscore locally using the provided model checkpoints of three Small Language Models 0.5B, 1B and 3B (ranging from 0 to 200 BT) along with the accompanying scoring algorithm (provided in a notebook in the starting kit). In contrast, the other two subscores cannot be computed independently, as the corresponding checkpoints—from 200 GT to 1 T tokens, as well as the 0.5 billion parameter model trained exclusively on web data—will remain hidden throughout the competition. Nonetheless, the global score will be automatically computed upon submission through the Hugging Face competition space, allowing participants to track their overall performance. This setup is intended to prevent overly customized solutions specifically tailored to the released checkpoints.

Further details about each evaluation metric, along with full scoring results on state-of-the-art benchmarks, are available in the competition proposal.

For inquiries and support, reach out to the task coordinators at e2lmc@tii.ae. You can also join our discord channel here to directly interact with us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced aims for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” notes misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

It has been revealed that the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto indicates, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

According to recent reports, for soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

According to recent reports, and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

Sources indicate that according to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

It has been revealed that “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch indicates. She aims to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

According to recent reports, still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

In a recent development, the “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

Industry observers note that as of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto claims, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto notes, “that would be a huge victory.”.

#173558. How to Self-Host Plex and Jellyfin: A Developer's Field Guide to Your Own Streaming Stack

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1245 w)

How to Self-Host Plex and Jellyfin: A Developer's Field Guide to Your Own Streaming Stack

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the first time I cancelled Netflix and tried to watch my own ripped movies on a hotel TV, nothing played.
  • Industry observers note that plex and Jellyfin both solve the same problem-your media library, served to your devices, with metadata, posters, and a Netflix-like UI.
  • It has been revealed that both projects are mature, both play every common format, both support hardware transcoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the first time I cancelled Netflix and tried to watch my own ripped movies on a hotel TV, nothing played. The file was H.265 10-bit in MKV. The TV didn't support it. The browser transcoder choked. My "save $20 a month" project turned into a weekend of reading about hardware transcoding, and that's the moment you realize media streaming is genuinely hard. This article is the guide I wish I'd had then.

Industry observers note that plex and Jellyfin both solve the same problem-your media library, served to your devices, with metadata, posters, and a Netflix-like UI. Plex is the polished commercial product with a paywall on the good features. Jellyfin is the AGPL-licensed fork of Emby that doesn't phone home and doesn't ask for a credit card. Most developers I know end up running both for a few weeks and picking a side. I'll show you how to run either (or both) on real hardware, with real transcoding, behind a real reverse proxy, reachable from anywhere.

It has been revealed that both projects are mature, both play every common format, both support hardware transcoding. The differences are about philosophy and friction.

I run Jellyfin in production. I run Plex on a second box for family members whose Smart TVs don't have a Jellyfin app. If your household is mostly Apple TV, Plex is still the safer bet. If everyone's on Roku/Fire Stick/web, Jellyfin is fine and you'll save the Plex Pass fee.

A typical self-hosted media stack looks like this:.

┌──────────────────────────┐ │ Internet / Tailscale │ └────────────┬─────────────┘ │ HTTPS ▼ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ Caddy reverse proxy │ │ (auto TLS via ACME) │ └────────────┬─────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────────┼───────────────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ Jellyfin │ │ Plex │ │ *arr stack │ │ (Docker) │ │ (Docker) │ │ (Radarr / │ │ │ │ │ │ Sonarr / │ │ /dev/dri │ │ /dev/dri │ │ Prowlarr) │ │ render │ │ render │ │ │ └─────┬──────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ /mnt/media ← mergerfs( /mnt/disk{1..N} ) │ │ │ │ SnapRAID parity: /mnt/parity (1 disk) │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘.

The key design decisions are: services in Docker, all media mounted read-only inside containers, hardware acceleration passed through /dev/dri, and one reverse proxy handling TLS for everything.

Industry observers note that keep the host layout boring and predictable. Every service gets a config dir under /opt, every persistent dataset under /mnt.

plaintext /opt/jellyfin/ # config, metadata cache, transcode dir /opt/plex/ /opt/caddy/Caddyfile /mnt/disk1/ # individual data disks, mounted at boot /mnt/disk2/ /mnt/parity/ # SnapRAID parity /mnt/media # mergerfs view of disk1..N ├── movies/ ├── tv/ ├── music/ └── photos/.

Recent findings suggest that /mnt/media is the only path the containers see. If you ever migrate disks or rebuild the pool, the container mounts don't change.

A single significant disk is the easy path until it dies. RAID 5 rebuilds are stressful on modern high-capacity drives and the array is slow while it runs. The homelab consensus is mergerfs (file-level concatenation, no striping) plus SnapRAID (snapshot parity, run nightly).

shell sudo apt install mergerfs snapraid.

conf /dev/disk/by-id/ata-WDC_WD40EFRX-1 /mnt/disk1 ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2 /dev/disk/by-id/ata-WDC_WD40EFRX-2 /mnt/disk2 ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2 /dev/disk/by-id/ata-WDC_WD40EFRX-3 /mnt/parity ext4 defaults,noatime 0 2.

/mnt/disk1:/mnt/disk2 /mnt/media fuse.mergerfs \ defaults,allow_other,category.create=mfs,moveonenospc=true,dropcacheonrename=true 0 0.

conf parity /mnt/parity/snapraid.parity content /mnt/disk1/snapraid.content content /mnt/disk2/snapraid.content content /opt/snapraid/snapraid.content data d1 /mnt/disk1/ data d2 /mnt/disk2/ exclude *.unrecoverable exclude /tmp/ exclude /lost+found/ exclude *.!sync exclude *.bak.

set -euo pipefail LOG=/var/log/snapraid.log { echo "=== $(date) ===" snapraid sync snapraid scrub -p 8 -o 1 } >> "$LOG" 2>&1.

Recent findings suggest that crucially: mergerfs is not RAID. If a disk dies before SnapRAID has run, the files written since the last sync are gone. SnapRAID is snapshot parity, not real-time. This is the trade-off. For movies you can re-rip, that's fine. For irreplaceable photos, back them up off-site too.

Direct play is when the client can decode the file as-is. Transcoding is when the server has to convert it on the fly. 4K HEVC to 1080p H.264 in software will pin 8 cores and deliver 4 FPS. The fix is hardware: pass /dev/dri into the container and let the iGPU do it.

Recent findings suggest that vainfo should list VAProfileHEVCMain10 and VAProfileVP9Profile0. If you don't have it, install intel-media-va-driver-non-free on Debian/Ubuntu.

Add your media user to the render group so the container can access the device:.

shell sudo usermod -aG render jellyfin sudo usermod -aG render plex.

It has been revealed that the classical symptom of "transcoding doesn't work" is the server going to 100% CPU and the video pausing every few seconds. That's software transcoding. The container is missing /dev/dri or the render group permission.

In a recent development, here's a production-ready compose file. Note the /dev/dri device, the render group ID mapped via group_add, and the explicit no-new-privileges security option.

services: jellyfin: image: jellyfin/jellyfin:10.9.11 container_name: jellyfin restart: unless-stopped user: "1000:1000" group_add:.

Inside Jellyfin, enable VAAPI under Dashboard → Playback → Transcoding. Pick /dev/dri/renderD128 as the device. Test with a 4K HEVC file forced to 1080p max and a 20 Mbps bitrate cap-CPU should stay under 10%.

Plex is similar but the image expects a claim token from plex.tv on first boot.

services: plex: image: plexinc/pms-docker:latest container_name: plex restart: unless-stopped hostname: plex devices:.

In a recent development, plex Pass is required for hardware transcoding. Without it, you'll see "Transcoding (cpu)" in the dashboard and CPU will spike. Don't waste a weekend debugging the /dev/dri perms if you haven't bought Plex Pass yet-it's gated behind the feature flag.

It has been revealed that plex uses network_mode: host because it broadcasts on multiple ports (32400 main, 32469 DLNA, 1900/5353 UDP for discovery). You can run bridge mode with explicit port mappings, but DLNA auto-discovery will break for clients that rely on it.

You want HTTPS for remote access and you want a single port forwarded. Caddy is the lowest-friction option because ACME is built in.

jellyfin.example.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8096 { flush_interval -1 } encode zstd gzip.

# Jellyfin's recommended headers header { Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload" X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Referrer-Policy no-referrer # don't apply Caddy's default CSP, Jellyfin sets its own ?Content-Security-Policy "" }.

@websockets { header Connection Upgrade header Upgrade websocket } reverse_proxy @websockets 127.0.0.1:8096 }.

plex.example.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:32400 encode zstd gzip }.

The flush_interval -1 is critical for Jellyfin-it disables buffering so streaming chunks reach the client immediately. Without it, you'll see 30-second startup stalls on every video.

services: caddy: image: caddy:2.8-alpine container_name: caddy restart: unless-stopped ports:.

If you'd rather not open ports on your router, skip this whole section and use Tailscale.

Cloudflare Tunnel's free ToS technically excludes "large file streaming." People do it anyway and most accounts never get flagged, but if you care about the letter of the agreement, don't. Use Tailscale for family-if they can install a phone app, they can use Tailscale. Use port forwarding + Caddy for yourself.

shell curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh sudo tailscale up --advertise-tags=tag:media.

Both Plex and Jellyfin have hard opinions about file layout. Get this wrong and metadata matching turns into a part-time job.

plaintext /mnt/media/movies/ The Matrix (1999)/ The Matrix (1999) [1080p] [Bluray].mkv The Matrix Reloaded (2003)/ The Matrix Reloaded (2003) [1080p] [Bluray].mkv.

/mnt/media/tv/ Breaking Bad (2008)/ Season 01/ Breaking Bad - S01E01 - Pilot.mkv Breaking Bad - S01E02 - Cat's in the Bag.mkv.

/mnt/media/music/ Artist/ Album (Year)/ 01 - Track.flac.

The patterns the metadata agents look for:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, sound familiar?
  • Industry observers note that in this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've got everything ready - data, model, a beefy GPU setup. You hit "run" and... wait. And wait some more. Your GPUs are barely breaking a sweat while your wallet's getting lighter by the hour.

In a recent development, sound familiar? We've been there. After some detective work on our nanoVLM project, we discovered the real culprit wasn't our model or hardware, it was our data pipeline being incredibly wasteful.

Industry observers note that in this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages. In each stage we add or remove from the previous step and comment on what went right and what did not.

According to recent reports, to make it easier to follow the data preparation tasks, we created a separate repo laser-focused on the data pipeline only. We hope this will be much easier to understand that reading the code once integrated with the nanoVLM repository. In addition, this could be useful to bootstrap other data pipelines!

Repository: https://github.com/ariG23498/mmdp.

Industry observers note that to follow along, all you need to do is clone the repository. It contains the final data preparation tasks, but it's designed to showcase each step of the way.

Before optimizing anything, we need to understand what we are working with. Our multimodal dataset has images, text prompts, and responses.

Getting familiar with your training data is crucial for success. The previous script demonstrates a random sample each time you run it; you may want to copy the snippet to a notebook and run it multiple times to get a feeling about the data.

Our first training attempt used the obvious (and very frequent) approach:.

It has been revealed that the results were painful. Look at this visualization:.

Sources indicate that see all that gray? That's padding. That's the GPU processing absolutely nothing while you pay for compute time. We were wasting roughly 60% of our batch on empty tokens.

Our next move was simple. Set a global maximum length and stick to it. If a sample was too long, we'd just drop it.

As you might have noticed that the batch now has one sample less. This is due to the filtering process. This helped, but we were still padding everything to the same fixed length regardless of actual content. Better than before, but still wasteful.

It has been revealed that now we’re ready to rethink batching entirely. Padding is the enemy, and we need a strategy to minimize it while maximizing how much data we can fit into each batch. Enter the knapsack problem, a classic from computer science that’s perfect for this.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you’re packing a backpack for a hike. It can only hold so much weight, and you want to cram in as many useful items as possible. In our case:.

Sources indicate that to test this idea, we start with a toy dataset: just a list of numbers from 1 to 25, each representing a sequence length. This lets us experiment without the complexity of images and text.

Sources indicate that most PyTorch datasets are map-style (you access them with dataset[i]). But for dynamic batching, we need something more flexible. So, we built an iterable-style dataset by subclassing torch.utils.data.IterableDataset. This lets us generate batches on the fly and handle tricks like sharding data across multiple workers:.

In a recent development, packing sequences can be slow, especially if we’re sorting or shuffling. To keep things moving, we use a producer-consumer pattern using Python queues:.

It has been revealed that the producer thread packs batches and puts them in a queue, while the main thread pulls them out as needed. This overlap keeps the pipeline flowing smoothly.

First, we try a simple greedy packing strategy:.

This walks through the data sequentially, adding items to a pack until it’s full, then starting a fresh one. It’s fast but not perfect. Here’s what the batches look like:.

Notice how later batches get sparse? We’re leaving gaps.

Let’s try a smarter approach: bin-packing (specifically, First Fit Decreasing):.

In a recent development, this sorts sequences by length (longest first) and tries to fit each one into the first pack that has room. If none fits, it starts a new pack. The result?

These batches are much tighter, with less wasted space. It’s like playing Tetris with your data, fitting pieces together snugly.

Now for the real deal, applying knapsack packing to our multimodal dataset.

We’re back to images, prompts, and responses, and we need to pack them efficiently while respecting both token limits and image budgets. Image budgeting is done so that images per sample are balanced. We would like to avoid the case where one GPU needs to process way more images than another.

In a recent development, our fresh ConstantLengthDataset class handles the heavy lifting. Here’s how it works, compared to Stage 4:.

The ConstantLengthDataset does it all:.

Look at that! The gray (padding) is minimal, and the batches are dense with useful data. It’s like packing a suitcase so well you can still zip it up without sitting on it.

The image might seem unintuive at the first glance, but let us look at the image side by side with constrained padding.

According to recent reports, here you will notice that the samples in knapsack are more evenly distributed. We also do not run into the concern of having less samples in the batch due to filtering.

What started as a simple "why is training so slow?" investigation led to a complete rethink of how we handle multimodal data.

The balanced knapsack strategy for data pipeline comes from the Eagle 2: Building Post-Training Data Strategies from Scratch for Frontier Vision-Language Models paper from NVIDIA.

Happy training (and may your GPUs stay busy)!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • SQL statements start with exec sql and end with a semicolon, and can span lines.
  • Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Embedded SQL in RPG is the default way to access Db2 for i in newly introduced code. It is also where I most often see sloppy code: no status checks, SELECT *, and cursors left open. This article gives a pattern you can paste into a real program.

SQL statements start with exec sql and end with a semicolon, and can span lines. The source member type is SQLRPGLE.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

Fixed format has no exec sql ...; one-liner: the statement sits between C/EXEC SQL and C/END-EXEC on C+ lines (/ in column 7, EXEC SQL in columns 8-16). SET OPTION goes there like any other statement.

SET OPTION is not executable; the precompiler reads it. IBM requires it to precede every other SQL statement in the source, and you can code only one, so put all options in that one statement. It lets the source carry its own compile options.

Prefix RPG variables with a colon inside SQL.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

In a recent development, A host structure maps columns by position, not name, so the select list order must match the structure. Always list columns explicitly.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

If no row matches you get SQLSTATE 02000 (SQLCODE 100). If more than one matches, you get an error (SQLSTATE 21000, SQLCODE -811) unless you add fetch first row only. Decide which you mean. A null in a column needs a null-indicator variable (:cust.balance :balInd) or you get SQLCODE -305.

According to recent reports, the precompiler gives you sqlstate and sqlcode automatically. Check after every statement. SQLSTATE is the portable value; SQLCODE is Db2-specific but handy.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

DSPLY needs a variable in fixed format, hence MSG. DSPLY also cuts the message at 52 characters, so keep it short. If CHECKSQL is called earlier in the same source, add a D CHECKSQL PR N prototype first.

Sources indicate that warnings start with 01, not found is 02, and 00 is success. Anything else (class 22, 23, 42 and so on) is an error you must handle. For details use GET DIAGNOSTICS CONDITION 1 :msg = MESSAGE_TEXT (the CONDITION 1 is required for condition items like MESSAGE_TEXT, RETURNED_SQLSTATE and DB2_MESSAGE_ID). Capture sqlstate into a variable before you run it, or any other statement, because every later SQL statement can overwrite what you were about to test.

Use a cursor when you expect many rows: declare, open, fetch in a loop, close.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

Sources indicate that DECLARE is not executable, but it must appear in the source before the OPEN that uses it, and the host variables it references must be declared before it. closqlcsr(*endmod) closes cursors when the module ends. The ILE default is *ENDACTGRP, so a cursor you forget to close stays open until the activation group ends, and the next call's OPEN fails with SQLSTATE 24502 (already open). Close cursors yourself anyway.

Fetching a block of rows in one call reduces overhead. Use an array data structure.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

SQLERRD(3) (short name SQLER3) holds the number of rows fetched. The last block is usually short: Db2 then returns SQLSTATE 02000 (SQLCODE 100) and the rows it did find, so process SQLERRD(3) rows first and stop afterwards. Reading it straight after the FETCH needs no extra statement; GET DIAGNOSTICS :fetched = ROW_COUNT gives the same count but is one more statement to get wrong.

When the statement text is built at run time, use PREPARE and EXECUTE. Use parameter markers (?), never concatenated user input, to avoid SQL injection.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

The statement literal is split with + because a single literal would run past column 80.

Recent findings suggest that for a one-off statement without parameters, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE :stmt is enough. A dynamic SELECT is prepared, then used with DECLARE CURSOR FOR s1 and OPEN c USING :value.

With COMMIT(*NONE) every statement is permanent immediately. With COMMIT(*CHG) (or *CS, *ALL) changes are held until you matter COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

Tables must be journaled to be used under commitment control; otherwise the statement fails at runtime (SQLCODE -7008, SQLSTATE 55019). The CRTSQLRPGI default is COMMIT(*CHG), so a program you compile without thinking about it hits this on any unjournaled file. On PUB400 a latest SQL schema is journaled automatically, but tables created with CRTPF (see DDS to SQL DDL migration) in a plain library are not.

Industry observers note that the precompiler produces a temporary source and then calls the RPG compiler. COMMIT(*NONE) is right for batch utilities (wrap the call in CL and use SBMJOB) and read-only programs; choose *CHG for transactional programs. The SET OPTION line in the source carries the same options with the member.

Defaults worth knowing before you rely on them:.

According to recent reports, the samples use mylib.customer. With OPTION(*SQL) an unqualified name goes to the default schema instead of the library list.

Same program in fixed format (what you will meet in most shops):.

Fixed format wants all D specs before the first C spec, so the declarations move up. SET OPTION is still the first SQL statement in the source, which is what the precompiler needs.
